title: Introduction
html:
Introduction

This guide walks through every book of the Bible, Genesis to Revelation, so you can see how each one fits the whole. It is modeled on the BibleProject book overview videos and posters (bibleproject.com/explore/book-overviews; posters and transcripts at bibleproject.com/downloads). Those videos are a great help for following a book's literary flow. This edition pairs the two: each book entry now ends with a BibleProject section showing BibleProject's own poster for that book (reproduced whole and unaltered, with credit) along with a short summary, in our words, of what the video covers, a link to watch it, and a Reformed response where one is needed. Everything outside the BibleProject sections is original to this guide.

Each book entry has:

  • A key verse (ESV) and a short note on the setting: author, audience, and historical situation.
  • Where it fits: the book's place on the timeline, linked to the timelines section.
  • The flow of the book: its major movements, similar to the panels on a BibleProject poster.
  • Main themes and main characters.
  • Key passages to read first.
  • How it points to Christ, because Jesus said the Scriptures "bear witness about me" (John 5:39).
  • A short Reformed note drawing on John Calvin, R.C. Sproul, J.I. Packer, Wayne Grudem, John Frame, D.A. Carson, and Doug Wilson. A view is credited to a named theologian only where it is well documented. Otherwise it is described as the view of "the Reformed tradition."
  • Going deeper: a fuller paragraph of Reformed reflection on the book.
  • Recommended free Reformed commentaries: two to four free, legal commentaries or sermon series for the book, each with a one-line note, plus links to the Monergism and Ligonier hubs for that book.
  • Occasionally, a Reading BibleProject well note. These point out, fairly and briefly, where BibleProject's framing differs from or needs filling out by Reformed theology.
  • The BibleProject section: the poster, a summary of the video, the video link, and sometimes A Reformed response to the video.

Perspective. This guide reads Scripture as the inerrant Word of God and works within Reformed, covenantal theology: God's sovereignty in creation, providence, and salvation; the unity of the Bible's story under the covenant of grace; penal substitutionary atonement; justification by faith alone; and hope for the gospel's advance in history. It is written from a covenantal Baptist position that leans a little Presbyterian. Where Reformed Baptists and Presbyterians differ, mainly on baptism and the children of believers, both views are given charitably. On the end times, the guide is friendly to Doug Wilson's postmillennialism, and other Reformed views are noted where they come up.

How to use it. Read one book entry before you start a book of the Bible, watch the linked BibleProject video with the poster in front of you, and come back to the "How it points to Christ" section when you finish. The book order follows the English Bible, grouped into seven parts.

title: The Big Story: Creation to New Creation
html:
The Big Story: Creation to New Creation

The Bible is one story told across 66 books, about 40 human authors, and roughly 1,500 years, with one divine Author. Its plot has four great movements:

1. Creation

God, who is sovereign and self-sufficient, creates a good world out of nothing and makes humanity in his image to rule it as his representatives, enjoying fellowship with him (Gen 1–2).

2. Fall

Adam, our covenant head, rebels. Sin and death enter the world, the image is defaced, creation is cursed, and all humanity is guilty and corrupt in him (Gen 3; Rom 5:12).

3. Redemption

God promises a Seed who will crush the serpent (Gen 3:15). He works out that promise through a series of covenants: Noah, Abraham, Israel, David, and finally the New Covenant in Jesus Christ, who lives the obedient life we failed to live, dies as our substitute under God's wrath, rises, and reigns.

4. Consummation

The risen Christ pours out his Spirit, builds his church among all nations, and will return to raise the dead, judge the world, and bring a new heaven and new earth where God dwells with his people forever (Rev 21–22).

BibleProject often tells this story as the story of heaven and earth coming together, with the garden as the first temple and the new creation as a garden-city temple. That framing is true and helpful. The Reformed tradition adds that the story turns on covenant and atonement. The main problem isn't only that heaven and earth are separated. Guilty sinners stand before a holy God, and only a substitute can reconcile them. The temple story and the cross story are the same story, because God dwells with his people only on the basis of the blood of the Lamb.

“The Lord, the Lord, a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abounding in steadfast love and faithfulness, ... but who will by no means clear the guilty.” Exodus 34:6–7 (ESV)

title: The Covenants
html:
The Covenants

Covenant theology holds that God relates to humanity through covenants, solemn binding relationships with promises, obligations, and signs. Reformed theologians usually speak of an eternal covenant of redemption among the Father, Son, and Spirit, a covenant of works with Adam, and a covenant of grace that God reveals progressively through the historical covenants below. Each one builds on the previous one, and all of them meet in Christ.

CovenantKey textsPromise and signFulfilled in Christ
Creation / Adam
(covenant of works)		Gen 1:26–28; 2:15–17; Hos 6:7Life through obedience, and death for disobedience. Dominion over creation.The last Adam obeys where Adam failed and wins life for his people (Rom 5:12–21).
Promise after the FallGen 3:15The woman's Seed will crush the serpent.Christ defeats Satan at the cross (Col 2:15; Heb 2:14).
NoahicGen 8:20–9:17God will preserve the created order until redemption is complete. Sign: the rainbow.A stable world as the stage for the gospel. Judgment by water anticipates the final judgment (2 Pet 3).
AbrahamicGen 12:1–3; 15; 17Land, offspring, and blessing to all nations. Sign: circumcision.Christ is the singular Offspring (Gal 3:16). Believers among all nations are Abraham's children (Gal 3:7–9, 29).
Mosaic (Sinai)Exod 19–24; DeuteronomyIsrael is a kingdom of priests, with law, tabernacle, and sacrifice. Sign: the Sabbath.Christ fulfills the law, is the true sacrifice and priest, and bears the law's curse (Matt 5:17; Gal 3:13).
Davidic2 Sam 7; Ps 89; Ps 110An eternal throne and kingdom for David's Son, who will build God's house.Jesus, Son of David, reigns now at the Father's right hand (Acts 2:30–36).
New CovenantJer 31:31–34; Ezek 36:25–27; Luke 22:20; Heb 8–10The law written on hearts, full forgiveness, the Spirit given, and all knowing the Lord. Signs: baptism and the Lord's Supper.Established in Christ's blood, once for all.
Baptist and Presbyterian Both traditions affirm one way of salvation, by grace through faith in Christ, across all of Scripture. Presbyterians (Westminster) see one covenant of grace under different administrations, so the children of believers receive the covenant sign as circumcision once was given. Doug Wilson argues this position in To a Thousand Generations. Covenantal (1689) Baptists see the covenant of grace promised in the Old Testament covenants and formally established in the New Covenant, whose members all "know the Lord" (Jer 31:34), so they baptize believers. This guide notes both views where they come up.
Hope for history Postmillennialists, Wilson most prominently, take the Abrahamic promise (all nations blessed), Psalm 110 (Christ reigns until his enemies are subdued), Daniel 2 (the stone becomes a mountain filling the earth), and the Great Commission (disciple the nations) to mean the gospel will substantially triumph in history before Christ returns. Amillennial and historic premillennial Reformed believers agree that Christ reigns now and will win, but they expect less visible victory before the end.

title: Reading BibleProject Well
html:
Reading BibleProject Well

BibleProject, founded by Tim Mackie and Jon Collins, has done a great service for Bible reading. Its videos show the literary design of books, trace themes across the canon, and keep the big story in view. This guide owes a lot to that approach. Since you're wary of parts of their theology, here are a few things to keep in mind, offered charitably:

  • Atonement. BibleProject's treatment of sacrifice stresses purification, ransom, "life for life," and Christ's victory over evil (Christus Victor). Those are all biblical. But they say comparatively little about penal substitution, that Christ bore the Father's just wrath against our sin in our place. The Reformed tradition (Calvin, Packer, Sproul, Grudem) holds that penal substitution is at the heart of the atonement and that the other aspects depend on it (Isa 53; Rom 3:25–26; 2 Cor 5:21; Gal 3:13; 1 John 4:10).
  • Justification. Their Paul material often follows recent "New Perspective" emphases on covenant membership and one multiethnic family. That is a real theme in Paul, but the Reformed reading keeps the forensic heart of the matter central: the ungodly are declared righteous by faith alone through Christ's imputed righteousness.
  • Temple-cosmos and spiritual beings. They draw heavily on scholars like John Walton (Genesis 1 as temple inauguration) and Michael Heiser (the "divine council"). These readings can shed light on texts, but they are scholarly proposals, not settled conclusions, and they sometimes push older Reformed readings aside.
  • Authorship and dating. Their videos sometimes follow mainstream scholarly conventions (on Isaiah, for example) more than traditional conservative positions.
  • Sovereignty and election. Their videos rarely get into God's sovereign, electing grace, which is central to Reformed reading of Romans 9, Ephesians 1, and John 6.

None of this means you should stop watching. Enjoy the art and the literary insight, and keep a Reformed confession (the 1689 London Baptist Confession or the Westminster Confession) and a good study Bible, such as the Reformation Study Bible, which Sproul edited, next to it.

title: BibleProject in This Guide
html:
BibleProject in This Guide

BibleProject (bibleproject.com) creates free animated videos, posters, transcripts, and study notes. This edition uses its material as follows, within what its Terms of Use allow:

  • Posters. BibleProject's book overview posters are reproduced whole and unaltered (scaled to fit the page, nothing cropped or changed), each with a notice right next to it naming BibleProject as author and owner and linking to bibleproject.com. BibleProject's terms allow this for free, non-commercial use only, so the guide is not for sale, and any printing should stay well under the terms' limit on copies (500).
  • Video summaries. The "What the video covers" lists are our own paraphrase of each video, written from BibleProject's published transcripts (Old Testament) and the videos' captions (New Testament). Only a few short phrases are quoted, always in quotation marks and attributed. They are not BibleProject's notes or scripts. For the real thing, watch the video at the link given.
  • Responses. "A Reformed response to the video" boxes are this guide's own commentary. BibleProject has not reviewed or endorsed this guide, its summaries, or its theology.
  • Shared videos. Where BibleProject covers several biblical books in one video (Kings, Chronicles, Ezra–Nehemiah, 1–3 John), the poster appears with the first book and the others point back to it. The Old and New Testament overview videos open the first Old and New Testament parts.

Posters © BibleProject. Used under the BibleProject Terms of Use for free, non-commercial display. BibleProject is the author and owner of this content. Visit bibleproject.com.

title: Free Reformed Commentaries
html:
Free Reformed Commentaries

Every book entry in this edition ends, just before the BibleProject section, with a box of recommended free Reformed commentaries. All of them are free and legal to read online, and every link was checked in November 2026. Each box usually draws on the sources below, in this order:

  • John Calvin, Commentaries, on CCEL. Calvin is the starting point wherever he wrote on a book. He wrote no commentary on Judges through Esther, Job (he preached sermons on it instead), Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, Song of Songs, 2–3 John, or Revelation. For those books, Matthew Henry (1662–1714), the warm Puritan-era expositor, takes his place. ccel.org/ccel/calvin/commentaries · ccel.org/ccel/henry/mhc
  • Douglas Wilson, "Surveying the Text": one sermon per book, delivered at Christ Church, Moscow, Idaho, and posted free on his blog. These are sermon-length overviews of a book's structure and themes, not verse-by-verse commentary. There is no post for 1–2 Timothy or Titus. dougwils.com/scripture-reference-index
  • A book-specific pick where a strong free one exists. Examples include Poythress (Frame's colleague) on Genesis 1–3, the Law of Moses, and Revelation; Calvin's Sermons on Deuteronomy; Sproul's verse-by-verse series on the Gospels, Acts, Romans, and Galatians; Spurgeon's Treasury of David; and the Puritan, Princeton, and Scottish divines (Owen on Hebrews, Manton on James and Jude, Hodge on 1–2 Corinthians and Ephesians, Bridges on Proverbs and Ecclesiastes, Leighton on 1 Peter, Caryl on Job, Durham on the Song, Bonar on Leviticus, Fairbairn on Ezekiel, Candlish on 1 John) plus Bullinger on Daniel.
  • TGC Bible Commentary, The Gospel Coalition's free online commentary in the Carson stream of Reformed evangelicalism. Each entry names its author, where TGC lists one. thegospelcoalition.org/commentary

A "More free material" line then links to the Monergism page for that book (sermons, manuscripts, MP3s, and older commentaries sorted by Scripture) and the Ligonier scripture page (Sproul's teaching and articles). Monergism's topical libraries are the best place to keep digging.

What is not free Several works these theologians are best known for cannot be read free and legally, so this guide does not link them. They include Grudem's Systematic Theology and his Tyndale commentary on 1 Peter, the ESV Study Bible and Reformation Study Bible notes (ESV Study Bible content sits behind a paid ESV.org subscription), Wilson's published commentaries and the Canon Press Surveying the Text book, Carson's Pillar and Expositor's commentaries on John and Matthew, and Frame's and Packer's printed books (Frame's free articles and some ebooks are on frame-poythress.org). They are worth buying, but they are not linked here.

title: Timelines: Master Timeline
html:
Timelines: The Story in Time

These timelines put the books of the Bible on one line of history, from Abraham to the death of the last apostle. They also show where each tribe and each key city stood in every era, and what the surrounding nations were doing at the same time. Seeing God's covenant story beside the rise and fall of Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome makes the Bible's own claim plain: "the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will" (Dan 4:17).

How the dates work This guide uses the conservative "early" chronology found in most Reformed and evangelical study Bibles (e.g. the ESV and Reformation Study Bibles). It takes 1 Kings 6:1 at face value: 480 years from the Exodus to Solomon's 4th year (c. 966 BC), which puts the Exodus c. 1446 BC. Exodus 12:40 (430 years in Egypt) then puts Jacob's descent into Egypt c. 1876 BC and Abraham's birth c. 2166 BC. Alternatives: many scholars, including some conservatives, prefer a "late" Exodus c. 1270–1260 BC under Ramesses II, reading the 480 years as twelve symbolic generations. Others take the 430 years to include the patriarchs' time in Canaan (following the Greek Septuagint at Exod 12:40 and Gal 3:17), which shortens the time in Egypt to about 215 years. Marking: "c." means approximate. † marks a date or identification that is seriously disputed. Kings' reign dates follow the widely used Thiele/ESV-style chronology and can vary by 1–2 years because of co-regencies and differences in calendar reckoning. Genesis 1–11 is left undated. Its genealogies may be selective (compare Matt 1:8 with 1 Chr 3:11–12), and Scripture gives no date for creation or the flood that all orthodox readers agree on.

text: Timelines: The Story in Time These timelines put the books of the Bible on one line of history, from Abraham to the death of the last apostle. They also show where each tribe and each key city stood in every era, and what the surrounding nations were doing at the same time. Seeing God's covenant story beside the rise and fall of Egypt, Assyria, Babylon, Persia, Greece, and Rome makes the Bible's own claim plain: "the Most High rules the kingdom of men and gives it to whom he will" (Dan 4:17). How the dates work This guide uses the conservative "early" chronology found in most Reformed and evangelical study Bibles (e.g. the ESV and Reformation Study Bibles). It takes 1 Kings 6:1 at face value: 480 years from the Exodus to Solomon's 4th year (c. 966 BC), which puts the Exodus c. 1446 BC . Exodus 12:40 (430 years in Egypt) then puts Jacob's descent into Egypt c. 1876 BC and Abraham's birth c. 2166 BC. Alternatives: many scholars, including some conservatives, prefer a "late" Exodus c. 1270–1260 BC under Ramesses II, reading the 480 years as twelve symbolic generations. Others take the 430 years to include the patriarchs' time in Canaan (following the Greek Septuagint at Exod 12:40 and Gal 3:17), which shortens the time in Egypt to about 215 years. The Maccabean revolt ends in the temple's rededication, remembered at Hanukkah (John 10:22) The Hasmonean dynasty rules an independent Judea until 63 BC. 63 Pompey enters the temple, even the Most Holy Place. Judea becomes subject to Rome The Roman Republic is in crisis. Julius Caesar is assassinated (44). 37–4 Herod the Great reigns and begins rebuilding the temple in 20/19 BC (compare John 2:20) Augustus is sole ruler (27 BC–AD 14). The Priene inscription (9 BC) hails his birthday as the "beginning of the good news ( euangelia )" for the world. The New Testament Era (c. 6 BC–AD 100) c. 6–4 BC Jesus born in Bethlehem, before Herod's death in 4 BC † Matthew, Mark, Luke, John Augustus' census (Luke 2:1). The dating of Quirinius' census is debated † . AD 28/29–30 (or 33) John the Baptist begins in Tiberius' 15th year (Luke 3:1). Jesus' public ministry. Crucifixion and resurrection in AD 30 or 33, both dates defended † Tiberius (r. AD 14–37). Pontius Pilate is prefect of Judea (AD 26–36), confirmed by the "Pilate Stone" found at Caesarea in 1961. c. 30–49 Pentecost. Stephen. Paul's conversion (c. 33–35). The gospel reaches Samaria, Cornelius, and Antioch. Paul's first missionary journey Acts. Letters: James (c. 45–49), Galatians (c. 48), 1–2 Thessalonians (c. 50–51), 1–2 Corinthians (c. 54–56), Romans (c. 57), Prison Epistles (c. 60–62), Pastorals (c. 62–67), Hebrews (60s), 1–2 Peter, Jude (60s) Caligula (r. 37–41) orders his statue set up in the temple, but the order is not carried out. Herod Agrippa I dies at Caesarea (AD 44; Acts 12). c. 49–57 Jerusalem Council (Acts 15). Second and third journeys. Paul spends 18 months at Corinth and about 3 years at Ephesus Claudius expels the Jews from Rome (c. 49; Acts 18:2). Suetonius says it was over a "Chrestus." An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio's proconsulship to c. 51–52 (Acts 18:12). c. 57–67 Paul is arrested in Jerusalem, held at Caesarea, and sent to Rome (c. 60–62). By tradition, Peter and Paul are martyred under Nero Nero (r. 54–68). After the fire of Rome (64), Tacitus says Christians were burned as living torches. 66–73 The Jewish War. Jerusalem and the temple destroyed (AD 70) , as Jesus foretold (Luke 21:20–24; Matt 24:1–2). Christians flee to Pella (Eusebius) John's Gospel and letters (c. 85–95); Revelation (c. 95, or c. 68 † ) Vespasian and Titus. The Arch of Titus in Rome shows the temple menorah carried in triumph. Masada falls (73/74). c. 81–100 John exiled on Patmos (Rev 1:9). By tradition, John dies at Ephesus c. AD 100, the last apostle Vesuvius buries Pompeii (79). Domitian (r. 81–96) liked to be addressed as "lord and god." Compare Rev 4:11: "Worthy are you, our Lord and God."

title: 2. The Tribes Through Time
html:
2. The Tribes Through Time

Jacob had twelve sons by four mothers. Joseph received a "double portion" through his two sons, Ephraim and Manasseh (Gen 48:5). Levi received no land and instead served as the priestly tribe. That leaves twelve land-holding tribes plus Levi. The census numbers below are the men of fighting age from Numbers 1 (at Sinai, c. 1445) and Numbers 26 (on the plains of Moab, c. 1406).

2a. From the patriarchs to the judges

TribePatriarchs: mother and Jacob's blessing (Gen 49)Egypt and wilderness (census Num 1 → 26)Conquest and allotmentJudges (c. 1380–1050)
ReubenLeah's firstborn. He loses the firstborn's preeminence for sleeping with Bilhah (35:22; 49:3–4)46,500 → 43,730. Dathan and Abiram rebel (Num 16)East of the Jordan, on the Moabite tableland north of the Arnon (Num 32; Josh 13:15–23)Stays "among the sheepfolds" instead of helping Deborah (Judg 5:15–16)
SimeonLeah. Simeon and Levi massacre Shechem (Gen 34), and Jacob says they will be "scattered in Israel" (49:5–7)59,300 → 22,200, the steepest fall. Zimri, the Simeonite at Baal-peor (Num 25:14). Simeon is left out of Moses' blessing (Deut 33)Towns inside Judah's territory in the Negev, including Beersheba (Josh 19:1–9). The scattering begins to come trueFights alongside Judah (Judg 1:3, 17)
LeviLeah. Joined Simeon in the Shechem violence and was also to be "scattered" (49:7)Moses and Aaron are Levites. Their zeal at the golden calf turns the curse into a calling (Exod 32:26–29). Numbered apart: 22,000 → 23,000 males from a month old (Num 3:39; 26:62)No territory: "the Lord is their inheritance." They receive 48 towns, including the 6 cities of refuge, scattered through every tribe (Num 35; Josh 21)Wandering Levites in Judges 17–19 show the nation coming apart
JudahLeah. Judah and Tamar (Gen 38). He offers himself in Benjamin's place (44:33). "The scepter shall not depart from Judah" (49:10)74,600 → 76,500, the largest. Judah marches first (Num 10:14). Nahshon and CalebThe southern hill country, the largest share (Josh 15). Hebron goes to CalebJudah "goes up first" (Judg 1:2; 20:18). Othniel, the first judge. Bethlehem: Ruth and Boaz
DanBilhah (Rachel's maid). "Dan shall judge… a serpent in the way" (49:16–17)62,700 → 64,400. Oholiab the craftsman (Exod 31:6)The coastal plain west of Benjamin (Josh 19:40–48), but the Amorites hem them in (Judg 1:34)Samson, a Danite (Judg 13). The tribe migrates north, seizes Laish, renames it Dan, and sets up an idol (Judg 18)
NaphtaliBilhah. "A doe let loose" (49:21)53,400 → 45,400Upper Galilee, west of the Sea of Galilee (Josh 19:32–39). Kedesh is a city of refugeBarak is from Kedesh in Naphtali (Judg 4:6). Naphtali "risked their lives" (Judg 5:18) and later rallies to Gideon
GadZilpah (Leah's maid). "Raiders shall raid him, but he shall raid at their heels" (49:19)45,650 → 40,500Gilead, east of the Jordan (Num 32; Josh 13:24–28). Ramoth-gilead is a city of refugeJephthah of Gilead fights the Ammonites (Judg 11). Mahanaim, a Levitical town in Gad (Josh 21:38), later becomes Ish-bosheth's capital and David's refuge (2 Sam 2:8; 17:24)
AsherZilpah. "His food shall be rich" (49:20)41,500 → 53,400The coast north of Carmel toward Tyre and Sidon (Josh 19:24–31). They fail to drive out the Canaanites (Judg 1:31–32)Stays by the coast instead of helping Deborah (Judg 5:17). Joins Gideon (Judg 6:35)
IssacharLeah. "A strong donkey… a servant at forced labor" (49:14–15)54,400 → 64,300The fertile Jezreel Valley, including Jezreel and Shunem (Josh 19:17–23)Its princes stand with Deborah (Judg 5:15). Tola the judge (Judg 10:1)
ZebulunLeah. "Shall dwell at the shore of the sea" (49:13)57,400 → 60,500Lower Galilee (Josh 19:10–16), including Gath-hepher"A people who risked their lives to the death" (Judg 5:18). Elon the judge (Judg 12:11)
Ephraim (Joseph)Rachel, through Joseph. Jacob crosses his hands and puts the younger son first (Gen 48:14–20). "Joseph is a fruitful bough" (49:22–26)40,500 → 32,500. Joshua son of Nun (Num 13:8)The central hill country (Josh 16). Shiloh, where the tabernacle stands (Josh 18:1)A proud tribe that quarrels with Gideon and Jephthah, ending in the "Shibboleth" slaughter (Judg 8:1; 12:1–6). Samuel's family lives in the hill country of Ephraim (1 Sam 1:1)
Manasseh (Joseph)Rachel, through Joseph. Joseph's firstborn, adopted by Jacob as his own (48:5)32,200 → 52,700. The daughters of Zelophehad win the right to inherit (Num 27; 36)Split in two: half in Bashan and northern Gilead (east), half north of Ephraim (west) (Josh 13:29–31; 17)Gideon of the clan of Abiezer (Judg 6:15). Jair of Gilead
BenjaminRachel. Born as Rachel dies near Bethlehem (35:16–19). "A ravenous wolf" (49:27)35,400 → 45,600A narrow strip between Judah and Ephraim that includes Jerusalem (Jebus), Jericho, Bethel, and Gibeon (Josh 18:11–28)Ehud, the left-handed Benjaminite (Judg 3:15). After the outrage at Gibeah, the tribe is nearly wiped out, leaving 600 survivors (Judg 19–21)

2b. From the monarchy to the New Testament

TribeUnited monarchy (c. 1051–931)Divided kingdom (931–722)732 / 722 BC586, exile, and returnNew Testament
ReubenEast of the Jordan. Joins David at Hebron (1 Chr 12:37)Pressed by Moab. The Mesha Stele (c. 840) boasts of taking Nebo and other towns in this regionDeported by Tiglath-pileser III c. 732 (1 Chr 5:26)Not named among the returneesListed among the sealed in Revelation 7:5
SimeonAbsorbed into Judah. Its towns were "theirs until David reigned" (1 Chr 4:31)Some Simeonites defect to Asa (2 Chr 15:9). Some settle in Seir under Hezekiah (1 Chr 4:39–43)Survives inside JudahAbsorbed into JudahRevelation 7:7
LeviDavid organizes the Levites into divisions of priests, singers, and gatekeepers (1 Chr 23–26). Zadok's lineNorthern Levites move to Judah when Jeroboam appoints priests from outside Levi (2 Chr 11:13–14)The Levites of Judah surviveEzekiel, a priest, prophesies in exile. 4,289 priests return but only 74 Levites (Ezra 2:36–40), so Ezra recruits more (Ezra 8:15–20)Zechariah, the priest (Luke 1:5). Barnabas, a Levite (Acts 4:36). Christ is priest after the order of Melchizedek, not Levi (Heb 7)
JudahDavid of Bethlehem, king at Hebron and then Jerusalem. The Davidic covenant (2 Sam 7)The southern kingdom, with Benjamin. The house of David continues for about 345 yearsSurvives Assyria. Hezekiah is delivered in 701Exiled to Babylon in 605, 597, and 586. Returns under Zerubbabel, a son of David (Hag 2:23). "Jew" comes from Judah"Our Lord was descended from Judah" (Heb 7:14). "The Lion of the tribe of Judah" (Rev 5:5)
Dan"From Dan to Beersheba" means all Israel (2 Sam 24:2)Jeroboam sets up a golden calf at Dan (1 Kgs 12:29). The Tel Dan Stele (c. 840) is later found thereThe north is overrun c. 732 (2 Kgs 15:29)—Left out of the tribal list in Revelation 7. Why is debated †; many connect it with Dan's idolatry
NaphtaliHiram, the temple's master bronze-worker, has a mother from Naphtali (1 Kgs 7:14)Raided by Ben-hadad of Damascus (1 Kgs 15:20)The first to go: "all the land of Naphtali" is deported in 732 (2 Kgs 15:29)—Isaiah 9:1–2 is fulfilled when Jesus lives in Capernaum "in the territory of Zebulun and Naphtali" (Matt 4:13–16)
GadGadite warriors "whose faces were like the faces of lions" join David (1 Chr 12:8)The Mesha Stele: "the men of Gad had lived in the land of Ataroth from of old"Deported c. 732 (1 Chr 5:26)—Revelation 7:5
AsherSolomon gives Hiram twenty Galilean towns, which Hiram dismisses as "Cabul" (1 Kgs 9:11–13)Some from Asher humble themselves and come to Hezekiah's Passover (2 Chr 30:11)Deported, though a remnant remains—Anna the prophetess, "of the tribe of Asher" (Luke 2:36). Northern tribal identity survived
Issachar"Men who had understanding of the times" (1 Chr 12:32)Baasha of Issachar seizes the northern throne (1 Kgs 15:27). Ahab's palace at Jezreel and Naboth's vineyard. The Shunammite woman (2 Kgs 4)Deported. Some had come to Hezekiah's Passover (2 Chr 30:18)—Revelation 7:7
ZebulunSends 50,000 men to David (1 Chr 12:33)Jonah son of Amittai, from Gath-hepher (2 Kgs 14:25)Deported. Some had come to Hezekiah's Passover (2 Chr 30:11)—"The land of Zebulun… Galilee of the Gentiles": the light dawns in Jesus' Galilean ministry (Matt 4:15–16)
EphraimThe hill country around Shiloh and Shechem. Jeroboam, an Ephraimite official under Solomon (1 Kgs 11:26)Jeroboam leads the split. "Ephraim" becomes another name for the northern kingdom (Isa 7; Hosea)Samaria falls in 722 and the people are deported (2 Kgs 17)Some from Ephraim and Manasseh live in Jerusalem (1 Chr 9:3)Jesus withdraws to "a town called Ephraim" (John 11:54). The Samaritans live on its old hills (John 4)
Manasseh18,000 "expressly named" from the half-tribe come to make David king (1 Chr 12:31)Some join Asa (2 Chr 15:9) and come to Hezekiah's Passover (2 Chr 30:11)East Manasseh is deported c. 732 (1 Chr 5:26) and the west in 722See EphraimRevelation 7:6 (Joseph is also listed, 7:8)
BenjaminSaul, the first king (1 Sam 9). Shimei's curses and Sheba's revolt (2 Sam 16; 20)Stays loyal to Judah's king (1 Kgs 12:21). Jeremiah comes from Anathoth in BenjaminSurvives with JudahMordecai the Benjaminite defeats Haman "the Agagite," a reprise of Saul against Agag (Esth 2:5; 3:1; 1 Sam 15). Benjamin returns with Judah (Ezra 1:5)Saul of Tarsus: "of the tribe of Benjamin" (Rom 11:1; Phil 3:5)
"The lost ten tribes"? Scripture never says the northern tribes vanished. Faithful northerners moved south (2 Chr 11:16), and remnants joined Hezekiah's and Josiah's Passovers (2 Chr 30; 34:9). The returning community saw itself as "all Israel" (Ezra 6:17, with twelve sin offerings). Anna of Asher was waiting in the temple, and James writes "to the twelve tribes in the Dispersion" (Jas 1:1). Revelation 7 numbers the twelve tribes as twelve thousand each, then pictures "a great multitude… from every nation" (7:9). Many Reformed interpreters read both as the one people of God in Christ, Jew and Gentile together (compare Gal 6:16; Eph 2:11–22).

title: 3. Key Cities Through Time
html:
3. Key Cities Through Time

Many places in the Bible keep coming back, and later events echo earlier ones in the same spot. Bethel, where God met Jacob, became a shrine for Jeroboam's golden calf. Shechem, where the covenant was renewed, is where the kingdom split. Jerusalem, where Abraham offered Isaac, is where the Father gave his Son. Each list below runs in time order.

CityKey moments (in time order)
The patriarchal heartland
Ur
southern Iraq		A great Sumerian city with the ziggurat of Ur-Nammu (c. 2100 BC). Abram's family leaves it (Gen 11:31; Acts 7:2–4). Some suggest a northern "Ur" near Haran instead †.
Haran
southern Turkey		Terah dies here. Abram leaves at 75 (Gen 12:4). Jacob serves Laban here for 20 years (Gen 29–31). Like Ur, it was a center of the moon-god Sin (compare Josh 24:2). Assyria makes its last stand here (610 BC).
Shechem
between Mts Ebal and Gerizim		Abram's first altar in Canaan (Gen 12:6–7). Jacob buys land and Dinah is defiled (Gen 33–34). The law is read on Ebal and Gerizim (Josh 8:30–35). Joshua's covenant renewal, "as for me and my house" (Josh 24), and Joseph's bones buried (24:32). Abimelech's failed kingship (Judg 9). Rehoboam's coronation goes wrong and the kingdom splits; Jeroboam's first capital (1 Kgs 12). Jesus talks with the Samaritan woman at Jacob's well nearby (John 4).
Bethel
12 mi N of Jerusalem		Abram's altar (Gen 12:8). Jacob's ladder: "this is… the house of God" (Gen 28). The ark is there during the judges (Judg 20:27). Jeroboam's golden calf (1 Kgs 12:29). Amos is told to leave "the king's sanctuary" (Amos 7:13). Josiah tears down its altar (2 Kgs 23:15), as a man of God foretold by name about 300 years earlier (1 Kgs 13:2).
Hebron
Judean hills		Abraham at Mamre. The cave of Machpelah, the family tomb of Abraham, Sarah, Isaac, Rebekah, Jacob, and Leah, and the first land Abraham owned (Gen 23; 49:29–32). The spies meet the Anakim (Num 13:22). Caleb's inheritance (Josh 14) and a city of refuge. David is king here for 7½ years (2 Sam 2:11). Absalom launches his revolt here (2 Sam 15). Herod's enclosure over the tomb still stands.
Beersheba
Negev		Abraham's well and oath (Gen 21). Isaac lives here. Jacob sets out from here twice, for Haran and later for Egypt (Gen 28:10; 46:1). The southern limit in "from Dan to Beersheba." Elijah flees here from Jezebel (1 Kgs 19:3).
Conquest and the tabernacle
Jericho
Jordan valley		The first city taken (Josh 6, c. 1406). Rahab. Joshua curses whoever rebuilds it, which comes true for Hiel in Ahab's day (1 Kgs 16:34). Elisha heals its spring (2 Kgs 2). Zedekiah is caught on its plains (2 Kgs 25:5). Bartimaeus and Zacchaeus (Luke 18–19). Archaeologists dispute the date of its fallen walls †.
Shiloh
Ephraim		The tabernacle is set up and the land allotted here (Josh 18). It stays Israel's worship center through the judges. Hannah's prayer and Samuel's call (1 Sam 1–3). The ark is lost at Aphek (1 Sam 4), and Shiloh becomes a byword for judgment: "Go now to my place that was in Shiloh" (Jer 7:12).
The kingdom cities
Jerusalem
Mt Zion / Moriah		Melchizedek, king of "Salem" (Gen 14:18, traditionally Jerusalem). Abraham offers Isaac on "Moriah" (Gen 22), where the temple later stands (2 Chr 3:1). A Jebusite stronghold until David takes it (c. 1004). Solomon's temple (966–959). Shishak's raid (925). Sennacherib's siege fails (701). Josiah's reform (622). Captured in 597 and destroyed in 586. The temple is rebuilt (516) and the walls restored (445). Antiochus' desecration (167). Pompey (63 BC). Herod's temple. Jesus' death and resurrection (AD 30/33). Pentecost. The Council of Acts 15. Destroyed by Titus (AD 70). Its final picture is the New Jerusalem (Rev 21).
Bethlehem
5 mi S of Jerusalem		Rachel's burial "on the way to Ephrath" (Gen 35:19). Ruth and Boaz. David anointed (1 Sam 16). Micah 5:2 promises a ruler from Bethlehem. Jesus born (c. 6–4 BC), and Herod murders its infants (Matt 2).
Dan (Laish)
source of the Jordan		Abram pursues the kings "as far as Dan" (Gen 14:14). The Danites seize Laish and set up an idol (Judg 18). Jeroboam's golden calf (1 Kgs 12:29). Excavators found a gate complex and a high place here, and the Tel Dan Stele naming the "House of David" (discovered 1993).
Samaria
central hills		Omri buys the hill for two talents of silver (1 Kgs 16:24, c. 880). Ahab's "ivory house" (1 Kgs 22:39); carved ivories have been found there. Ben-hadad's siege and famine (2 Kgs 6–7). Amos' "cows of Bashan" (Amos 4:1). Falls in 722 after a three-year siege, and Assyria resettles it with foreigners (2 Kgs 17), the origin of the Samaritans. Herod rebuilds it as "Sebaste" in honor of Augustus. Philip preaches Christ there (Acts 8).
Imperial capitals
Nineveh
Mosul, Iraq		Founded in Nimrod's realm (Gen 10:11). Jonah's preaching leads to repentance (c. 780–750 †). Sennacherib makes it the capital (c. 700) and builds his "palace without rival," lined with the Lachish reliefs. His sons murder him there (2 Kgs 19:37, 681). Ashurbanipal's library. Destroyed in 612 by the Babylonians and Medes, as Nahum and Zephaniah 2:13 foretold.
Babylon
south of Baghdad		Babel (Gen 11). Hammurabi's capital (18th cent. BC). Merodach-baladan's envoys court Hezekiah (Isa 39). Nebuchadnezzar's city (605–562), with its Ishtar Gate and the walls Daniel would have seen. Falls to Cyrus in 539 (Dan 5). In the New Testament it is a code name for the proud world-city (1 Pet 5:13; Rev 17–18).
Susa (Shushan)
SW Iran		Daniel's vision "in Susa the citadel" (Dan 8:2). Darius I's palace. Esther's story is set in its court (Esth 1:2). Nehemiah serves there as cupbearer to Artaxerxes (Neh 1:1, 445).
The Gospels
Nazareth
lower Galilee		An obscure village never named in the Old Testament. Jesus' hometown (Luke 2:39, 51). His sermon there ends with an attempt to throw him off a cliff (Luke 4:16–30). "Can anything good come out of Nazareth?" (John 1:46).
Capernaum
N shore, Sea of Galilee		Jesus' base, "his own city" (Matt 4:13; 9:1). Peter's house. A centurion who built the synagogue (Luke 7:5). The Bread of Life sermon (John 6:59). Woe pronounced on it for its unbelief (Matt 11:23). A basalt foundation, likely from the first-century synagogue, lies under the later limestone one.
Caesarea Maritima
coast		Herod's harbor city (c. 22–10 BC) and Rome's seat of government in Judea. The "Pilate Stone" was found here. Cornelius, the first Gentile convert (Acts 10). Herod Agrippa I is struck down here (Acts 12:23, AD 44). Paul is held here for two years (Acts 23–26).
The church goes to the nations
Antioch (Syria)
SE Turkey		The empire's third city. Disciples are first called "Christians" here (Acts 11:26). It sends out Paul and Barnabas (Acts 13:1–3). Paul confronts Peter here (Gal 2:11).
Ephesus
W Turkey		The temple of Artemis, one of the Seven Wonders. Paul ministers here about 3 years (Acts 19; 20:31). The silversmiths' riot in the great theater. Ephesians. Timothy's charge (1 Tim 1:3). Christ's letter to Ephesus, which had "abandoned the love you had at first" (Rev 2:4). By tradition, John's later home.
Corinth
Greece		Refounded as a Roman colony by Julius Caesar (44 BC). Paul spends 18 months here (Acts 18:11, c. 50–52); Gallio is proconsul. 1–2 Corinthians. Romans is written from here (Rom 16:23). A pavement inscription names an aedile "Erastus," possibly the city treasurer of Romans 16:23 †.
Athens
Greece		Paul speaks at the Areopagus and quotes Greek poets: "In him we live and move and have our being" (Acts 17:28).
Rome
Italy		Founded by tradition in 753 BC. Augustus' census decree (Luke 2:1). Claudius expels the Jews (c. 49). Romans (c. 57). Paul under house arrest (Acts 28, c. 60–62). The fire and Nero's persecution (64). By tradition, Peter and Paul are martyred there. The Arch of Titus celebrates the fall of Jerusalem.

title: 4. Meanwhile in the World: Moments That Light Up the Themes
html:
4. Meanwhile in the World: Moments That Light Up the Themes

These are short, documented moments from the surrounding nations, each paired with the biblical theme it helps illustrate. They aren't proofs of the Bible. They are windows into the world God's people actually lived in, and they often sharpen the contrast between the Lord and the gods of the nations.

c. 1754 BC · Hammurabi's Code

Babylon's famous law stele uses the same "if a man…" form as the case laws in Exodus 21–23, and both include "eye for eye" (Hammurabi §196). The differences matter more. Hammurabi grounds his law in his own glory, and his penalties vary by social class. Moses' law grounds obedience in redemption: "I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt" (Exod 20:2). It also protects slaves and sojourners (Exod 21:26–27; 22:21). Theme: law flows from grace.

14th–13th cent. BC · Hittite treaties

Hittite treaties between a great king and his vassals follow a fixed pattern: preamble, historical prologue, stipulations, provision for storing and reading the document, witnesses, and blessings and curses. Meredith Kline (Treaty of the Great King) showed that Deuteronomy follows this shape, which supports dating it to the second millennium. Theme: covenant. The Lord is Israel's Great King.

c. 1208 BC · Merneptah's boast

Pharaoh Merneptah carved a victory hymn claiming, "Israel is laid waste; his seed is not." It is the first mention of Israel outside the Bible, and it announces Israel's destruction. Egypt's dynasties are gone, and Abraham's seed is not. Theme: the promise to Abraham outlasts empires (Gen 12:3).

c. 1177 BC · The Sea Peoples

Ramesses III's reliefs at Medinet Habu show his battle with the "Sea Peoples," including the Peleset, or Philistines, who then settle the coast of Canaan. This explains why Philistines dominate Judges and Samuel, and why Israel had no smiths (1 Sam 13:19–22). Theme: God raises up enemies to discipline his people and deliverers to save them.

853 / 841 BC · Ahab and Jehu in Assyrian records

Shalmaneser III's Kurkh Monolith credits "Ahab the Israelite" with 2,000 chariots at Qarqar, the largest force there. Kings, however, gives Ahab's military record barely a line and judges him for his idolatry (1 Kgs 16:30–33). Twelve years later the Black Obelisk shows Jehu, or his envoy, bowing to Assyria. Theme: God judges kings by covenant faithfulness, not power.

763 BC · The eclipse at Nineveh

An Assyrian list records a solar eclipse in the year of the official Bur-Sagale, fixed by astronomy at 15 June 763. It is the anchor for ancient Near Eastern dating. Revolts and plague troubled Assyria in those years. Some suggest these omens prepared Nineveh for Jonah's warning, and that Amos 8:9 ("I will make the sun go down at noon") alludes to it †, though both are only possibilities. Theme: God's mercy reaches even Israel's enemies (Jonah 4:11).

753 BC · Romulus and Remus

By legend, Rome was founded when Romulus killed his brother Remus, around the time of Amos and Hosea. Augustine (City of God 15.5) compared this with Cain, who killed his brother and built the first city (Gen 4:17). The earthly city is founded on fratricide; the heavenly city is founded by a Brother who dies for his brothers. Theme: the two cities.

701 BC · "Like a bird in a cage"

Sennacherib's prism lists 46 Judean cities he took and says he shut Hezekiah up in Jerusalem "like a bird in a cage." He never claims to have taken Jerusalem. His palace walls show the siege of Lachish instead, as if to fill the gap. Compare 2 Kings 19:32–36 and Isaiah 37. Theme: "I will defend this city… for my own sake" (Isa 37:35).

7th cent. BC · Gilgamesh at Nineveh

Ashurbanipal's library preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh, with its flood story. In the related Atrahasis epic, the gods send the flood because human noise keeps them awake, and they crowd around the sacrifice "like flies." Genesis tells of one holy God who judges sin, saves Noah by grace, and makes a covenant (Gen 6–9). Theme: one sovereign, moral God.

605–562 BC · Nebuchadnezzar's bricks

Thousands of Babylon's bricks are stamped with Nebuchadnezzar's name. That gives force to his boast in Daniel 4:30, "Is not this great Babylon, which I have built… for the glory of my majesty?" It also gives force to his humbling, and to his confession that God's "dominion is an everlasting dominion" (4:34). Theme: pride and the sovereignty of God.

c. 592 BC · Rations for a captive king

Cuneiform tablets from Babylon list oil rations for "Yaukin, king of the land of Yahudu," and his sons. This is Jehoiachin, the captive heir of David. Kings ends with him lifted up from prison to eat at the king's table (2 Kgs 25:27–30). Theme: the lamp of David is not snuffed out (2 Sam 7:16).

c. 800–300 BC · The "Axial Age"

Historian Karl Jaspers noticed that Confucius (551–479), the Buddha (dates disputed †), the Upanishads, and the Greek philosophers all appear within a few centuries. This is the same era as Isaiah, Jeremiah, the exile, and the return. As the nations sought wisdom by searching, God spoke "at many times and in many ways… by the prophets" (Heb 1:1). Theme: revelation versus speculation (1 Cor 1:21).

539 BC · The Cyrus Cylinder

Cyrus' clay cylinder boasts that Marduk chose him, and it records his policy of sending deported peoples and their gods home. Isaiah had named him over a century earlier as the Lord's "shepherd" and "anointed," raised up "though you do not know me" (Isa 44:28–45:4). Theme: providence. "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord" (Prov 21:1).

483–479 BC · Xerxes, Greece, and Esther

Herodotus describes Xerxes' great council before he invaded Greece. Esther 1 sets a lavish 180-day display in his 3rd year (483). Then came Thermopylae and Salamis (480). Esther is taken to the king in his 7th year (c. 479/478), after he comes home defeated. While the West remembers Salamis, God was quietly preparing a Jewish queen in Susa. Theme: hidden providence. God is never named in Esther, yet he is everywhere.

c. 430–399 BC · Malachi and Socrates

The Old Testament closes with Malachi about the time Athens reaches its peak with Pericles, the Parthenon, and Socrates. In Plato's Phaedo (85d), Socrates' friend Simmias wishes for "some divine word" to carry us more safely through life. Malachi ends with a promise: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet" (Mal 4:5). Theme: four hundred years of waiting.

333–323 BC · Alexander

Alexander's lightning conquest fits Daniel's "male goat" that crosses the earth "without touching the ground" (Dan 8:5–8, 21). Josephus tells a story, probably legendary, that the high priest showed Alexander the book of Daniel (Antiquities 11.337). Alexander's lasting gift was the Greek language. The New Testament would be written in it. Theme: "the fullness of time" (Gal 4:4).

9 BC · The "gospel" of Augustus

A calendar inscription from Priene says the birthday of the god Augustus was "the beginning of the good tidings (euangelia) for the world." Mark opens with a direct challenge: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (Mark 1:1). Luke sets Jesus' birth under Augustus' decree (Luke 2:1). Theme: Jesus is Lord, and Caesar is not.

AD 49–52 · Claudius and Gallio

Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because of riots "at the instigation of Chrestus," probably a garbled report about Christ. This is how Aquila and Priscilla came to Corinth (Acts 18:2). An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio's proconsulship to c. 51–52, and it is the fixed point for dating Paul's letters. Theme: the gospel travels on Rome's own roads.

AD 64 · Nero's torches

After the great fire, Tacitus writes, Nero blamed the Christians. Some were sewn into animal skins and torn by dogs, and others were burned as torches in his gardens (Annals 15.44). First Peter and Hebrews speak to churches facing that "fiery trial" (1 Pet 4:12). Theme: suffering, then glory.

AD 70 · The temple falls

Josephus describes Titus' siege in harrowing detail: famine, faction, and fire. The temple burned in the month of Ab, about forty years after Jesus said "there will not be left here one stone upon another" (Matt 24:2). The Arch of Titus still shows the menorah carried through Rome. Eusebius says Christians, heeding Luke 21:20–21, fled to Pella. Many Reformed interpreters, including Wilson and Gentry, read much of the Olivet Discourse as fulfilled here †. Theme: Jesus is the true temple (John 2:19–21).

AD 81–96 · "Our lord and god"

Suetonius reports that Domitian liked to be called dominus et deus noster, "our lord and god." In Revelation 4:11 the elders sing, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God." Whether Revelation dates to Domitian's reign or before AD 70 †, its worship is aimed straight at Caesar's claims. Theme: the Lamb on the throne.

This is Jehoiachin, the captive heir of David. Kings ends with him lifted up from prison to eat at the king's table (2 Kgs 25:27–30). Theme: the lamp of David is not snuffed out (2 Sam 7:16). c. 800–300 BC · The "Axial Age" Historian Karl Jaspers noticed that Confucius (551–479), the Buddha (dates disputed † ), the Upanishads, and the Greek philosophers all appear within a few centuries. This is the same era as Isaiah, Jeremiah, the exile, and the return. As the nations sought wisdom by searching, God spoke "at many times and in many ways… by the prophets" (Heb 1:1). Theme: revelation versus speculation (1 Cor 1:21). 539 BC · The Cyrus Cylinder Cyrus' clay cylinder boasts that Marduk chose him, and it records his policy of sending deported peoples and their gods home. Isaiah had named him over a century earlier as the Lord 's "shepherd" and "anointed," raised up "though you do not know me" (Isa 44:28–45:4). Theme: providence. "The king's heart is a stream of water in the hand of the Lord " (Prov 21:1). 483–479 BC · Xerxes, Greece, and Esther Herodotus describes Xerxes' great council before he invaded Greece. Esther 1 sets a lavish 180-day display in his 3rd year (483). Then came Thermopylae and Salamis (480). Esther is taken to the king in his 7th year (c. 479/478), after he comes home defeated. While the West remembers Salamis, God was quietly preparing a Jewish queen in Susa. Theme: hidden providence. God is never named in Esther, yet he is everywhere. c. 430–399 BC · Malachi and Socrates The Old Testament closes with Malachi about the time Athens reaches its peak with Pericles, the Parthenon, and Socrates. In Plato's Phaedo (85d), Socrates' friend Simmias wishes for "some divine word" to carry us more safely through life. Malachi ends with a promise: "Behold, I will send you Elijah the prophet" (Mal 4:5). Theme: four hundred years of waiting. 333–323 BC · Alexander Alexander's lightning conquest fits Daniel's "male goat" that crosses the earth "without touching the ground" (Dan 8:5–8, 21). Josephus tells a story, probably legendary, that the high priest showed Alexander the book of Daniel ( Antiquities 11.337). Alexander's lasting gift was the Greek language. The New Testament would be written in it. Theme: "the fullness of time" (Gal 4:4). 9 BC · The "gospel" of Augustus A calendar inscription from Priene says the birthday of the god Augustus was "the beginning of the good tidings ( euangelia ) for the world." Mark opens with a direct challenge: "The beginning of the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" (Mark 1:1). Luke sets Jesus' birth under Augustus' decree (Luke 2:1). Theme: Jesus is Lord, and Caesar is not. AD 49–52 · Claudius and Gallio Suetonius says Claudius expelled the Jews from Rome because of riots "at the instigation of Chrestus," probably a garbled report about Christ. This is how Aquila and Priscilla came to Corinth (Acts 18:2). An inscription at Delphi dates Gallio's proconsulship to c. 51–52, and it is the fixed point for dating Paul's letters. Theme: the gospel travels on Rome's own roads. AD 64 · Nero's torches After the great fire, Tacitus writes, Nero blamed the Christians. Some were sewn into animal skins and torn by dogs, and others were burned as torches in his gardens ( Annals 15.44). First Peter and Hebrews speak to churches facing that "fiery trial" (1 Pet 4:12). Theme: suffering, then glory. AD 70 · The temple falls Josephus describes Titus' siege in harrowing detail: famine, faction, and fire. The temple burned in the month of Ab, about forty years after Jesus said "there will not be left here one stone upon another" (Matt 24:2). The Arch of Titus still shows the menorah carried through Rome. Eusebius says Christians, heeding Luke 21:20–21, fled to Pella. Many Reformed interpreters, including Wilson and Gentry, read much of the Olivet Discourse as fulfilled here † . Theme: Jesus is the true temple (John 2:19–21). AD 81–96 · "Our lord and god" Suetonius reports that Domitian liked to be called dominus et deus noster , "our lord and god." In Revelation 4:11 the elders sing, "Worthy are you, our Lord and God." Whether Revelation dates to Domitian's reign or before AD 70 † , its worship is aimed straight at Caesar's claims. Theme: the Lamb on the throne.

title: The Old Testament as a Whole
html:
The Old Testament as a Whole

BibleProject overview
BibleProject video: TaNaK / Old Testament bibleproject.com/videos/tanak-old-testament/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The Protestant "Old Testament" contains the same books as the Jewish TaNaK, an acronym for Torah ("instruction"), Nevi'im ("prophets") and Ketuvim ("writings"), but in a different order. Jesus himself refers to the three-part shape (compare Luke 24:44).
  • BibleProject argues that the books are deliberately linked by cross-references into one unified library. It describes generations of "prophetic scribes" shaping the material, guided by God's Spirit so that through human words God speaks.
  • Torah: God gives humanity the rule of a very good world, but humans seize autonomy to define good and evil, are exiled, and build Babylon. God promises a new human who will crush the snake, and he works through Abraham's family and Moses's covenant, though Israel fails. The Torah ends by noting that no prophet like Moses has arisen since.
  • Nevi'im: the Former Prophets retell Israel's failure in the land, ending in exile in Babylon, with the promise of a Davidic king as the bright spot. The Latter Prophets (three major and twelve shorter prophets, echoing three patriarchs and twelve sons) announce the Day of the Lord, but also a purified new Israel in a new covenant under a ruler "called by the name David." They close by looking for a coming "Elijah."
  • Ketuvim: Psalms 1–2 introduce the righteous one and the messianic King, and the Psalms teach God's people to pray while they wait. Proverbs, Job and Ecclesiastes carry on a conversation about living wisely. Daniel sees the new human trampled and then raised to rule. Chronicles retells the whole story and ends hoping that one "whose God is with him" will "go up" to Jerusalem.
  • The TaNaK is a unified story of God's covenant promise to Israel and to all humanity, meant for a lifetime of reading.
A Reformed response to the video Reformed readers welcome the emphasis on a unified, Christ-anticipating canon (Luke 24:27, 44). They are more cautious about BibleProject's account of a long, mostly anonymous editorial process. The Reformed confessions (WCF 1; 1689 LBCF 1) locate inspiration in the writings themselves, and conservative Reformed scholars generally defend substantial Mosaic authorship of the Pentateuch (affirmed by Jesus in John 5:46–47).

title: Genesis
html:
Genesis

50 chapters

“And he believed the Lord, and he counted it to him as righteousness.” (Genesis 15:6, ESV)

Setting. Traditionally attributed to Moses, Genesis was given to Israel as they came out of Egypt to tell them who their God is, where the world came from, why it is broken, and why they in particular were chosen. It covers the time from creation to Joseph's death in Egypt.

Where it fits. Patriarchs — Covers creation to Joseph's death (c. 1805 BC). Abraham's call is c. 2091 BC. Written by Moses in the wilderness, c. 1446–1406 BC. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Creation (1–2): God makes an ordered, good world and crowns it with humanity as his image-bearers.
  2. Fall and spread of sin (3–11): Rebellion in the garden, Cain, the flood, and Babel show sin multiplying; God keeps judging and keeps showing mercy.
  3. Abraham and Isaac (12–26): God calls one man and promises land, offspring, and blessing to all nations.
  4. Jacob (27–36): A deceiver is mastered, renamed Israel, and becomes the father of twelve tribes.
  5. Joseph (37–50): Through betrayal and slavery God preserves the family and saves many lives.
Main themes. Creation and the image of God; sin and death; blessing and curse; covenant promise; God's providence over human evil; the chosen line or "seed".
Main characters. Adam and Eve, Cain and Abel, Noah, Abraham and Sarah, Isaac and Rebekah, Jacob and Esau, Rachel and Leah, Judah, Joseph.
Key passages
  • 1:26–28 — the image of God and the creation mandate
  • 3:15 — the first promise of the gospel
  • 12:1–3 — the call of Abram and blessing to the nations
  • 15 — the covenant ceremony where God alone walks between the pieces
  • 22 — the binding of Isaac and "the Lord will provide"
  • 50:20 — "you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good"

How it points to Christ. The promise that the woman's offspring would crush the serpent (3:15) launches the whole Bible's hope. Christ is the true offspring of Abraham (Gal 3:16), the ram provided in Isaac's place (22), the king from Judah (49:10), and the greater Joseph, rejected by his brothers and exalted to save them.

Going deeper. Genesis gives us the categories the rest of the Bible depends on: a good creation, human beings made as God's image to rule under him, sin as rebellion that brings death, and grace that promises a Deliverer. Frame's "lordship" emphasis helps here. God speaks and it is (control), he defines good and evil (authority), and he walks with his people (presence). The creation mandate (1:28) and the promise to bless "all the families of the earth" (12:3) are why postmillennial writers like Wilson expect the gospel to bear cultural fruit in history. The Great Commission is the creation mandate renewed in Christ. Joseph's story is the Bible's great lesson in providence: human sin is real and culpable, yet God governs it for good (WCF 5).

Reformed note Reformed theology calls 3:15 the first announcement of the gospel and reads Genesis through the covenant of grace. In Genesis 15, God alone passes between the pieces, so the covenant rests on his oath and not on Abraham's performance. Postmillennial writers like Doug Wilson take "all the families of the earth shall be blessed" (12:3) as a promise the gospel will actually fulfill in history.
Reading BibleProject well BibleProject splits Genesis into two videos (1–11 and 12–50). It reads Genesis 1 as God building a cosmic temple and Genesis 6's "sons of God" as rebellious spiritual beings. Both are defensible readings, but they aren't the only Reformed options. Calvin, for example, took the "sons of God" to be the godly line of Seth.
Recommended free Reformed commentaries: Genesis
  • Calvin's Commentaries: Commentary on Genesis — John Calvin. The fountainhead of Reformed exegesis: plain sense, Christ-centred, and pastoral (vols. 1–2; link opens vol. 1).ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom01
  • Surveying the Text: Genesis — Douglas Wilson. Wilson's one-sermon panorama of the whole book: its structure, themes, and Christ, with postmillennial and covenantal punch.dougwils.com/the-church/s8-expository/surveying-the-text-genesis.html
  • Interpreting Eden (Gen 1–3), on the Frame–Poythress free eBooks page — Vern Poythress. Frame's longtime colleague on reading creation and the fall faithfully; free PDF, personal use only.frame-poythress.org/ebooks/
  • TGC Bible Commentary: Genesis — The Gospel Coalition (Carson Center for Theological Renewal). A free, modern, section-by-section commentary in TGC's Reformed-evangelical stream, with good help on biblical theology.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/genesis/
More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Genesis 1-11 bibleproject.com/videos/genesis-1-11/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Genesis has two parts, God and the whole world (1–11) and God and one family (12–50), joined by a "hinge" at the start of chapter 12.
  • God brings order and goodness out of darkness and makes humans in his image, which BibleProject explains as a role: to reflect God's character and rule his world on his behalf, harnessing its potential.
  • The tree of the knowledge of good and evil is a choice between trusting God's definition of good and seizing autonomy to define it for ourselves, and turning from the giver of life means death.
  • The snake, a creature in rebellion, retells the story, and the humans grasp at being "like God" when they already bore his image. Shame, hiding and blame follow.
  • God's poetic sentence includes grace: a seed of the woman will strike the snake's head and be struck on the heel, a "wounded victor."
  • Chapters 4–11 trace the ripple effect: Cain's murder and city, Lamech's violence, the "sons of God" (fallen angels or god-claiming kings, left open), the flood, Noah failing "in a garden" like a new Adam, and Babylon's tower.
  • The point: God keeps giving humans the chance to do right with his world and they keep ruining it, but God is determined to bless and rescue it.

“We live in a good world that we have turned bad.” — BibleProject, Genesis 1-11 video

BibleProject video: Genesis 12-50 bibleproject.com/videos/genesis-12-50/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Out of Babel's scattering, the story narrows to Abram. God promises land, a great nation, a great name (the name Babel grasped for) and blessing, renewing the blessing of Eden.
  • The purpose clause is the key to the whole Bible: in Abraham "all the families of the earth" will be blessed. This is why Israel becomes "a kingdom of priests," and the prophets later tie the promise to a messianic king.
  • Two themes run through every generation: the family's repeated failure, which puts the promise at risk, and God's faithfulness in rescuing them from themselves.
  • Abraham lies about Sarah twice and takes Hagar, yet he looks at the stars and trusts God's promise. God formalizes this in covenant (15, 17) and gives circumcision as its sign.
  • Jacob the "deceiver" is deceived by Laban, wrestles with God for a blessing and is renamed Israel.
  • Joseph is betrayed and enslaved but raised up to save many lives. His words "you meant evil… God meant it for good" summarize the book.
  • The seed promise of Genesis 3 is traced through Abraham to Judah. Jacob's blessing (49) foresees a king from Judah who will command the obedience of the nations and restore the garden blessing.

“You all planned this for evil, but God planned it for good.” — BibleProject, Genesis 12-50 video

title: Exodus
html:
Exodus

40 chapters

“I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” (Exodus 20:2, ESV)

Setting. Moses wrote Exodus for the redeemed nation. It picks up centuries after Genesis, with Abraham's family enslaved in Egypt, and follows them out of Egypt to Mount Sinai, probably in the 15th or 13th century BC.

Where it fits. Israel in Egypt → Wilderness — From the oppression in Egypt through the Exodus (c. 1446 BC) to the tabernacle (1445 BC). On the early date, the pharaoh is likely of Egypt's 18th Dynasty. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Slavery and the call of Moses (1–4): Pharaoh oppresses Israel, and God reveals his name at the burning bush.
  2. Plagues and Passover (5–13): God judges Egypt's gods, and the firstborn of Israel are spared under the blood of the lamb.
  3. The sea and the wilderness (14–18): Israel passes through the waters and learns to trust God for bread and water.
  4. Covenant at Sinai (19–24): God makes Israel his treasured possession and gives the Ten Commandments.
  5. Tabernacle, golden calf, and glory (25–40): God gives instructions for his dwelling, Israel commits idolatry, Moses intercedes, and God's glory fills the tabernacle.
Main themes. Redemption; the name and character of God (34:6–7); law given to a rescued people; God dwelling with his people; idolatry and intercession.
Main characters. Moses, Aaron, Miriam, Pharaoh, Jethro, Joshua.
Key passages
  • 3:14 — "I AM WHO I AM"
  • 12 — the Passover lamb
  • 14 — the crossing of the sea
  • 19:5–6 — a kingdom of priests and a holy nation
  • 20 — the Ten Commandments, given to an already-redeemed people
  • 32–34 — the golden calf, Moses' intercession, and God's name proclaimed
  • 40:34 — the glory fills the tabernacle

How it points to Christ. Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Cor 5:7) and leads a greater exodus out of slavery to sin (Luke 9:31, where his "departure" is literally his exodus). He is the bread from heaven, the rock that was struck (1 Cor 10:4), and the Word who "tabernacled" among us (John 1:14).

Going deeper. The order matters: God redeems first (chs. 1–18) and then gives the law (chs. 19–24). The law is the shape of life for those already rescued, not a ladder for climbing up to God. This is why the Reformed tradition speaks of the "third use" of the law as a guide for the grateful believer (Calvin, Institutes 2.7.12; Heidelberg Catechism, Part 3, "Gratitude"). Sproul's The Holiness of God draws heavily on scenes like the burning bush and Sinai: God's holiness is both terrifying and beautiful. The tabernacle chapters, which readers often skip, are the point of the book. The God who judged Egypt's gods comes to live among his people, which John 1:14 says happens fully in Jesus.

Reformed note The order matters: redemption comes first (20:2) and the law follows, so obedience is a grateful response to grace and never a way of earning it. John Frame organizes Christian ethics around the Ten Commandments (The Doctrine of the Christian Life) and draws his "lordship attributes" of God's control, authority, and presence from passages like the revelation of the divine name in Exodus 3.
Recommended free Reformed commentaries: Exodus
  • Calvin's Commentaries: Harmony of the Law (Exodus–Deuteronomy) — John Calvin. The fountainhead of Reformed exegesis: plain sense, Christ-centred, and pastoral (vols. 3–6; link opens vol. 3).ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom03

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Exodus 1-18 bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-1-18/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Israel was "fruitful and multiplied," echoing Eden's blessing. But a new Pharaoh sees them as a threat, enslaves them and orders the boys drowned.
  • BibleProject calls Pharaoh the worst character in the Bible so far, a "new Babylon" who has redefined good and evil so far that killing children seems good to him.
  • God turns Pharaoh's evil upside down: Moses floats in a basket into Pharaoh's own house, then meets God at the burning bush.
  • On the hardening of Pharaoh's heart, BibleProject reads the sequence closely. In the first plagues Pharaoh hardens his own heart. Only in the later plagues does God harden it, once Pharaoh's evil has passed "a point of no return" and God bends it toward redemption.
  • Passover: God provides escape through the blood of a spotless lamb, which Israel re-enacts yearly to celebrate God's justice and mercy.
  • The Song of the Sea ends "the Lord will reign," showing what God's kingdom is about: confronting evil and freeing those enslaved to it.
  • Grumbling in the wilderness raises the question of whether Israel's heart is as hard as Pharaoh's.
BibleProject video: Exodus 19-40 bibleproject.com/videos/exodus-19-40/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • At Sinai God invites Israel into covenant, developing the promise to Abraham: if they keep it they will be "a kingdom of priests," showing the nations what God is like.

  • God wants his presence to dwell among them, restoring what was lost in Eden. The tabernacle's detailed blueprints are full of garden imagery, "a portable Eden."
  • The golden calf breaks the first two commands at the foot of the mountain. Moses intercedes by appealing to God's promises to Abraham and his reputation among the nations, and God relents.

“Israel "has become its own worst enemy.” — BibleProject, Exodus 19-40 video

A Reformed response to the video BibleProject treats Pharaoh's hardening as God confirming a choice Pharaoh had already made. Reformed readers agree the text shows Pharaoh hardening himself, but with Paul (Rom 9:17–18) also see God's sovereign purpose announced before the plagues began (Exod 4:21; 7:3). On this view both are true at once, as with Joseph's brothers in Gen 50:20.
text: Exodus 40 chapters “I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, out of the house of slavery.” (Exodus 20:2, ESV) Setting. Moses wrote Exodus for the redeemed nation. It picks up centuries after Genesis, with Abraham's family enslaved in Egypt, and follows them out of Egypt to Mount Sinai, probably in the 15th or 13th century BC. Where it fits. Israel in Egypt → Wilderness — From the oppression in Egypt through the Exodus (c. 1446 BC) to the tabernacle (1445 BC). On the early date, the pharaoh is likely of Egypt's 18th Dynasty. ( Timelines ) The Flow of the Book Slavery and the call of Moses (1–4) : Pharaoh oppresses Israel, and God reveals his name at the burning bush. Plagues and Passover (5–13) : God judges Egypt's gods, and the firstborn of Israel are spared under the blood of the lamb. The sea and the wilderness (14–18) : Israel passes through the waters and learns to trust God for bread and water. Covenant at Sinai (19–24) : God makes Israel his treasured possession and gives the Ten Commandments. Tabernacle, golden calf, and glory (25–40) : God gives instructions for his dwelling, Israel commits idolatry, Moses intercedes, and God's glory fills the tabernacle. Main themes. Redemption; the name and character of God (34:6–7); law given to a rescued people; God dwelling with his people; idolatry and intercession. Main characters. Moses, Aaron, Miriam, Pharaoh, Jethro, Joshua. Key passages 3:14 — "I AM WHO I AM" 12 — the Passover lamb 14 — the crossing of the sea 19:5–6 — a kingdom of priests and a holy nation 20 — the Ten Commandments, given to an already-redeemed people 32–34 — the golden calf, Moses' intercession, and God's name proclaimed 40:34 — the glory fills the tabernacle How it points to Christ. Christ is our Passover lamb (1 Cor 5:7) and leads a greater exodus out of slavery to sin (Luke 9:31, where his "departure" is literally his exodus). He is the bread from heaven, the rock that was struck (1 Cor 10:4), and the Word who "tabernacled" among us (John 1:14). Going deeper. The order matters: God redeems first (chs. 1–18) and then gives the law (chs. 19–24). The law is the shape of life for those already rescued, not a ladder for climbing up to God. This is why the Reformed tradition speaks of the "third use" of the law as a guide for the grateful believer (Calvin, Institutes 2.7.12; Heidelberg Catechism, Part 3, "Gratitude"). Sproul's The Holiness of God draws heavily on scenes like the burning bush and Sinai: God's holiness is both terrifying and beautiful. The tabernacle chapters, which readers often skip, are the point of the book. The God who judged Egypt's gods comes to live among his people, which John 1:14 says happens fully in Jesus. Reformed note The order matters: redemption comes first (20:2) and the law follows, so obedience is a grateful response to grace and never a way of earning it. John Frame organizes Christian ethics around the Ten Commandments ( The Doctrine of the Christian Life ) and draws his "lordship attributes" of God's control, authority, and presence from passages like the revelation of the divine name in Exodus 3. title: Leviticus
html:
Leviticus

27 chapters

“You shall be holy, for I the Lord your God am holy.” (Leviticus 19:2, ESV)

Setting. Leviticus is God's instruction through Moses at Sinai. It answers the question Exodus leaves open: how can a holy God live among a sinful people?

Where it fits. Wilderness — Given at Sinai in the year after the Exodus, c. 1445 BC. The tabernacle has just been set up (Exod 40:17). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Sacrifices (1–7): Five kinds of offering for worship, fellowship, and atonement.
  2. Priesthood (8–10): Aaron's sons are ordained, and Nadab and Abihu are struck down for "strange fire."
  3. Clean and unclean (11–15): Laws about food, birth, skin disease, and bodily discharges teach the distance between life and death.
  4. Day of Atonement (16): The center of the book. One goat dies and the other carries sin away.
  5. Holiness in all of life (17–27): Holiness covers sex, justice, love of neighbor (19:18), festivals, Sabbath and Jubilee, and covenant blessings and curses.
Main themes. Holiness; atonement by blood (17:11); priestly mediation; purity; sacred time (Sabbath, feasts, Jubilee).
Main characters. Moses, Aaron, Nadab and Abihu.
Key passages
  • 1–7 — the five offerings
  • 10 — Nadab and Abihu's "strange fire"
  • 11–15 — clean and unclean
  • 16 — the Day of Atonement and the scapegoat
  • 17:11 — "the life of the flesh is in the blood"
  • 19:18 — "love your neighbor as yourself"
  • 26 — covenant blessings and curses

How it points to Christ. Hebrews 9–10 reads Leviticus as a shadow of Christ. He is both the priest and the sacrifice. He offered himself once for all, took our uncleanness on himself, and opened the way into the true Holy Place.

Going deeper. Leviticus answers a question Exodus leaves hanging: how can a holy God dwell among sinful people? The answer is substitution. A spotless animal dies in the worshiper's place, and blood makes atonement. Hebrews 9–10 says these sacrifices were "a shadow of the good things to come," fulfilled once for all in Christ, which is why Christians don't offer them. Reformed theology classically divides the law into moral, ceremonial and civil parts (WCF 19.3–4). The ceremonial law is fulfilled in Christ. The moral law, summed up in the Ten Commandments and in 19:18, still binds. The "general equity" of the civil laws still teaches wisdom. Wilson and other theonomy-sympathetic writers press that last point further than many Reformed teachers do.

Reformed note The Reformed tradition stresses that the sacrifices teach substitution: the animal dies in the sinner's place, and the blood turns away God's just wrath (propitiation, Rom 3:25). Calvin and the Reformed confessions divide Moses' law into moral, ceremonial, and civil parts. The ceremonial laws are fulfilled in Christ, while the moral law still guides believers.
Reading BibleProject well BibleProject's material on sacrifice stresses purification and "life for life" ransom, and that is good and biblical. Reformed readers will want to add the penal side, which the text also teaches: the sacrifice bears guilt and satisfies God's justice (Lev 16:21–22; Isa 53:5–6).

What the video covers (our summary)
  • Leviticus opens with "the Lord called to Moses from the tent" because Moses could not go in. The book is about how God graciously makes a way for sinful people to live in his holy presence.
  • "Holy" means set apart or unique. God is the author of life, so the space around him is full of goodness and life, and impure, unjust people must be made holy to live near him.
  • The book is symmetrical. Rituals (1–7; 23–25), priests (8–10; 21–22) and purity (11–15; 18–20) are arranged around the Day of Atonement at the center (16).
  • The sacrifices include thank-you offerings and sorry offerings. In the sorry offerings an animal dies in the worshiper's place and "covers" (atones for) sin. The seven feasts retell the story of redemption.
  • Nadab and Abihu show the paradox: God's presence is pure goodness, but it becomes dangerous to those who insult it.
  • Ritual impurity is linked to death (fluids, skin disease, mold, corpses). Being impure was not sin. Bringing death into God's presence was. The food laws and moral purity laws (care for the poor, sexual integrity, justice) teach that holiness reaches every part of life.
  • On the Day of Atonement, one goat purifies and the scapegoat carries sins away. Numbers then opens with God speaking to Moses in the tent. "Leviticus worked."

title: Numbers
html:
Numbers

36 chapters

“God is not man, that he should lie, or a son of man, that he should change his mind.” (Numbers 23:19, ESV)

Setting. Numbers follows Israel's forty years between Sinai and the plains of Moab. It is named for its two censuses, one of the generation that died in the desert and one of the generation that would enter the land.

Where it fits. Wilderness — From the Sinai census (c. 1445 BC) to the plains of Moab, almost 40 years later (c. 1406 BC). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Ordering the camp at Sinai (1–10): Israel is counted, arranged around the tabernacle, and sets out.
  2. Rebellion in the wilderness (11–25): The people complain, the spies bring a faithless report, Korah rebels, and Moses sins at Meribah. The bronze serpent and Balaam's blessings show God's grace in the middle of it.
  3. A new generation (26–36): A second census, inheritance laws, and preparation to enter Canaan.
Main themes. Unbelief and its consequences; God's patient faithfulness; holiness of the camp; blessing that can't be reversed (Balaam).
Main characters. Moses, Aaron, Miriam, Joshua and Caleb, Korah, Balaam, Phinehas.
Key passages
  • 6:24–26 — the priestly blessing
  • 13–14 — the spies and the refusal to enter the land
  • 20 — Moses strikes the rock
  • 21:4–9 — the bronze serpent (see John 3:14)
  • 22–24 — Balaam's oracles
  • 24:17 — "a star shall come out of Jacob"

How it points to Christ. Jesus himself compares his cross to the bronze serpent lifted up so that whoever looks may live (John 3:14–15). Balaam's oracle of a star from Jacob and a scepter from Israel (24:17) looks ahead to the Messiah King.

Going deeper. Numbers is the story of a generation that saw miracles and still didn't believe. Hebrews 3–4 uses it as a warning to the church: "they were unable to enter because of unbelief." It also shows the persistence of grace. God sustains Israel for forty years, turns Balaam's curses into blessings, and brings the next generation to the border. Jesus himself draws the lesson of the bronze serpent (John 3:14–15): it shows the pattern of the gospel: the very sign of judgment becomes the means of life, received simply by looking. That pattern points to the cross.

Reformed note Paul says these things "were written down for our instruction" (1 Cor 10:11), and Hebrews 3–4 uses the wilderness generation to warn against unbelief. The Reformed tradition reads such warnings as one of the means God uses to keep his elect persevering.
