title: Deuteronomy
html:
Deuteronomy

34 chapters

“Hear, O Israel: The Lord our God, the Lord is one. You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart...” (Deuteronomy 6:4–5, ESV)

Setting. Deuteronomy is Moses' farewell sermons on the plains of Moab, given to the new generation just before they cross the Jordan. Its name means "second law," because Moses restates the covenant for them.

Where it fits. Wilderness — Moses' farewell sermons on the plains of Moab in the 40th year, c. 1406 BC. Its shape resembles Hittite treaties of the 2nd millennium BC. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Looking back (1–4): Moses retells the wilderness story.
  2. The heart of the covenant (5–11): The Ten Commandments are repeated, followed by the Shema and calls to love God and teach your children.
  3. Covenant stipulations (12–26): Laws for worship, leaders, justice, and family life.
  4. Blessings and curses (27–30): Life or death. Moses predicts Israel's failure and promises that God will circumcise their hearts (30:6).
  5. Moses' song, blessing, and death (31–34): Leadership passes to Joshua.
Main themes. Covenant love and loyalty; remembering; teaching the next generation; one God, one place of worship; blessing and curse; heart circumcision.
Main characters. Moses, Joshua, the new generation of Israel.
Key passages
  • 6:4–9 — the Shema
  • 7:6–8 — chosen because God loved them, not because they were great
  • 10:16 and 30:6 — circumcise your hearts / the Lord will circumcise your heart
  • 18:15 — a prophet like Moses
  • 28 — blessings and curses
  • 30:15–20 — choose life

How it points to Christ. Jesus answered the devil's temptations with quotations from Deuteronomy (Matt 4). He is the Prophet like Moses (18:15; Acts 3:22), and he bore the covenant curse by being hanged on a tree (21:23; Gal 3:13).

Going deeper. Deuteronomy is shaped like an ancient treaty between a great king and his vassal, and it is the covenant document Jesus quoted most. All three of his answers to Satan in the wilderness come from it. It is also deeply realistic. Moses expects Israel to fail (31:16–29), and 30:6 promises that God himself will one day do the heart-work they can't do. Reformed theology sees that promise fulfilled in the new covenant (Jer 31; Ezek 36). Deuteronomy 6 is also a charter for the covenant home: teach these words to your children as you sit, walk, lie down and rise. Wilson champions that vision in his writing on covenant child-rearing and Christian education (Standing on the Promises; Recovering the Lost Tools of Learning).

Reformed note Meredith Kline showed that Deuteronomy is structured like an ancient suzerain treaty, a covenant document between a great king and his vassal. Doug Wilson's long work for classical Christian education and household discipleship leans heavily on 6:6–7: "you shall teach them diligently to your children."

What the video covers (our summary)
  • Moses speaks to the new generation on the plains of Moab, explaining the Torah. The name means "second law," because many Sinai laws are repeated around a central law collection (12–26).
  • Moses retells the wilderness story and preaches covenant loyalty, centered on the Shema. "Hear" (shema) means listen and respond, and "love" means wholehearted devotion of will and emotion.
  • Obedience would make Israel a kingdom of priests, showing the nations God's wisdom and justice. Worshiping one God, the Creator and Redeemer, brings life, while Canaan's idols "degrade humans and destroy communities."
  • The laws cover worship tied to care for the poor (a tithe for the needy), leaders placed under the law and held accountable by prophets (unlike divine kings), and civil justice for widows, orphans and immigrants.
  • Reading tips: these are terms of the Sinai covenant for ancient Israel, so compare them with Assyria and Babylon rather than modern law, and look for the principle underneath (as Paul does with Deut 25:4 in 1 Cor 9:9).
  • "Choose life," but Moses expects Israel to rebel and go into exile. He promises that God will one day "circumcise your heart," the root of Jeremiah's and Ezekiel's new-heart hope.
  • The Torah closes with its big tensions unresolved: the seed of the woman, blessing for the nations, holiness with sinners, and new hearts.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject puts the new heart mainly in the future and in exile. Reformed readers agree that Deuteronomy 30:6 points to the new covenant (Rom 10:6–8), and add that regeneration was always God's gift to the faithful remnant (Rom 2:28–29; 4). The heart is circumcised by grace, not reached by effort.

title: Joshua
html:
Joshua

24 chapters

“Not one word of all the good promises that the Lord had made to the house of Israel had failed; all came to pass.” (Joshua 21:45, ESV)

Setting. Joshua tells how Israel entered and took the promised land under Moses' successor. It was written for Israel living in the land as a witness to God's faithfulness.

Where it fits. Conquest — The conquest and allotment of Canaan, c. 1406–1380 BC, in Egypt's Amarna age. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Entering the land (1–5): Joshua is commissioned, Rahab is spared, Israel crosses the Jordan, and the men are circumcised.
  2. Conquest (6–12): Jericho falls, Achan sins and Ai is defeated, the Gibeonites deceive Israel, and campaigns sweep south and north.
  3. Dividing the inheritance (13–21): The tribes receive their allotments, and cities of refuge are set apart.
  4. Covenant renewal (22–24): "Choose this day whom you will serve."
Main themes. God keeps his promises; holy war and judgment; faith versus compromise; rest in the land; covenant renewal.
Main characters. Joshua, Rahab, Caleb, Achan, the Gibeonites.
Key passages
  • 1:8–9 — be strong and courageous, meditate on the Book of the Law
  • 2 — Rahab and the scarlet cord
  • 5:13–15 — the commander of the Lord's army
  • 6 — Jericho
  • 7 — Achan's sin
  • 21:43–45 — every promise fulfilled
  • 24:15 — "choose this day whom you will serve"

How it points to Christ. "Joshua" and "Jesus" are the same name, meaning "the Lord saves." Joshua gave Israel only a partial rest, and Hebrews 4:8–10 points past him to the Sabbath rest Christ gives. Rahab, a Canaanite saved by faith, appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:5).

Going deeper. Joshua shows God keeping the land promise he made to Abraham. The conquest is hard reading. Reformed teachers generally treat it as a unique, limited act of divine judgment on long-ripened Canaanite sin (Gen 15:16), not a model for Christians to imitate. The church's warfare is now spiritual (2 Cor 10:3–5; Eph 6). Rahab, a Canaanite saved by faith and later listed in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:5; Heb 11:31), shows that the line between Israel and the nations was always about faith, not ethnicity. Hebrews 4:8 says Joshua's rest wasn't final, so a greater "Jesus" (the Greek form of Joshua) was still needed.

Reformed note The Reformed tradition presents the conquest as God's just judgment on Canaanite sin that had reached its full measure (Gen 15:16), not as ethnic aggression. Postmillennial readers like Doug Wilson see in it a picture of the gospel's advance, now carried out with word and sacrament rather than the sword (2 Cor 10:4–5).

BibleProject video: Joshua bibleproject.com/videos/joshua/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The book has four movements: entering the land (1–5), battles (6–12), dividing the land (13–22) and Joshua's farewell speeches (23–24).
  • Joshua is presented as a new Moses. He calls Israel to the Torah, sends spies (with a better result this time, as Rahab turns to Israel's God) and leads Israel across the parted Jordan behind the ark.
  • The commander of the Lord's army answers "Neither" when asked whose side he is on. The real question is whether Israel is on God's side, and the battle is God's.
  • Jericho and Ai are paired. At Jericho Israel trusts and waits and God brings the walls down. At Ai, Achan's theft brings defeat, showing that Israel gets no special treatment.
  • On the violence, BibleProject points to Canaanite corruption (Lev 18) and child sacrifice (Deut 12). It argues that phrases like "left no survivor" are ancient hyperbole (Hebron and Debir are still populated later), that "genocide" does not fit, that converts like Rahab and the Gibeonites were welcomed, and that Israel was to seek peace with all other nations (Deut 20).
  • The boundary lists, "a map with no pictures," mattered because they show God's promise to Abraham fulfilled in detail. Joshua's farewell leaves Israel with a choice.
A Reformed response to the video Many evangelical and Reformed scholars accept that conquest reports use stylized, hyperbolic language. Reformed readers add that the conquest was real judgment by the righteous Judge on sin that had "reached its full measure" (Gen 15:16). It also prefigures the final judgment, from which only those sheltered by God's mercy are spared, like Rahab under the scarlet cord.

title: Judges
html:
Judges

21 chapters

“In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did what was right in his own eyes.” (Judges 21:25, ESV)

Setting. Judges covers roughly the 300 years between Joshua and the monarchy. It was probably written early in the kingdom period to show why Israel needed a faithful king.

Where it fits. Judges — Overlapping judgeships from c. 1380 to c. 1050 BC. The Philistines arrive c. 1177 BC, during the Bronze Age collapse. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. A failed conquest (1:1–3:6): Israel compromises, and a cycle begins: sin, oppression, crying out, deliverance.
  2. The judges (3:7–16:31): Othniel, Ehud, Deborah and Barak, Gideon, Jephthah, and Samson. Each one is more flawed than the last.
  3. Total collapse (17–21): Idolatry in Micah's house, the Levite's concubine, and civil war against Benjamin.
Main themes. The downward cycle of sin; God's mercy in raising deliverers; Canaanization of Israel; the need for a king.
Main characters. Deborah, Barak, Gideon, Jephthah, Samson, Delilah.
Key passages
  • 2:11–19 — the cycle of sin, oppression, crying out, and deliverance
  • 4–5 — Deborah, Barak and Jael
  • 6–8 — Gideon
  • 13–16 — Samson
  • 17–21 — the moral collapse that closes the book, under the refrain "no king in Israel"

How it points to Christ. Every judge is a flawed and temporary savior. The book leaves us longing for a righteous King and Deliverer who doesn't fail, and Christ is that King.

Going deeper. Judges is a downward spiral. Each judge is more flawed than the last, and by the end Israel looks like Sodom (19, compare Gen 19). The refrain "everyone did what was right in his own eyes" diagnoses the problem as the human heart, not just poor leadership. Reformed readers see total depravity on display: left to themselves, even God's people decay. Yet God keeps raising deliverers out of sheer mercy. Hebrews 11:32 still lists Gideon, Barak, Samson and Jephthah among the faithful, which is a reminder that salvation is by grace and that God uses deeply imperfect people.

Reformed note Judges is a case study in human depravity, even among God's people. Hebrews 11:32 still counts Gideon, Barak, Samson, and Jephthah among the faithful, which shows that God saves weak people through faith and not through their merit.

BibleProject video: Judges bibleproject.com/videos/judges/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Judges tells how Israel failed completely after Joshua. The judges were regional military chieftains, not courtroom figures, and BibleProject warns that the book is disturbing by design.
  • The introduction (1–2) shows the tribes failing to drive out the Canaanites and adopting their gods. The narrator then previews a downward-spiral cycle: sin, oppression, crying out, a deliverer, peace, and sin again.
  • Othniel, Ehud and Deborah are bloody but heroic. Then the judges get worse. Gideon starts as a coward, wins with 300 men, then murders Israelites and makes an idol. Jephthah treats God like a Canaanite god and vows his daughter. Samson is "by far the worst."
  • God's Spirit empowers these flawed leaders, but that does not mean he approves of their choices. He is committed to saving his people and works with what he has.
  • In the final stories (Micah's idol and the Danites, the Levite's concubine and civil war), Israel as a whole hits bottom: "everyone did what was right in their own eyes."
  • The repeated line "Israel had no king" is the glimmer of hope, setting up Ruth (David's family) and 1 Samuel (the start of kingship). Israel needs to be delivered from itself.

In the final stories (Micah's idol and the Danites, the Levite's concubine and civil war), Israel as a whole hits bottom: "everyone did what was right in their own eyes." The repeated line "Israel had no king" is the glimmer of hope, setting up Ruth (David's family) and 1 Samuel (the start of kingship). Israel needs to be delivered from itself.

title: Ruth
html:
Ruth

4 chapters

“Your people shall be my people, and your God my God.” (Ruth 1:16, ESV)

Setting. Ruth is set "in the days when the judges ruled." It is a short story of faithfulness that ends with the genealogy of David, so it was probably written in the time of the monarchy.

Where it fits. Judges — Set "in the days when the judges ruled" (1:1), probably late in the period (c. 1100 BC †). Boaz is David's great-grandfather. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Emptiness (1): Naomi loses her husband and sons in Moab, and Ruth clings to her.
  2. Gleaning (2): Ruth "happens" to glean in Boaz's field.
  3. The threshing floor (3): Ruth asks Boaz to act as kinsman-redeemer.
  4. Redemption (4): Boaz redeems, Obed is born, and the line leads to David.
Main themes. Hesed (steadfast, loyal love); hidden providence; redemption; inclusion of a Gentile.
Main characters. Naomi, Ruth, Boaz.
Key passages
  • 1:16–17 — Ruth's vow to Naomi
  • 2 — Ruth gleans in Boaz's field "by chance"
  • 3 — the threshing floor and the request for redemption
  • 4 — Boaz redeems, and the genealogy ends with David

How it points to Christ. Boaz the kinsman-redeemer (go'el) pictures Christ, who took on our flesh to become our near kinsman and paid the price to redeem us (Gal 4:4–5). Ruth the Moabite is in Jesus' family line (Matt 1:5).

Going deeper. There are no miracles in Ruth, and that is the point. God's providence works through ordinary harvests, kindness and lawful process. The key word is hesed, steadfast covenant love, shown by Ruth to Naomi, by Boaz to Ruth, and by God through both. Boaz as kinsman-redeemer is a clear picture of Christ, who became our kin in order to redeem us (Heb 2:14–17). Ruth also shows that the nations come into Israel's blessing: a Moabite woman becomes David's great-grandmother.

Reformed note Ruth shows the Reformed doctrine of providence in narrative form: God governs even "chance" (2:3) for the good of his people and the coming of his King.

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Ruth bibleproject.com/videos/ruth/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Ruth is "a brilliant work of theological art" about how God is involved in ordinary joys and hardships. It has three characters: Naomi the widow, Ruth the Moabite and Boaz the farmer.
  • Chapter 1 is set "when the judges ruled." Famine, exile to Moab and three deaths leave Naomi empty. Ruth's loyalty ("your God my God") goes back with her, and Naomi renames herself Mara, "bitter."
  • It "just so happens" that Ruth gleans in Boaz's field. Boaz keeps the Torah's command to be generous to the immigrant and the poor. Naomi calls him a "family redeemer," a relative responsible to protect a dead man's widow and land.
  • At the threshing floor Ruth boldly asks Boaz to redeem the family. He calls her a "woman of noble character," the phrase used for the woman of Proverbs 31.
  • A nearer relative declines because marrying a Moabite is involved. Boaz redeems the land and marries Ruth, and their son reverses chapter 1's tragedy.
  • Each chapter follows the same pattern: a plan, a providential meeting, rejoicing. The narrator never says God acts directly, yet his providence weaves everything together through human loyalty and choice.
  • The genealogy shows that Obed is David's grandfather, so ordinary events become part of God's story of redemption.

title: 1 Samuel
html:
1 Samuel

31 chapters

“For the Lord sees not as man sees: man looks on the outward appearance, but the Lord looks on the heart.” (1 Samuel 16:7, ESV)

Setting. First Samuel tells how Israel moved from judges to kings, around 1100–1010 BC. Its author is unknown. 1 and 2 Samuel were originally one book.

Where it fits. United Monarchy — Samuel and Saul, c. 1105–1011 BC. The ark is lost and Shiloh falls. Israel gets a king. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Hannah and Samuel (1–7): A barren woman's prayer, Hannah's song, and Eli's corrupt house.
  2. Saul's rise (8–15): Israel demands a king "like the nations." Saul starts well and is then rejected for disobedience.
  3. David and Saul (16–31): David is anointed, defeats Goliath, is hunted by Saul, and spares Saul's life. Saul dies on Mount Gilboa.
Main themes. God opposes the proud and exalts the humble (Hannah's song, 2:1–10); obedience over sacrifice (15:22); God chooses the king; faithful waiting.
Main characters. Hannah, Eli, Samuel, Saul, Jonathan, David, Goliath, Abigail.
Key passages
  • 2:1–10 — Hannah's song (the Lord raises the poor, gives strength to his king)
  • 3 — the call of Samuel
  • 8 — Israel demands a king "like all the nations"
  • 15:22 — "to obey is better than sacrifice"
  • 16 — David anointed
  • 17 — David and Goliath
  • 24 and 26 — David spares Saul

How it points to Christ. Hannah's song speaks of the Lord's "anointed" (2:10), the first time that messianic title appears. David, the overlooked shepherd who defeats the giant for his people, foreshadows the Son of David who defeats our great enemy.

Going deeper. The contrast between Saul and David is the lesson. Saul is impressive on the outside but disobedient and quick to make excuses. David is overlooked but has a heart after God's, trusts God's timing, and refuses to seize the throne by violence. Reformed preachers warn against reading David and Goliath as mainly "how to face your giants." The main point is that God's anointed king fights for his helpless people and wins the victory they share, as Christ does. Hannah's song (2:10) is the first place in the Bible where the word for God's "anointed" (messiah) appears in connection with a king.

Reformed note Reformed readers stress God's sovereign choice: David was chosen by God's grace and not for his outward qualities (16:7). Saul's rejection teaches that God wants heart obedience more than religious ritual.

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: 1 Samuel bibleproject.com/videos/1-samuel/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • 1–2 Samuel is one story split by scroll length. It moves Israel from tribal judges to a united kingdom through three figures: Samuel, Saul and David.
  • Hannah's song (ch. 2) introduces the book's themes: God opposes the proud and lifts up the humble, works his purposes through human evil and will raise up an anointed king.
  • Israel uses the ark like a magic trophy, and God lets it be captured. He then defeats Dagon without an army. "God is not Israel's trophy."
  • Israel asks for a king "like all the nations." God grants it despite their motives. Saul is tall and promising but dishonest and unable to admit fault, and he disqualifies himself by disobedience.
  • David, the unlikely shepherd, is chosen for his humble trust, shown in his fight with Goliath. Saul falls into jealous madness, and David twice spares him and waits on God's timing. Many psalms come from this period.
  • BibleProject presents Saul and David as character studies: Saul a warning to deal with our dark side, David an example of patience and trust in God's timing.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject reads Saul and David mostly as character studies. Reformed readers welcome the moral lessons but stress that the story's main point is God's anointed king. David's trust and his sparing of his enemy foreshadow the greater Son of David. The aim is less "be like David" than "look for David's Lord."

title: 2 Samuel
html:
2 Samuel

24 chapters

“And your house and your kingdom shall be made sure forever before me. Your throne shall be established forever.” (2 Samuel 7:16, ESV)

Setting. Second Samuel covers David's forty-year reign. It is honest about both his greatness and his failures.

Where it fits. United Monarchy — David's 40-year reign, c. 1011–971 BC. Jerusalem is taken c. 1004 BC. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. David's rise (1–10): David becomes king over Judah and then all Israel, takes Jerusalem, and brings up the ark. God makes the Davidic covenant (7).
  2. David's fall (11–12): Adultery with Bathsheba, the murder of Uriah, and Nathan's rebuke: "You are the man!"
  3. Consequences (13–20): Amnon, Absalom's rebellion, and David's flight and grief.
  4. Epilogue (21–24): David's songs and the census and plague, ending at the site of the future temple.
Main themes. The Davidic covenant; sin and its consequences; repentance and forgiveness; kingship under God.
Main characters. David, Bathsheba, Nathan, Joab, Absalom, Mephibosheth.
Key passages
  • 5 — David captures Jerusalem
  • 6 — the ark comes to the city, and Uzzah dies
  • 7 — the Davidic covenant
  • 11–12 — Bathsheba, Uriah and Nathan's "You are the man!"
  • 13–18 — Absalom's rebellion
  • 22–23 — David's song and last words

How it points to Christ. The covenant in chapter 7 promises an eternal throne to David's son, and the New Testament proclaims Jesus as that Son (Luke 1:32–33; Acts 2:30). David's kindness to lame Mephibosheth (9) pictures grace to the undeserving.

Going deeper. The Davidic covenant (ch. 7) is one of the hinges of the whole Bible. God promises David an eternal house, throne and kingdom, and Psalm 2, Psalm 110, Isaiah 9 and Luke 1:32–33 all build on it. Then the king falls. Chapters 11–12 show that even the best human king needs a better King, and Psalm 51 shows true repentance. Sproul often used Uzzah (ch. 6) to show that God's holiness is not to be trifled with. Reformed covenant theology reads the Davidic covenant as a stage within the one covenant of grace, fulfilled in Christ's present reign at the Father's right hand (Acts 2:30–36). Postmillennial writers stress that this reign is active now and expanding.

Reformed note The Reformed tradition counts the Davidic covenant as one of the key administrations of the covenant of grace. Psalm 51, David's prayer after Nathan's rebuke, became a model of true repentance for Calvin and the Puritans.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • 2 Samuel tells David's reign in two movements, success and blessing (1–10) followed by moral failure and its consequences (11–20), and ends with a crafted epilogue (21–24).
  • David laments Saul, the man who tried to kill him. All the tribes make him king. He takes Jerusalem (Zion), wins battles and brings in the ark.
  • In 2 Samuel 7 David offers to build God a house, and God promises to build David a house: a dynasty, a future king who will build God's temple and reign forever. BibleProject calls this a key chapter for the whole Bible, later tied to the Abraham promise to bless the nations.
  • David takes Bathsheba and has Uriah killed. Confronted by Nathan, he repents and is forgiven, but the consequences remain: Amnon and Tamar, Absalom's murder of Amnon and Absalom's rebellion. David flees again, "this time… not an innocent man."

  • The book's hope reaches beyond David to the Messiah who will bring God's kingdom to the nations.

title: 1 Kings
html:
1 Kings

22 chapters

“How long will you go limping between two different opinions? If the Lord is God, follow him.” (1 Kings 18:21, ESV)

Setting. Kings was originally one book, written during the exile to explain why Israel and Judah fell. First Kings runs from Solomon (about 970 BC) to Ahab's era.

Where it fits. United → Divided Kingdom — From Solomon (c. 971–931 BC) and the temple (966 BC) to Ahab and Elijah (c. 853 BC). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Solomon's glory (1–10): Wisdom, the temple, and the Queen of Sheba.
  2. Solomon's fall (11): Many wives and their idols.
  3. The divided kingdom (12–16): Rehoboam and Jeroboam. Jeroboam's golden calves set the north on a path of idolatry.
  4. Elijah versus Ahab (17–22): The drought, Mount Carmel, the still small voice, and Naboth's vineyard.
Main themes. Covenant faithfulness determines blessing or exile; wisdom and its corruption; idolatry; the prophetic word always comes true.
Main characters. Solomon, Rehoboam, Jeroboam, Ahab, Jezebel, Elijah, the widow of Zarephath.
Key passages
  • 3 — Solomon asks for wisdom
  • 8 — the temple dedication prayer
  • 11 — Solomon's heart turned by many wives
  • 12 — the kingdom divided
  • 17–19 — Elijah, the widow, Mount Carmel and the still small voice
  • 21 — Naboth's vineyard

How it points to Christ. Jesus is "greater than Solomon" (Matt 12:42) and the true temple (John 2:19–21). Elijah prepares for John the Baptist (Mal 4:5; Matt 11:14).

Going deeper. 1 Kings shows how quickly glory can turn to ruin. Solomon breaks, one by one, the king's laws in Deuteronomy 17 (horses, wives, gold), and the kingdom splits under his son. The writer judges every king by one standard: covenant loyalty to the Lord and rejection of idols. At Carmel, Elijah's challenge ("If the Lord is God, follow him") is still the call to every generation that wants to keep both God and its idols. Jesus as "something greater than Solomon" (Matt 12:42) is the wise king who builds the true temple, his people (Eph 2:19–22).

Reformed note Kings shows God's sovereignty over history: every prophecy comes to pass, and even wicked kings serve his purposes. This is the Reformed doctrine of providence on a national scale.

title: 2 Kings
html:
2 Kings

25 chapters

“Before him there was no king like him, who turned to the Lord with all his heart and with all his soul and with all his might.” (2 Kings 23:25, ESV)

Setting. Second Kings continues the story from Elijah's departure to Jerusalem's fall in 586 BC. It explains the exile to the people living through it.

Where it fits. Divided Kingdom → Exile — From Elisha (c. 850 BC) through the fall of Samaria (722) and Jerusalem (586) to Jehoiachin's release (562 BC). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Elisha's ministry (1–8): Miracles of life and provision.
  2. The northern kingdom falls (9–17): Jehu's purge, decline, and Assyria's conquest in 722 BC. Chapter 17 explains why.
  3. Judah's final years (18–25): Hezekiah's faith, Manasseh's evil, Josiah's reform, and Babylon's destruction of Jerusalem.
Main themes. Judgment for persistent covenant-breaking; reform and relapse; God's patience; hope for David's line.
Main characters. Elisha, Naaman, Jehu, Hezekiah, Isaiah, Manasseh, Josiah, Nebuchadnezzar.
Key passages
  • 2 — Elijah taken up and Elisha's double portion
  • 5 — Naaman healed
  • 17 — the fall of Samaria, with the reasons given
  • 18–19 — Hezekiah and the Assyrian siege
  • 22–23 — Josiah finds the Book of the Law
  • 25 — Jerusalem falls and Jehoiachin is released

How it points to Christ. The book ends with David's heir, Jehoiachin, released from prison and eating at the king's table (25:27–30). It is a small sign that God hasn't forgotten his promise of a Son of David. Elisha's ministry of healing, cleansing a Gentile, and feeding many anticipates Jesus' miracles (Luke 4:27).

Going deeper. 2 Kings is a theological account of why the exile happened. Chapter 17 says it plainly: Israel "feared other gods" and refused the prophets. Sin has consequences for whole nations, not just for individuals, a theme Wilson often presses when he writes about cultural decline. Even the best reform (Josiah) can't reverse the judgment, because the people's heart needs a deeper cure. The book ends on a quiet note of hope. David's heir is released from prison and eats at the king's table (25:27–30). The line survives, waiting for its true King.

Reformed note Even Josiah's wholehearted reform couldn't change the people's hearts. The Reformed tradition reads this as the law's inability to produce new hearts, which drives the story toward the New Covenant (Jer 31; Ezek 36).

title: 1 Chronicles
html:
1 Chronicles

29 chapters

“Yours, O Lord, is the greatness and the power and the glory and the victory and the majesty.” (1 Chronicles 29:11, ESV)

Setting. Chronicles was written after the exile, traditionally by Ezra, for returnees rebuilding life around the temple. It retells Israel's history with a focus on David, worship, and hope.

Where it fits. United Monarchy (written after the Return) — Genealogies from Adam, then David's reign (c. 1011–971 BC). Compiled for the returned community, c. 450–400 BC. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Genealogies from Adam to the return (1–9): God's people are tied to the whole human story.
  2. David's reign (10–29): Saul's death is told briefly, the ark comes to Jerusalem, God makes the Davidic covenant, and David prepares for the temple and organizes worship.
Main themes. Continuity of God's people; true worship; the Davidic king and the temple; God's sovereignty over history.
Main characters. David, Solomon, Levites and singers.
Key passages
  • 1–9 — genealogies from Adam to the returned exiles
  • 11–12 — David made king by all Israel
  • 16 — the ark comes to Jerusalem and David's psalm of thanks
  • 17 — the Davidic covenant retold
  • 22–29 — David prepares for the temple
  • 29:10–19 — David's prayer

How it points to Christ. Chronicles keeps Israel looking for a Son of David who will build God's house and reign forever (17:11–14). Jesus is that Son, and he builds his church as God's temple.

Going deeper. Chronicles retells Israel's history for the community that returned from exile, and it does so with a purpose. It skips David's sin with Bathsheba, not to hide it (Samuel had already told it) but to present David as a model of worship and as a pattern for the coming Messiah. The genealogies, starting with Adam, tell the returnees that they belong to God's story for all humanity. Chronicles is the last book of the Hebrew Bible, so it is fitting that its focus is worship ordered by God's word, a theme the Reformed "regulative principle" of worship takes seriously.

Reformed note The genealogies remind Reformed readers that God saves a covenant people across generations. Here covenantal Baptists and Presbyterians draw different conclusions about the children of believers, but they agree on God's faithfulness across generations.
Reading BibleProject well BibleProject's Chronicles video (one video for both books) notes that Chronicles comes last in the Hebrew order of the Old Testament, so the Hebrew Bible ends with an invitation to "go up" to Jerusalem. That's a helpful observation.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • Originally one book, split in two because of scroll length. It overlaps heavily with Samuel and Kings, so readers often skip it, but it has its own message. In the Jewish ordering it is the last book of the Bible. It begins with "Adam" and ends with the return from exile.
  • The anonymous author wrote a couple of centuries after the return, when the hopes of a rebuilt temple, God dwelling with his people, the Messiah and the nations at peace had not come true. He retells the past to give hope, with two themes: a coming messianic king and a new temple.
  • 1 Chronicles 1–9: genealogies that sum up the whole Old Testament story, highlighting two lines: Judah to David and on to the author's day, and the priestly line of Aaron.
  • 1 Chronicles 10–29: David's story without Saul's pursuit or the Bathsheba affair. New material shows David preparing for the temple (materials, builders, Levites, choirs) and receiving its plans from God, as Moses received the tabernacle's. The aim is not to hide his flaws but to present an ideal David as a type of the coming Messiah.
  • 1 Chronicles 17, compared with 2 Samuel 7, makes clear that neither David nor Solomon nor any later king was the promised one. The Messiah is still to come.
  • 2 Chronicles: only Judah's Davidic kings. New stories show faithful kings blessed and unfaithful kings bringing disaster, leading to an exile of Judah's own making. These are character studies for later generations.
  • The ending: Cyrus lets the exiles return. The last line, "Let him go up," is left hanging. The author's hope looks past Ezra and Nehemiah to another return, when the Messiah rebuilds the temple. The Old Testament ends as "a story in search of an ending."
A Reformed response to the video The video's emphasis on an idealized David fits much of the book. Note, though, that the Chronicler does include David's sinful census and the plague (1 Chr 21), and that is how he leads into the temple site. Even the ideal king needs atonement. The "search for an ending" is answered in the New Testament, which opens with a genealogy that starts with Abraham and David (Matt 1:1). Jesus, the true Son of David, rebuilds the temple in himself and his people (John 2:19–21; 1 Pet 2:5). The Chronicler's pattern of reform, repentance and blessing (2 Chr 7:14) has also encouraged Reformed hopes for revival and the reformation of nations.

title: 2 Chronicles
html:
2 Chronicles

36 chapters

“If my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven.” (2 Chronicles 7:14, ESV)

Setting. Second Chronicles continues the post-exilic retelling from Solomon to the decree of Cyrus (538 BC). It focuses on Judah and David's line.

Where it fits. United → Exile (written after the Return) — From Solomon to Cyrus' decree (538 BC), told from Judah's side. Compiled c. 450–400 BC. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Solomon and the temple (1–9): God's glory fills the house.
  2. The kings of Judah (10–36): The book is organized around reform and revival (Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah) and around apostasy. Those who seek the Lord are blessed. It ends with exile and Cyrus's decree to rebuild.
Main themes. Seeking the Lord; humility and repentance; temple worship; immediate consequences of faithfulness and unfaithfulness.
Main characters. Solomon, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Manasseh (who repents), Josiah, Cyrus.
Key passages
  • 1–9 — Solomon and the temple
  • 7:14 — "if my people… humble themselves"
  • 20 — Jehoshaphat's prayer and the battle won by singing
  • 29–31 — Hezekiah's Passover
  • 33 — Manasseh's repentance
  • 36:22–23 — Cyrus: "let him go up"

How it points to Christ. Christ is the greater Solomon and the true temple. The final word, "let him go up" (36:23), invites God's people home, and Christ completes that homecoming.

Going deeper. The central message of 2 Chronicles is that seeking the Lord brings blessing and forsaking him brings ruin, and that repentance is always welcome. Manasseh, the worst king of all, humbles himself and is restored (33:12–13), a striking picture of grace. 7:14 is often applied directly to modern nations. Carefully understood, it was spoken to Israel about the temple, and its principle reaches the church as God's people now. The Hebrew Bible ends with Cyrus's decree, "let him go up," so the whole Old Testament closes facing forward, waiting for the return of the King.

Reformed note Manasseh's repentance (33:12–13) shows sovereign grace to the worst of sinners. Note that 7:14 was given to Israel as a covenant nation. Christians apply it through Christ and his church rather than directly to a modern nation.

text: 2 Chronicles 36 chapters “If my people who are called by my name humble themselves, and pray and seek my face and turn from their wicked ways, then I will hear from heaven.” (2 Chronicles 7:14, ESV) Setting. Second Chronicles continues the post-exilic retelling from Solomon to the decree of Cyrus (538 BC). It focuses on Judah and David's line. Where it fits. United → Exile (written after the Return) — From Solomon to Cyrus' decree (538 BC), told from Judah's side. Compiled c. 450–400 BC. ( Timelines ) The Flow of the Book Solomon and the temple (1–9) : God's glory fills the house. The kings of Judah (10–36) : The book is organized around reform and revival (Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Josiah) and around apostasy. Those who seek the Lord are blessed. It ends with exile and Cyrus's decree to rebuild. Main themes. Seeking the Lord ; humility and repentance; temple worship; immediate consequences of faithfulness and unfaithfulness. Main characters. Solomon, Asa, Jehoshaphat, Hezekiah, Manasseh (who repents), Josiah, Cyrus. Key passages 1–9 — Solomon and the temple 7:14 — "if my people… humble themselves" 20 — Jehoshaphat's prayer and the battle won by singing 29–31 — Hezekiah's Passover 33 — Manasseh's repentance 36:22–23 — Cyrus: "let him go up" How it points to Christ. Christ is the greater Solomon and the true temple. The final word, "let him go up" (36:23), invites God's people home, and Christ completes that homecoming. Going deeper. The central message of 2 Chronicles is that seeking the Lord brings blessing and forsaking him brings ruin, and that repentance is always welcome. Manasseh, the worst king of all, humbles himself and is restored (33:12–13), a striking picture of grace. 7:14 is often applied directly to modern nations. Carefully understood, it was spoken to Israel about the temple, and its principle reaches the church as God's people now. The Hebrew Bible ends with Cyrus's decree, "let him go up," so the whole Old Testament closes facing forward, waiting for the return of the King. Reformed note Manasseh's repentance (33:12–13) shows sovereign grace to the worst of sinners. Note that 7:14 was given to Israel as a covenant nation. Christians apply it through Christ and his church rather than directly to a modern nation. title: Ezra
html:
Ezra

10 chapters

“For Ezra had set his heart to study the Law of the Lord, and to do it and to teach his statutes and rules in Israel.” (Ezra 7:10, ESV)

Setting. Ezra and Nehemiah were one book in Hebrew. Ezra covers two returns from Babylon: Zerubbabel's in 538 BC, which rebuilt the temple, and Ezra's in 458 BC, which reformed the community around the Torah.

Where it fits. Return — From the first return (538 BC) and the second temple (516/515 BC) to Ezra's mission (458 BC). Persian period. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Return and rebuilding (1–6): Cyrus's decree, the altar and foundation, opposition, and the temple finished with help from Haggai and Zechariah.
  2. Ezra's reform (7–10): Ezra arrives, teaches the law, and confronts intermarriage with idolaters.
Main themes. God moves pagan kings to fulfill his word; rebuilding worship; the Word of God at the center; repentance and purity.
Main characters. Cyrus, Zerubbabel, Jeshua the priest, Ezra.
Key passages
  • 1 — Cyrus's decree
  • 3 — the altar and the temple foundation, with weeping and shouting
  • 4–6 — opposition and the completion of the temple
  • 7:10 — Ezra sets his heart to study, do and teach
  • 9–10 — Ezra's prayer of confession and the problem of intermarriage

How it points to Christ. The rebuilt temple was modest (3:12), so it left Israel waiting for the greater glory Haggai promised. That glory came when Christ, the true temple, entered it.

Going deeper. Ezra shows God moving the heart of a pagan emperor to keep his promise (1:1, Prov 21:1). That is sovereignty at work through ordinary politics. Ezra himself is a model for every Christian teacher: study the word, do it, then teach it, in that order. The intermarriage crisis troubles modern readers. The issue was idolatry, not ethnicity (compare Ruth and Rahab), and it threatened the survival of the people through whom the Messiah would come (Mal 2:11, 15).

Reformed note Ezra's pattern of study, practice, and teaching (7:10) is a classic Reformed model for ministers. The decree of a pagan king (1:1) shows God "stirring up" hearts in fulfillment of prophecy (Prov 21:1).

BibleProject video: Ezra-Nehemiah bibleproject.com/videos/ezra-nehemiah/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Ezra-Nehemiah was originally one book. It has three parallel parts (Zerubbabel and the temple, Ezra and the Torah, Nehemiah and the walls), and each follows the same pattern: a Persian king sends the leader with God's prompting, opposition is overcome, and the ending is "a strange anticlimax."
  • Cyrus's decree fulfills Jeremiah and raises hopes for a Davidic king, a glorious temple and the nations' blessing. But when the second temple is dedicated, no fiery cloud descends and the old men weep. Zerubbabel's refusal of help ("you have no part") sits uneasily with the prophets' vision of all the tribes and nations gathered.
  • Ezra, a Torah scholar, finds that returnees have married locals. He prays a heartfelt confession, but the divorce decree is driven by the leaders and only partly carried out. BibleProject points out that God never commanded it and that Malachi says God hates divorce.
  • Nehemiah rebuilds the walls with courage and integrity, under armed guard. But Zechariah pictured a Jerusalem without walls, open to the nations, which leads BibleProject to ask whether the conflict could have been handled differently.
  • There is a high point when the Torah is read for seven days, the Feast of Tabernacles is celebrated, sins are confessed and the covenant renewed. In chapter 13 everything has unraveled: the temple is neglected, the Sabbath broken and mixed marriages are back, and Nehemiah ends up pulling out hair.
  • The point is that being back in the land has not changed hearts. The book shows the need Jeremiah and Ezekiel identified, the transformation of the heart.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject is openly critical of Ezra's marriage reform and Nehemiah's walls. Many Reformed and conservative commentators read both more positively, as costly covenant faithfulness at a time when intermarriage meant importing idolatry (Mal 2:11; Neh 13:26 cites Solomon). They agree with BibleProject that the book ends showing that reform without regeneration cannot last.

title: Nehemiah
html:
Nehemiah

13 chapters

“For the joy of the Lord is your strength.” (Nehemiah 8:10, ESV)

Setting. Nehemiah's memoir (around 445 BC) tells how a Persian court official returned to rebuild Jerusalem's walls and renew the covenant.

Where it fits. Return — Nehemiah rebuilds the walls in 445 BC and returns for a second term c. 432 BC, under Artaxerxes I, in Pericles' day. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Rebuilding the walls (1–7): Prayer, permission, opposition from Sanballat and Tobiah, and the walls done in 52 days.
  2. Covenant renewal (8–10): Ezra reads the law publicly, the people confess sin, and they sign a covenant.
  3. Repopulating and backsliding (11–13): Jerusalem is dedicated, but the people quickly compromise again.
Main themes. Prayer and action together; public reading of Scripture; opposition; covenant renewal and quick relapse.
Main characters. Nehemiah, Ezra, Sanballat, Tobiah, Artaxerxes.
Key passages
  • 1 — Nehemiah's prayer
  • 2 — the request to the king
  • 4–6 — building with a sword in one hand
  • 8 — the public reading of the Law and "the joy of the Lord is your strength"
  • 9 — the great prayer of confession retelling Israel's history
  • 13 — Nehemiah's final reforms

How it points to Christ. The book ends in disappointment (13): even a godly reformer can't change hearts. Israel was left waiting for the Messiah, who rebuilds God's people from within.

Going deeper. Nehemiah combines prayer and planning, trusting God while posting guards. It is a fine study in godly leadership. Chapter 8 is a model of Reformed worship: the word read publicly, explained so that people understand (8:8), and answered with confession and joy. The anticlimax of chapter 13, where the people slide back into the same sins, shows that walls, reforms and covenants can't change hearts. That makes the reader long for the new covenant.

Reformed note Reformed churches have long read chapter 8 as a picture of preaching: the Word is read clearly, and its sense is explained so the people understand (8:8).

title: Esther
html:
Esther

10 chapters

“And who knows whether you have not come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14, ESV)

Setting. Esther is set in Persia under Xerxes (Ahasuerus) around 480 BC among Jews who stayed in exile. God is never named in the book, but he is at work everywhere in it.

Where it fits. Exile / Persian period — Set in Susa under Xerxes I, c. 483–473 BC, around his failed invasion of Greece (480–479 BC). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Esther becomes queen (1–2): Vashti is deposed, Esther is chosen, and Mordecai uncovers a plot.
  2. Haman's plot (3–4): Mordecai won't bow, and Haman decrees genocide.
  3. Reversal (5–10): Esther's banquets, the sleepless king, Haman hanged on his own gallows, the Jews delivered, and Purim established.
Main themes. Hidden providence; reversal (the proud brought low); courage; preservation of the covenant people.
Main characters. Esther, Mordecai, Ahasuerus, Haman.
Key passages
  • 3 — Haman's plot
  • 4:14 — "for such a time as this"
  • 5–7 — the banquets and Haman's fall
  • 6 — the king's sleepless night
  • 8–9 — the reversal and the feast of Purim

How it points to Christ. God preserves the people through whom the Messiah will come. Esther risks death to intercede for her people, a faint picture of Christ, who didn't just risk death but died to save his own.

Going deeper. God's name never appears in Esther, yet his hand is on every page: a sleepless king, a timely reading of the records, a gallows that turns back on the man who built it. Reformed teachers treat it as the Bible's great textbook on providence. God works through "coincidences" without suspending human choices (WCF 5.2–3). The theme of reversal (9:1) points forward to the cross, where the enemy's greatest apparent victory became his defeat (Col 2:15).

Reformed note Esther may be the Bible's best illustration of the Reformed doctrine of providence: God governs all things, including sleepless nights and "coincidences," without suspending human choices.

title: Wisdom & Poetry
html:
Part

Wisdom & Poetry

These books show how to live wisely in God's world: how to fear him, praise him, suffer before him, enjoy his gifts, and love well.

Job · Psalms · Proverbs · Ecclesiastes · Song of Songs

title: Job
html:
Job

42 chapters

“For I know that my Redeemer lives, and at the last he will stand upon the earth.” (Job 19:25, ESV)

Setting. Job is set in the patriarchal era in the land of Uz. Its author and date are unknown. It is a masterpiece of poetry about the suffering of a righteous man.

Where it fits. Patriarchs? (setting) — No date is given. The setting looks patriarchal: wealth counted in herds, Job as his family's priest, and no mention of the Law. The date of writing is unknown. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Prologue (1–2): A heavenly scene. Satan is permitted to test Job, who loses everything.
  2. Dialogues (3–37): Job's three friends argue he must have sinned, Job protests his innocence and demands a hearing, and Elihu speaks.
  3. The Lord speaks (38–41): God answers from the whirlwind with a tour of creation, not with an explanation.
  4. Epilogue (42): Job repents in dust and ashes, the friends are rebuked, and Job is restored.
Main themes. Suffering and God's justice; the limits of human wisdom; bad theology from good friends; God's sovereignty over Satan and chaos; faith that holds on through pain.
Main characters. Job, Job's wife, Eliphaz, Bildad, Zophar, Elihu, Satan ("the accuser").
Key passages
  • 1–2 — the heavenly court and Job's losses
  • 1:21 — "the Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away"
  • 19:25–27 — "I know that my Redeemer lives"
  • 28 — the poem on where wisdom is found
  • 38–41 — the Lord speaks from the whirlwind
  • 42:1–6 — Job repents in dust and ashes

How it points to Christ. Job longs for a Redeemer and a mediator to stand between him and God (9:33; 19:25). Christ is that mediator and truly innocent sufferer, and he is vindicated in resurrection.

Going deeper. Job dismantles the neat formula that suffering always matches sin, which was the error of Job's friends. It does this without making God any less sovereign. The accuser can do nothing without permission, and Job himself sees God's hand behind it all (1:21; 2:10). Carson's How Long, O Lord? is a good companion. God doesn't give Job reasons. He gives Job himself, and that is enough. Job longs for a mediator (9:33) and a living Redeemer (19:25), and the New Testament shows him in Jesus, the righteous sufferer who was truly innocent.

Reading BibleProject well BibleProject rightly stresses that God doesn't explain Job's suffering. Reformed readers would add that the prologue does show the reader that suffering serves God's purposes and glory, so it is mysterious but never meaningless.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • The setting is Uz, the hero is not an Israelite, and the period is unspecified, so that we focus on the questions suffering raises. A prose prologue and epilogue frame dense poetry.

title: Psalms
html:
Psalms

150 psalms

“The Lord says to my Lord: "Sit at my right hand, until I make your enemies your footstool."” (Psalm 110:1, ESV)

Setting. The Psalms are Israel's prayer and hymn book, written over roughly 1,000 years by David, Asaph, the sons of Korah, Moses, and others. They were arranged in five books after the exile.

Where it fits. United Monarchy → Return — Mostly David's era (c. 1011–971 BC), with Psalm 90 (Moses) and exilic psalms such as Psalm 137. Collected in its final form after the Return. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Gateway (1–2): The blessed man who delights in Torah, and the Messiah King whom the nations must "kiss."
  2. Book I (3–41) and Book II (42–72): Mostly Davidic. Lament turns to trust.
  3. Book III (73–89): The crisis of exile. The Davidic covenant seems to have failed (Ps 89).
  4. Book IV (90–106): "The Lord reigns!" God is king even when the king is gone.
  5. Book V (107–150): Return, the Songs of Ascents, Torah (119), and a final cascade of praise ending in "Hallelujah."
Main themes. Praise and lament; Torah meditation; the messianic King; the reign of God; trust in suffering; judgment on the wicked.
Main characters. David, Asaph, the sons of Korah, Moses (Ps 90), Solomon.
Key passages
  • 1–2 — the gateway (the righteous and the Messiah)
  • 22 — "My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?"
  • 23 — the Lord my shepherd
  • 51 — David's confession
  • 73 — the prosperity of the wicked and the sanctuary
  • 110 — the priest-king at God's right hand
  • 119 — the Torah alphabet poem
  • 150 — let everything praise the Lord

How it points to Christ. The New Testament quotes the Psalms more than any other Old Testament book. Psalm 2, 22, 110, and 118 are fulfilled in Christ's sonship, his crucifixion, his ascension, and his rejection and exaltation. Psalm 110 is the Old Testament text the New Testament quotes most.

Going deeper. Calvin called the Psalms "an anatomy of all the parts of the soul": every human emotion is here, brought before God. The Psalms are the prayer book of Jesus. He prays Psalm 22 and Psalm 31 on the cross, and the New Testament quotes Psalms 2 and 110 more than almost any other Old Testament texts to show that he is the enthroned King. Reformed churches have a long tradition of singing the Psalms, from the Genevan Psalter to the Scottish metrical psalms. Wilson is among those who have defended praying and singing even the hard imprecatory psalms. Read as Christ's prayers against his unrepentant enemies, those psalms teach the church to long for justice and to leave vengeance to God.

Reformed note Calvin called the Psalms "an anatomy of all the parts of the soul." Doug Wilson and his church community have urged believers to recover singing the whole Psalter, imprecatory psalms included, as prayers for Christ's victory over his enemies. Psalm 110's picture of Christ reigning "until" his enemies are subdued is a key text for postmillennial hope.

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Psalms bibleproject.com/videos/psalms/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • 150 poems from many periods: 73 linked to David, along with Asaph, the sons of Korah, Solomon and Moses, and about a third anonymous. They were arranged after the exile into a deliberately designed book, "not a hymn book."
  • Its structure: a five-hallelujah conclusion (146–150), five books marked by doxologies, and an introduction (Psalms 1–2).
  • Psalm 1: blessed is the one who meditates on Torah, and the five books form a "new Torah" of prayer. Psalm 2: God's promise to David of a Messiah who rules the nations, "Blessed are all who take refuge in him." Torah and Messiah are the two themes.
  • Book 1 centers on Psalm 19 (Torah) between David the faithful king (16–18) and the future king (20–23). Book 2 ends with Psalm 72, the king blessing all nations as promised to Abraham. Book 3 ends with Psalm 89, the Davidic promise seemingly broken in exile. Book 4 answers with Moses' prayer (90) and "The Lord reigns" (93–99). Book 5 has the Hallel, the Songs of Ascents and Psalm 119, the Torah alphabet poem, and hopes for a new exodus. Psalm 148: God "has raised up a horn for his people."
  • Laments dominate Books 1–3 and praise grows in Books 4–5: lament is a fitting response to evil, and faith looks forward. "Torah and messiah, lament and praise, faith and hope."

title: Proverbs
html:
Proverbs

31 chapters

“The fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge; fools despise wisdom and instruction.” (Proverbs 1:7, ESV)

Setting. Proverbs is mostly Solomon's work, with collections from "the wise," Agur, and King Lemuel. It was compiled in the monarchy and later (25:1) to train young people in godly skill for living.

Where it fits. United Monarchy — Mostly Solomon (c. 971–931 BC). Hezekiah's men copied out chapters 25–29 (c. 700 BC). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. A father's speeches (1–9): Two ways, two women (Lady Wisdom and Folly), and the call to choose wisdom.
  2. Solomon's proverbs (10–22:16): Short sayings on speech, work, money, family, and justice.
  3. Other collections (22:17–30): The sayings of the wise, Hezekiah's collection, and Agur.
  4. The valiant woman (31): Lemuel's mother's counsel and the acrostic poem of the woman of strength.
Main themes. The fear of the Lord; wisdom versus folly; speech; work and diligence; family; justice and generosity.
Main characters. Solomon, Lady Wisdom, Lady Folly, the son, the woman of valor.
Key passages
  • 1:7 — the fear of the Lord is the beginning of knowledge
  • 3:5–6 — trust in the Lord with all your heart
  • 8 — wisdom present at creation
  • 9 — Lady Wisdom and Folly's two invitations
  • 22:6 — train up a child
  • 31:10–31 — the excellent wife

How it points to Christ. Christ is the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24, 30), and in him "are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 2:3). Proverbs 8's picture of Wisdom at creation echoes in John 1 and Colossians 1.

Going deeper. Proverbs teaches that God's world has a moral grain. Wisdom runs with it and folly runs against it, and in the end the grain wins. This is the doctrine of creation applied to daily life: work, speech, money, sex, friendship and politics. Frame's emphasis that all of life is lived before the Lord fits Proverbs well, because it refuses any divide between "sacred" and "secular." Christ is the wisdom of God (1 Cor 1:24) "in whom are hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge" (Col 2:3). Following Proverbs is ultimately about being joined to him.

Reformed note John Frame grounds all true knowledge in the fear of the Lord, using Proverbs 1:7 as a foundation for a Christian theory of knowledge. Doug Wilson's writing on households, money, and manhood draws a great deal from Proverbs.
Recommended free Reformed commentaries: Proverbs

  • Surveying the Text: Proverbs — Douglas Wilson. Wilson's one-sermon panorama of the whole book: its structure, themes, and Christ, with postmillennial and covenantal punch.dougwils.com/the-church/s8-expository/surveying-the-text-proverbs.html

  • TGC Bible Commentary: Proverbs — Ivan De Silva (TGC Bible Commentary). A free, modern, section-by-section commentary in TGC's Reformed-evangelical stream, with good help on biblical theology.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/proverbs/
More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Proverbs bibleproject.com/videos/proverbs/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The book is linked to Solomon (1 Kings 3–4), the source of Israel's wisdom tradition, though not every part is his. Wisdom (khokhmah) is skill, applied knowledge, the word used of the craftsmen in Exodus 31.
  • "The fear of the Lord" is reverence, not terror: recognizing that I am not God and don't define good and evil myself.
  • Chapters 1–9: ten speeches from a father to his son, along with four poems by Lady Wisdom, who is woven into the fabric of creation, so living wisely is living "along the grain of the universe." Wisdom literature is the accumulated insight of God's people, gathered "as God's word."
  • Chapters 10–29: hundreds of sayings about family, work, money, sex, anger, alcohol and debt. Proverbs deal in probabilities, not promises. They state the general rule, while Job and Ecclesiastes explore the exceptions ("Train up a child…").
  • Chapter 30: Agur confesses his ignorance and finds wisdom in God's word, a model reader. Chapter 31: King Lemuel's mother, and the acrostic poem of the "excellent wife" who puts wisdom into practice at home and in the community. The book opens with a father and closes with a mother.
A Reformed response to the video Reformed and Wilson-style readers agree that individual proverbs are not mechanical formulas. Wilson (Standing on the Promises) still presses the covenant promises God makes to faithful households more firmly than the "probabilities" framing suggests. The New Testament also identifies Christ as "the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24, 30; Col 2:3), so Lady Wisdom ultimately points to him.

What the video covers (our summary) The book is linked to Solomon (1 Kings 3–4), the source of Israel's wisdom tradition, though not every part is his. Wisdom (khokhmah) is skill, applied knowledge, the word used of the craftsmen in Exodus 31. "The fear of the Lord " is reverence, not terror: recognizing that I am not God and don't define good and evil myself. Chapters 1–9: ten speeches from a father to his son, along with four poems by Lady Wisdom, who is woven into the fabric of creation, so living wisely is living "along the grain of the universe." Wisdom literature is the accumulated insight of God's people, gathered "as God's word." Chapters 10–29: hundreds of sayings about family, work, money, sex, anger, alcohol and debt. Proverbs deal in probabilities, not promises. They state the general rule, while Job and Ecclesiastes explore the exceptions ("Train up a child…"). Chapter 30: Agur confesses his ignorance and finds wisdom in God's word, a model reader. Chapter 31: King Lemuel's mother, and the acrostic poem of the "excellent wife" who puts wisdom into practice at home and in the community. The book opens with a father and closes with a mother. A Reformed response to the video Reformed and Wilson-style readers agree that individual proverbs are not mechanical formulas. Wilson ( Standing on the Promises ) still presses the covenant promises God makes to faithful households more firmly than the "probabilities" framing suggests. The New Testament also identifies Christ as "the wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24, 30; Col 2:3), so Lady Wisdom ultimately points to him.

title: Ecclesiastes
html:
Ecclesiastes

12 chapters

“Fear God and keep his commandments, for this is the whole duty of man.” (Ecclesiastes 12:13, ESV)

Setting. Ecclesiastes is the reflection of "the Preacher" (Qoheleth), son of David, traditionally Solomon. It looks at life "under the sun."

Where it fits. United Monarchy — Traditionally Solomon in his later years (c. 940 BC). Many scholars date it later. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Prologue (1:1–11): "Vanity of vanities." Everything is hevel: vapor, breath.
  2. The Preacher's experiments (1:12–6:9): Pleasure, work, wisdom, wealth. None of it lasts or satisfies.
  3. Wisdom for an uncertain world (6:10–12:7): Death comes for all, so enjoy God's gifts now and remember your Creator in youth.
  4. Epilogue (12:8–14): Fear God, keep his commandments, and expect judgment.
Main themes. The fleeting nature of life; the limits of wisdom; death; enjoying God's gifts as a gift; the fear of God.
Main characters. The Preacher (Qoheleth).
Key passages
  • 1:2 — "vanity of vanities"
  • 2 — the experiment with pleasure, building and wealth
  • 3:1–11 — a time for everything and eternity in the heart
  • 5:18–20 and 9:7–10 — enjoy your food and work as God's gift
  • 12:1–8 — remember your Creator before old age
  • 12:13–14 — fear God and keep his commandments

How it points to Christ. Creation was "subjected to futility" (Rom 8:20), the same idea as Ecclesiastes' vapor. In Christ, our labor is "not in vain" (1 Cor 15:58), because his resurrection redeems life under the sun.

Going deeper. Ecclesiastes is the Bible's honest look at life "under the sun," life seen without reference to God's revelation and coming judgment. It undercuts every idol that promises lasting meaning. It is not nihilistic. Again and again it tells us to receive food, work and marriage as gifts from God's hand. Wilson's Joy at the End of the Tether develops exactly this: when we stop trying to grasp the vapor, we're free to enjoy it in gratitude. In Christ, our labor "in the Lord is not in vain" (1 Cor 15:58), which is the gospel's answer to the Preacher's question.

Reformed note Doug Wilson's Joy at the End of the Tether reads hevel as vapor rather than "meaninglessness." For Wilson, the book teaches us to stop trying to grasp and control life and to receive it gladly as a gift. Eat your bread with joy (9:7).

BibleProject video: Ecclesiastes bibleproject.com/videos/ecclesiastes/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Qohelet means "the one who gathers," the Teacher, a son of David (Solomon, a later king, or a teacher writing in Solomon's persona). The Teacher is a character, and an anonymous author introduces and evaluates him.
  • "Hevel, hevel… everything is hevel": vapor or smoke, which appears 38 times. Life is fleeting and enigmatic, not simply "meaningless."
  • The Teacher deconstructs every attempt to build meaning apart from God. Time erases everything (the mountains and the sea don't care). Death "devours the wise and the fool." Work, wealth, status and pleasure all slip away, and "Monday always comes."
  • Wisdom and the fear of the Lord have real advantages, but even they are hevel, because they guarantee nothing.
  • The paradoxical answer: accept hevel and receive "the gift of God," simple joys (food, friends, family, a sunny day), in trust.
  • The author's verdict: the Teacher's words are goads, but don't bury yourself in books. "Fear God and keep his commandments… for God will bring every deed into judgment." The hope of judgment gives life its meaning.
A Reformed response to the video This closely matches Wilson's own reading, Joy at the End of the Tether, which takes hevel as vapor and joy as God's gift received by faith. Reformed readers add that the "under the sun" limits are answered in Christ, who subjected himself to futility to free creation from it (Rom 8:20–21; 1 Cor 15:58).

title: Song of Songs
html:
Song of Songs

8 chapters

“Set me as a seal upon your heart, as a seal upon your arm, for love is strong as death.” (Song of Songs 8:6, ESV)

Setting. Song of Songs (Song of Solomon) is a collection of love poems connected with Solomon. It celebrates the love of a bride and groom.

Where it fits. United Monarchy — Solomon's era, c. 971–931 BC. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Longing and union (1–5:1): Desire, courtship, the wedding procession, and union.
  2. Separation and reunion (5:2–8:4): The bride searches for her beloved, they are reunited, and love deepens.
  3. Climax (8:5–14): Love is as strong as death and can't be bought.
Main themes. Marital love and desire as God's good gift; faithfulness; beauty; longing; exclusive covenant love.
Main characters. The bride (the Shulammite), the beloved (the king), the daughters of Jerusalem.
Key passages
  • 1–2 — mutual delight and longing
  • 2:7 — do not stir up love until it pleases
  • 3 and 5 — searching for the beloved
  • 4 — the bride praised, the garden locked
  • 8:6–7 — love strong as death

How it points to Christ. Scripture uses marriage to picture God and his people (Hos 2; Eph 5:32). The Song's love points beyond itself to Christ, the Bridegroom, who loves his church.

Going deeper. The Song celebrates married love and physical desire as God's good gift, a needed corrective to both lust and prudishness. Historically, much of the church (including many Puritans) read it mainly as a picture of Christ and the church. Many Reformed interpreters today read it first as a poem about marriage and then, because marriage itself is a picture of Christ and the church (Eph 5:32), as pointing beyond itself. Wilson's writing on marriage (Reforming Marriage) likewise treats sexual delight within the marriage covenant as something to celebrate, not merely tolerate.

Reformed note The Reformed tradition, including many Puritans, read the Song as a picture of Christ and the church. More recent Reformed writers also stress its plain sense as a celebration of married love. Both readings can stand together, as Ephesians 5 suggests.

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Song of Songs bibleproject.com/videos/song-of-songs/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • "Song of Songs" is a Hebrew superlative: the greatest song. It is a collection of love poems meant to be enjoyed as a flowing whole, not a linear story.
  • BibleProject takes "of Solomon" to mean "in Solomon's wisdom tradition." The main voice is the woman, "the beloved," and the male voice does not seem to be Solomon's. With his 700 wives, Solomon makes an odd fit with lovers who are exclusive to each other.
  • Repeated cycles of seeking and finding, longing and embrace (each scene ends just as things become intimate) and elaborate metaphors of attraction that are about meaning, not visual pictures.
  • The climax (8:6–7): love is strong as death and a flame that many waters cannot quench, and love cannot be bought. It is beautiful but dangerous, like fire, and a gift from God. Solomon's attempt to buy love is rejected, and the book ends open-ended.
  • Interpretations: Jewish allegory (God and Israel), Christian allegory (Christ and the church, inspired by Ephesians 5) and, since ancient Near Eastern love poetry was discovered, most scholars' reading of it as real love poetry.
  • The garden imagery echoes Eden, where a man and woman were naked and unashamed. The Song holds out hope that love is a transcendent gift pointing to God's love, which will one day transform his world.
A Reformed response to the video Reformed interpreters have read the Song both ways. Many Puritans and older Reformed commentators read it as Christ and the church. More recent Reformed commentators often read it first as marriage poetry and then, by way of Ephesians 5:31–32, as a picture of Christ and his bride. Two cautions: (1) the tradition has generally held to Solomonic authorship ("of Solomon," 1:1), and (2) BibleProject's description of the couple as engaged should be balanced by noting that the consummation scenes (e.g., 4:16–5:1) are framed by the wedding procession (3:6–11), consistent with the refrain "do not stir up or awaken love until it pleases" (2:7; 3:5; 8:4).

title: The Prophets
html:
Part

The Prophets

The prophets were God's covenant enforcers. They called Israel back to the covenant, warned of judgment, and promised a new covenant, a new David, and a new creation. BibleProject treats the twelve "minor" prophets as one scroll, "The Twelve."

title: Isaiah
html:
Isaiah

66 chapters

“But he was pierced for our transgressions; he was crushed for our iniquities; upon him was the chastisement that brought us peace.” (Isaiah 53:5, ESV)

Setting. Isaiah son of Amoz ministered in Jerusalem from about 740 to 700 BC under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. The book looks ahead to the exile and beyond. Conservative scholarship holds that the whole book comes from Isaiah.

Where it fits. Divided Kingdom → Judah alone — Isaiah ministers c. 740–681 BC, through the Assyrian crisis and Sennacherib (701). Chapters 40–66 address the exile and Cyrus. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Judgment and the coming King (1–12): Zion is corrupt, Isaiah sees the Lord in the temple (6), and Immanuel and the child-king are promised (7, 9, 11).
  2. Oracles against the nations (13–27): God judges every proud power.
  3. Woes and hope (28–35): Trust in God, not Egypt.
  4. Hezekiah's story (36–39): A bridge to Babylon.
  5. Comfort and the Servant (40–55): A new exodus, Cyrus, and the Servant Songs, climaxing in the suffering Servant (52:13–53:12).
  6. New creation (56–66): Servants of the Servant, the nations streaming to Zion, and new heavens and a new earth.
Main themes. The holiness of God; judgment and remnant; the messianic King; the suffering Servant; new exodus; new creation; the nations drawn to Zion.
Main characters. Isaiah, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Sennacherib, Cyrus, the Servant.
Key passages
  • 6 — Isaiah's vision of the thrice-holy God
  • 7:14 — Immanuel
  • 9:6–7 — "unto us a child is born"
  • 11 — the shoot from Jesse and the peaceable kingdom
  • 40 — "comfort, comfort my people"
  • 52:13–53:12 — the suffering servant
  • 55 — the free invitation
  • 65–66 — new heavens and new earth

How it points to Christ. Isaiah has been called "the fifth Gospel." Christ is Immanuel (7:14), the child whose government has no end (9:6–7), the root of Jesse (11), and above all the Servant who bore our sins in our place (53). Jesus began his ministry by reading Isaiah 61.

Going deeper. Isaiah is the Old Testament's fullest portrait of the gospel, and Jesus begins his ministry by reading it (Luke 4:16–21). Chapter 6 is the root of Sproul's The Holiness of God: seeing God's holiness leads to "Woe is me," then cleansing, then sending. Isaiah 53 is the clearest Old Testament statement of penal substitution: the Servant is "pierced for our transgressions" and the Lord lays our iniquity on him. Postmillennial writers lean heavily on Isaiah's kingdom texts: the increase of his government with no end (9:7), the earth full of the knowledge of the Lord (11:9), and all nations streaming to Zion (2:2–4). They read them as promises being fulfilled through the gospel age.

Reformed note R.C. Sproul's The Holiness of God is built around Isaiah 6. Isaiah 53 is the clearest Old Testament statement of penal substitution: "the Lord has laid on him the iniquity of us all" (53:6). Postmillennialists, Wilson among them, treasure 9:7 ("of the increase of his government... there will be no end") and 2:2–4 as promises of the gospel's growing triumph in history.
Reading BibleProject well BibleProject splits Isaiah into two videos (1–39 and 40–66) and follows the scholarly convention of distinguishing later sections. Reformed and conservative readers usually defend the unity of the book and point to the New Testament quoting "Isaiah" from both halves (John 12:38–41).

BibleProject video: Isaiah 1-39 bibleproject.com/videos/isaiah-1-39/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Isaiah of Jerusalem warns Judah's corrupt leaders that covenant rebellion will bring judgment through Assyria and then Babylon. He joins this to hope: a Davidic king, renewed covenant faithfulness and blessing flowing to the nations, as promised to Abraham.
  • Structure: chapters 1–39 build toward the fall of Jerusalem and the exile foreshadowed in chapter 39, and chapters 40–66 develop the hope.
  • 1–12: judgment works like a purifying fire that turns the old Jerusalem into a new Jerusalem of a repentant remnant, to which the nations stream. At the center is Isaiah's throne-room vision, "holy, holy, holy": a burning coal purifies rather than destroys, and he is commissioned to preach a message that will harden. Israel will be cut down to a burned stump, but "the holy seed" remains.
  • That seed is the coming king: Immanuel, "God with us," the shoot from Jesse's stump, empowered by the Spirit to bring justice for the poor and peace to all creation.
  • 13–27: oracles against Babylon and the nations for their pride, then a "tale of two cities." The proud city of rebellious humanity falls, and a new Jerusalem rises where God reigns over a redeemed humanity from all nations, with no more death.
  • 28–39: Judah trusts Egypt instead of God. Hezekiah humbles himself and Jerusalem is saved overnight from Assyria, but he then courts Babylon, and Isaiah foretells the exile, which fulfills his words and proves him a true prophet.

“God's judgment is never the final word for Israel or the nations.” — BibleProject, Isaiah 1-39 video

What the video covers (our summary)
  • 40–48: "Comfort": exile is over, sin is dealt with, and God will bring his kingdom. BibleProject presents two views of the voice here: Isaiah speaking prophetically to the future, or Isaiah's disciples applying his sealed scroll (chs. 8, 29, 30) after the exile. Its own explanation leans toward the second, but it says everyone agrees God is fulfilling Isaiah's promises.
  • Exiled Israel complains that God ignores them, so 41–47 is staged as a trial. The exile was God's judgment, and he raised up Cyrus of Persia to bring them home. The Lord, not the idols, is King of history. Israel, still hard-hearted, is disqualified as his servant (ch. 48).
  • 49–55: a new Servant, given the title "Israel," will restore Israel and be a light to the nations, Spirit-empowered like the messianic king of chapters 9 and 11. He is rejected and killed, dying for his people's sin as a sacrifice of atonement, then lives again and makes many righteous.

On chapters 65–66, postmillennialists (e.g., Kenneth Gentry and, in his preaching, Doug Wilson) note that 65:20 still has death and old age, and read the "new heavens and new earth" as beginning now in the gospel age before the final consummation.

Isaiah son of Amoz ministered in Jerusalem from about 740 to 700 BC under Uzziah, Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. The book looks ahead to the exile and beyond. Conservative scholarship holds that the whole book comes from Isaiah. Where it fits. Divided Kingdom → Judah alone — Isaiah ministers c. 740–681 BC, through the Assyrian crisis and Sennacherib (701). Chapters 40–66 address the exile and Cyrus. ( Timelines ) The Flow of the Book Judgment and the coming King (1–12) : Zion is corrupt, Isaiah sees the Lord in the temple (6), and Immanuel and the child-king are promised (7, 9, 11). Oracles against the nations (13–27) : God judges every proud power. Woes and hope (28–35) : Trust in God, not Egypt. Hezekiah's story (36–39) : A bridge to Babylon. Comfort and the Servant (40–55) : A new exodus, Cyrus, and the Servant Songs, climaxing in the suffering Servant (52:13–53:12). New creation (56–66) : Servants of the Servant, the nations streaming to Zion, and new heavens and a new earth. Main themes. Isaiah, Ahaz, Hezekiah, Sennacherib, Cyrus, the Servant. Key passages 6 — Isaiah's vision of the thrice-holy God 7:14 — Immanuel 9:6–7 — "unto us a child is born" 11 — the shoot from Jesse and the peaceable kingdom 40 — "comfort, comfort my people" 52:13–53:12 — the suffering servant 55 — the free invitation 65–66 — new heavens and new earth How it points to Christ. Christ is Immanuel (7:14), the child whose government has no end (9:6–7), the root of Jesse (11), and above all the Servant who bore our sins in our place (53). title: Jeremiah
html:
Jeremiah

52 chapters

“I will put my law within them, and I will write it on their hearts. And I will be their God, and they shall be my people.” (Jeremiah 31:33, ESV)

Setting. Jeremiah, a priest from Anathoth, prophesied from about 627 to 586 BC, through Josiah's reform, Judah's last kings, and Jerusalem's fall. He is "the weeping prophet."

Where it fits. Judah alone → Exile — Jeremiah ministers c. 627–580 BC, from Josiah's reform through the fall of Jerusalem (586) and the flight to Egypt. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Call and indictment (1–25): Covenant lawsuit, the temple sermon, Jeremiah's laments, and symbolic acts.
  2. Conflict and hope (26–45): False prophets, a letter to the exiles (29), the Book of Comfort with the New Covenant (30–33), Jerusalem's fall, and its aftermath.
  3. Oracles against the nations (46–51): Even Babylon will fall.
  4. Epilogue (52): Jerusalem destroyed, and Jehoiachin shown kindness.
Main themes. Covenant unfaithfulness; false security in the temple; the suffering prophet; judgment by Babylon; the New Covenant.
Main characters. Jeremiah, Baruch, Josiah, Jehoiakim, Zedekiah, Hananiah, Nebuchadnezzar.
Key passages
  • 1 — Jeremiah's call ("before I formed you in the womb")
  • 7 — the temple sermon
  • 17:9 — the heart is deceitful above all things
  • 18 — the potter and the clay
  • 29 — letter to the exiles, "seek the welfare of the city"
  • 31:31–34 — the new covenant
  • 36 — the king burns the scroll

How it points to Christ. Jesus inaugurated the New Covenant of 31:31–34 in his blood (Luke 22:20; Heb 8). Jeremiah, rejected and suffering for speaking God's word, foreshadows Jesus, and some even thought Jesus was Jeremiah (Matt 16:14).

Going deeper. Jeremiah preached for forty years with almost no visible success, a model of faithfulness over results. His diagnosis of the heart (17:9) is the backbone of the Reformed doctrine of total depravity. His promise of the new covenant (31:31–34) is the longest Old Testament passage quoted in the New Testament (Heb 8). Reformed Baptists and Presbyterians disagree about what 31:34, "they shall all know me," means for who belongs to the new covenant, and that disagreement is one of the roots of the baptism debate. Chapter 29 has become a key text for Christians living as faithful minorities: build, plant, marry, and pray for the city.

Reformed note Covenantal Baptists stress that in the New Covenant "they shall all know me" (31:34), so the covenant community is to be made up of believers, and they baptize believers. Presbyterians stress the continuity of God's promise to believers and their children. Both agree that the New Covenant is unbreakable because God writes his law on the heart.
