BibleProject video: Jeremiah bibleproject.com/videos/jeremiah/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Jeremiah, a priest in Jerusalem in Judah's last decades, warned that covenant-breaking idolatry and injustice would bring Babylon as God's servant of judgment. He lived through the siege and the exile.
  • Chapter 36: after 20 years of preaching, Jeremiah dictated his messages to the scribe Baruch, who also gathered stories about him. That is why the book reads like "a collection of collections."
  • His calling: a prophet to Israel and the nations, to "uproot and tear down" and to "plant and build up."
  • 1–24: Israel's idolatry pictured as adultery. Corrupt priests, kings and prophets, and the oppression of widows, orphans and immigrants. In the temple sermon (ch. 7), worship goes on as normal while idolatry and even child sacrifice continue, and God will destroy his own temple.
  • Chapter 25 is the hinge: in Nebuchadnezzar's first year, 70 years of exile are announced, and Babylon is the cup of God's wrath for Israel and the nations.
  • 26–45: Jeremiah is rejected, persecuted, sees the siege and is taken to Egypt. At the center are messages of hope (30–33): building on Deuteronomy 30, God will make a new covenant, write the Torah on hearts, heal rebellion, bring Israel home and raise up the Davidic messiah.
  • 46–51: judgment on the nations, longest of all on Babylon, the archetype of rebellion from Genesis 11. God used Babylon but does not endorse its violence.
  • Chapter 52: the fall of Jerusalem, then the captive Davidic king Jehoiachin released to eat at the Babylonian king's table. It is a glimmer of hope that the line of David endures.

“God's own faithfulness will bring about the fulfillment of his promises, no matter what.” — BibleProject, Jeremiah video

A Reformed response to the video The new covenant of 31:31–34 is quoted in full in Hebrews 8, and it is at the center of the Baptist–Presbyterian discussion. Covenantal Baptists (1689 LBCF 7) stress "they shall all know me." Presbyterians (WCF 7) stress continuity with the household administration of the one covenant of grace. Both agree it is fulfilled in Christ's blood (Luke 22:20). Jeremiah's call, "before I formed you in the womb I knew you" (1:5), is a common Reformed text on God's sovereign choosing for service.

title: Lamentations
html:
Lamentations

5 chapters

“The steadfast love of the Lord never ceases; his mercies never come to an end; they are new every morning; great is your faithfulness.” (Lamentations 3:22–23, ESV)

Setting. Lamentations is five poems of grief written soon after Jerusalem fell in 586 BC, traditionally by Jeremiah. Four of them are acrostics, grief put in order from A to Z.

Where it fits. Exile — Laments written just after Jerusalem's destruction in 586 BC. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Jerusalem the widow (1): The city mourns.
  2. The Lord as enemy (2): Judgment is acknowledged.
  3. Hope in the middle (3): One man's suffering turns to hope in God's steadfast love.
  4. Before and after (4): Then and now.
  5. A communal prayer (5): "Restore us to yourself, O Lord."
Main themes. Grief and lament; honest confession of sin; God's justice in judgment; hope in his steadfast love.
Main characters. Daughter Zion, the suffering man (3).
Key passages
  • 1 — Jerusalem as a widow
  • 2 — the Lord as an enemy
  • 3:22–33 — steadfast love and new mercies at the center
  • 4 — the horrors of siege
  • 5 — the closing prayer, "restore us to yourself"

How it points to Christ. Christ wept over Jerusalem (Luke 19:41) and bore God's wrath at the cross so that his mercies might be new every morning for his people.

Going deeper. Lamentations gives God's people permission and words to grieve under judgment, including the judgment they deserve. Its careful acrostic structure means grief is given form, not just let loose. Hope sits at the exact center (3:22–23), surrounded by ruin. The book doesn't pretend the pain away. Reformed pastoral theology values this. Lament is an act of faith, because it brings complaints to God rather than away from him. The book's final unresolved question (5:22) is answered at the cross, where Christ endured the wrath that fell on Jerusalem.

Reformed note Lamentations teaches that lament is faith speaking, not unbelief. It also shows that judgment comes from the Lord's hand (3:37–38), which is a sobering affirmation of his sovereignty.

BibleProject video: Lamentations bibleproject.com/videos/lamentations/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Five poems by an anonymous survivor of Jerusalem's fall to Babylon in 587 BC, a memorial to the pain of losing land, king, temple and city.
  • Lament in the Bible protests evil, processes emotion and voices confusion. These human words to God became God's word, giving "a sacred dignity to human suffering."
  • Chapters 1–4 are acrostics (one verse or more per Hebrew letter). Their order contrasts with the chaos of grief, as if exploring suffering from A to Z.
  • Chapter 1: Lady Zion as a widow, alone and uncomforted. Chapter 2: the fall as God's justified wrath for covenant violation. BibleProject stresses that God's wrath is not volatile but his slow-to-anger justice.
  • Chapter 3, the longest: a lone sufferer representing the people. He echoes Job, the psalms and Isaiah's servant, and he speaks the book's only hopeful words: God's mercies "new every morning." If God is consistent in justice, he will be consistent in keeping his covenant promises.
  • Chapter 4: the siege in shocking before-and-after contrasts. Chapter 5 drops the alphabet order, as if grief has broken down: a communal plea ending unresolved, "unless you have utterly rejected us."
  • Lament, prayer and grief are a crucial part of faith in a broken world.

“God's judgment is the seedbed of hope for the future.” — BibleProject, Lamentations video

A Reformed response to the video Reformed readers agree that God's wrath is not capricious, but they stress that it is personal and holy opposition to sin, not just consequences. Lamentations says plainly that the Lord did it (2:1–8, 17; 3:37–38). That is why the cross is a propitiation, God's wrath borne by Christ (Rom 3:25), and why 3:22–23 can be sung with confidence by those in him.

Chapter 1: Lady Zion as a widow, alone and uncomforted. Chapter 2: the fall as God's justified wrath for covenant violation. BibleProject stresses that God's wrath is not volatile but his slow-to-anger justice. Chapter 3, the longest: a lone sufferer representing the people. He echoes Job, the psalms and Isaiah's servant, and he speaks the book's only hopeful words: God's mercies "new every morning." If God is consistent in justice, he will be consistent in keeping his covenant promises. Chapter 4: the siege in shocking before-and-after contrasts. Chapter 5 drops the alphabet order, as if grief has broken down: a communal plea ending unresolved, "unless you have utterly rejected us." Lament, prayer and grief are a crucial part of faith in a broken world. “God's judgment is the seedbed of hope for the future.” — BibleProject, Lamentations video A Reformed response to the video Reformed readers agree that God's wrath is not capricious, but they stress that it is personal and holy opposition to sin, not just consequences. Lamentations says plainly that the Lord did it (2:1–8, 17; 3:37–38). That is why the cross is a propitiation, God's wrath borne by Christ (Rom 3:25), and why 3:22–23 can be sung with confidence by those in him.

title: Ezekiel
html:
Ezekiel

48 chapters

“And I will give you a new heart, and a new spirit I will put within you.” (Ezekiel 36:26, ESV)

Setting. Ezekiel was a priest taken to Babylon in 597 BC. He prophesied among the exiles from about 593 to 571 BC, before and after Jerusalem's fall.

Where it fits. Exile — Oracles dated 593–571 BC, among the exiles at the Chebar canal in Babylonia. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Vision and commission (1–3): God's throne-chariot glory appears in Babylon.
  2. Judgment on Jerusalem (4–24): Sign acts, and God's glory departs from the temple (10–11).
  3. Oracles against the nations (25–32).
  4. Restoration (33–39): The watchman, the good shepherd, a new heart, the valley of dry bones, and Gog defeated.
  5. The new temple (40–48): The glory returns, and a river flows out to heal the land.
Main themes. The glory of God; individual responsibility; judgment for idolatry; the Spirit giving new life; the return of God's presence.
Main characters. Ezekiel, the elders of Israel, the "shepherds" of Israel.
Key passages
  • 1 — the chariot-throne vision
  • 8–11 — the glory leaves the temple
  • 18 — each one's own sin, and "turn and live"
  • 34 — the true Shepherd
  • 36:25–27 — new heart and Spirit
  • 37 — the valley of dry bones
  • 40–48 — the new temple and the river of life

How it points to Christ. Jesus is the Good Shepherd (34; John 10) and the true temple from whom living water flows (47; John 7:37–39). He sends the Spirit, who gives new hearts.

Going deeper. Ezekiel is a book about God's presence: lost through idolatry (ch. 10) and promised again in glory (ch. 43). The final name of the city is "The Lord is there" (48:35). Ezekiel 36–37 is one of the clearest texts on monergistic regeneration. God removes the heart of stone, gives a new heart, puts his Spirit within, and "causes" his people to walk in his ways. Dead bones live only when God speaks. Reformed interpreters generally read the visionary temple of chapters 40–48 as fulfilled in Christ and his church, not as a future physical temple with restored animal sacrifices (Heb 10:18). The river flowing out to heal the nations (47) is a favorite image for postmillennial hope.

Reformed note Ezekiel 36:26–27 is a key text for the Reformed view of regeneration. God gives the new heart before we can respond, so new birth comes before faith. Postmillennial readers like Wilson see the river that grows deeper as it flows (47) as a picture of the kingdom's steady growth.
Reading BibleProject well BibleProject's two Ezekiel videos focus on God's presence and temple. Their temple-and-presence framing is a real strength here.
Recommended free Reformed commentaries: Ezekiel
  • Calvin's Commentaries: Commentary on Ezekiel 1–20 — John Calvin. Calvin died before finishing Ezekiel (covers chs. 1–20). The fountainhead of Reformed exegesis: plain sense, Christ-centred, and pastoral (vols. 22–23; link opens vol. 22).ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom22
  • Surveying the Text: Ezekiel — Douglas Wilson. Wilson's one-sermon panorama of the whole book: its structure, themes, and Christ, with postmillennial and covenantal punch.dougwils.com/the-church/s8-expository/surveying-the-text-ezekiel.html
  • An Exposition of Ezekiel — Patrick Fairbairn. Covers the whole book, including chs. 21–48, which Calvin never reached; strong on typology.monergism.com/exposition-ezekiel-ebook
  • TGC Bible Commentary: Ezekiel — Donna Petter (TGC Bible Commentary). A free, modern, section-by-section commentary in TGC's Reformed-evangelical stream, with good help on biblical theology.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/ezekiel/
More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Ezekiel 1-33 bibleproject.com/videos/ezekiel-1-33/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Ezekiel is a priest taken to Babylon in the first wave of exiles. Five years later, on his 30th birthday, the age he would have begun serving as a priest, he sees a storm cloud, four living creatures with wheels, and a throne carrying a glowing human-like figure: "the appearance of the likeness of the glory of the Lord."
  • "Glory" (Hebrew kavod) means heaviness or significance: God's visible presence, as at Sinai and over the ark. The shock is that this glory has appeared in Babylon.
  • Chapters 1–11: God commissions Ezekiel to charge Israel with idolatry and the injustice and violence it bred, and to warn that Jerusalem and the temple will fall. He acts out sign acts, a kind of street theater: a model siege, shaved and chopped hair, lying on his side for over a year. He is told no one will listen.
  • In a vision tour of the temple he sees idols and elders and women worshipping other gods. Then the glory departs east toward Babylon. God has left his temple, but he goes into exile with his people. Chapter 11 promises a remnant, a heart of stone replaced with a heart of flesh.
  • That hinge shapes the book: three sections of judgment (Israel, the nations, Jerusalem), then three of hope (Israel, the nations, all creation).
  • Chapters 12–24: parables and allegories (a burnt stick, an unfaithful wife, two promiscuous sisters) and a lawyer's case that judgment is deserved. Even Noah, Daniel and Job could not stop it.
  • Chapters 25–32: judgment on Israel's neighbors, then on Egypt and Tyre, whose kings made themselves gods who define right and wrong. Chapter 33: a refugee reports that Jerusalem has fallen.
BibleProject video: Ezekiel 34-48 bibleproject.com/videos/ezekiel-34-48/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • After Jerusalem falls, did God abandon Israel for good? The rest of the book answers with hope for Israel, for the nations, and for creation.
  • Chapters 34–37: God promises a new David, the king Israel needed but never had, and a transformed people. He will remove hard hearts and put his Spirit within them, as Moses promised in Deuteronomy.
  • The valley of dry bones pictures Israel's exile as a death, both literal and covenantal. The Spirit-wind brings the bones together and gives them breath, echoing Genesis 2, where God forms humans from dust and divine breath. The only hope is a new act of creation.
  • Chapters 38–39: Gog of Magog, a name drawn from the ancient nations of Genesis 10, is allied with nations from every direction. Gog is an archetype of all violent kingdoms, described with images used earlier for Tyre and Pharaoh. The overlapping scenes of his defeat (earthquake, fire twice, unburied armies) are symbolic, not a literal sequence. God finally defeats evil to clear the way for new creation.
  • Chapters 40–48: a heavenly guide tours a new temple larger than Solomon's, with a new altar, priests and worship. God's glory returns to it. The video notes that some expect a literal temple and others read the vision symbolically.
  • A trickle from the temple threshold becomes a river that turns the Dead Sea into a living sea lined with trees. This is Eden imagery. The city is never called Jerusalem. Its name is "The Lord is there."
A Reformed response to the video The video's three-part shape is helpful. Reformed readers add that the heart transplant of 11:19 and 36:26–27 is regeneration, the sovereign work of the Spirit that comes before and causes repentance and faith (WCF 10.1–2; John 3:3–8). The glory leaving and returning is fulfilled in the Word who "tabernacled" among us (John 1:14) and in the church as God's temple (1 Cor 3:16; Eph 2:21–22). The video presents literal and symbolic readings of chapters 40–48 evenly. Most Reformed interpreters take the symbolic view and see it fulfilled in Christ, the church and the new creation (Rev 21–22). They do not expect a rebuilt temple with renewed animal sacrifices, since Hebrews says Christ's one sacrifice ended them (Heb 10:12–18).
A Reformed response to the video God's promise to be the shepherd himself (34:11–16) and to set over them "my servant David" (34:23–24) come together in Jesus, who calls himself the good shepherd (John 10:11). That fits the Reformed confession of Christ as fully God and fully man. On Gog, many postmillennial and amillennial interpreters see the final defeat of the nations' rebellion as fulfilled in Christ's victory (Rev 20:8–9). The river of 47:1–12 grows as it flows, which some postmillennial writers take as a picture of the gospel's gradual spread, as in the parable of the leaven (Matt 13:33). Its fulfillment is clearly Revelation 22:1–2.

title: Daniel
html:
Daniel

12 chapters

“The God of heaven will set up a kingdom that shall never be destroyed.” (Daniel 2:44, ESV)

Setting. Daniel was taken to Babylon as a young man in 605 BC and served in the courts of Babylon and Persia. The book encourages faithfulness under pagan empires.

Where it fits. Exile → Persian period — From 605 BC to Cyrus' 3rd year (c. 536 BC). Covers Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar (539), and Darius the Mede. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Court stories (1–6): The diet test, Nebuchadnezzar's statue dream, the fiery furnace, the king humbled, the writing on the wall, and the lions' den.
  2. Visions (7–12): The four beasts and the Son of Man, the ram and the goat, the seventy weeks (9), and the final vision of conflict and resurrection.
Main themes. God's sovereignty over empires; faithfulness under pressure; the kingdom of God; the Son of Man; resurrection.
Main characters. Daniel, Shadrach, Meshach, Abednego, Nebuchadnezzar, Belshazzar, Darius.
Key passages
  • 1 — faithfulness in Babylon's court
  • 2 — the statue and the stone that becomes a mountain
  • 3 — the fiery furnace
  • 4 — Nebuchadnezzar humbled
  • 6 — the lions' den
  • 7 — the Son of Man receives the kingdom
  • 9:24–27 — the seventy weeks

How it points to Christ. Jesus' favorite title for himself, "Son of Man," comes from 7:13–14, where the Son of Man ascends to the Ancient of Days and receives an everlasting kingdom. Christ is the stone that becomes a great mountain filling the earth (2:35).

Going deeper. Daniel teaches God's people how to live faithfully inside a hostile empire. They serve competently, refuse idolatry, and trust God with the outcome. The book's theology is the absolute sovereignty of God over kings: "the Most High rules the kingdom of men" (4:17). Chapter 2 is central for postmillennialism. The stone cut without hands, Christ's kingdom set up in the days of Rome, grows until it fills the whole earth. Many postmillennial and partial-preterist interpreters (for example Kenneth Gentry) read the seventy weeks (9:24–27) as fulfilled in Christ's first coming and the events of AD 70, not as a future seven-year tribulation. Jesus' favorite title for himself, "Son of Man," comes from Daniel 7.

Reformed note Many Reformed interpreters see the seventy weeks fulfilled in Christ's first coming and in Jerusalem's fall in AD 70, not in a future period separated by a gap. Postmillennialists, Wilson included, take 2:35 to mean that Christ's kingdom will grow until it fills the whole earth before he returns. Many read 7:13 as fulfilled in Christ's ascension.
Recommended free Reformed commentaries: Daniel
  • Calvin's Commentaries: Commentary on Daniel — John Calvin. The fountainhead of Reformed exegesis: plain sense, Christ-centred, and pastoral (vols. 24–25; link opens vol. 24).ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom24
  • Surveying the Text: Daniel — Douglas Wilson. Wilson's one-sermon panorama of the whole book: its structure, themes, and Christ, with postmillennial and covenantal punch.dougwils.com/the-church/s8-expository/surveying-the-text-daniel.html
  • Daniel, the Wisest Prophet of God — Heinrich Bullinger. A Reformation-era exposition by Zwingli's successor in Zurich.monergism.com/daniel-wisest-prophet-god-ebook
  • TGC Bible Commentary: Daniel — Mitchell L. Chase (TGC Bible Commentary). A free, modern, section-by-section commentary in TGC's Reformed-evangelical stream, with good help on biblical theology.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/daniel/
More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Daniel bibleproject.com/videos/daniel/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Set after Babylon's first attack on Jerusalem. Daniel (Belteshazzar) and his friends Shadrach, Meshach and Abednego, young men of the royal house, try to keep hope and faithfulness in their conquerors' land.
  • The book's shape: stories in chapters 1–6 and visions in 7–12. Its languages also mark a section: Hebrew, then Aramaic for 2–7, then Hebrew again. This shows that 2–7 is a unit framed by chapters 2 and 7.
  • Chapter 1: they refuse the king's food to stay faithful to the Torah. God delivers and promotes them.
  • The Aramaic section is a symmetrical arrangement. Chapter 2 (a statue of four metals, a train of violent kingdoms, smashed by a stone that becomes a mountain: God's kingdom) pairs with chapter 7. Chapter 3 (the furnace) pairs with chapter 6 (the lions' den). At the center are two proud kings: Nebuchadnezzar becomes like a beast, is humbled and is restored, while Belshazzar refuses and dies that night.
  • Drawing on Genesis 1–2 and Psalm 8, the video argues that humans are God's royal image, but kingdoms that make their power a god become beastly, less than human.
  • Chapter 7, the center: four beasts and a boastful horn, then the Ancient of Days takes his throne and "one like a son of man" comes with the clouds to share God's rule. The video reads the son of man as an image of both God's people and their Davidic king.
  • Chapters 8–12: a ram (Medo-Persia), a goat (Greece), and an arrogant horn who defiles the temple. In chapter 9 Daniel reads Jeremiah's 70 years, and an angel says the exile will last "seven times" longer. Chapters 10–12 trace Persia, Greece and a final northern king.
  • Readers have tied these visions to Antiochus (160s BC), to Rome and AD 70, or to the future. The video suggests that in a sense all may be right: a pattern and a promise for every generation.

“God will confront the beast.” — BibleProject, Daniel video

A Reformed response to the video The video leaves the referent of the visions open. Reformed commentators have usually been more definite on two points. First, the stone and the kingdom of chapter 2 are set up "in the days of those kings" (2:44), during the fourth empire, so many identify it with Rome and with Christ's first coming. That kingdom then grows to fill the earth (2:35). Postmillennialists stress that this growth takes place within history. Second, Jesus' favorite title, "the Son of Man," and his answer at his trial (Mark 14:62) claim Daniel 7:13–14 for himself. The son of man ascends to the Ancient of Days, which the New Testament sees fulfilled in the ascension (Acts 1:9; Eph 1:20–22). Many Reformed interpreters likewise read the seventy weeks (9:24–27) as fulfilled in Christ's atoning work and Jerusalem's fall. They do not see them as a gap-theory timeline still waiting to be fulfilled.

In chapter 9 Daniel reads Jeremiah's 70 years, and an angel says the exile will last "seven times" longer. Chapters 10–12 trace Persia, Greece and a final northern king. Readers have tied these visions to Antiochus (160s BC), to Rome and AD 70, or to the future. The video suggests that in a sense all may be right: a pattern and a promise for every generation. “God will confront the beast.” — BibleProject, Daniel video A Reformed response to the video The video leaves the referent of the visions open. Reformed commentators have usually been more definite on two points. First, the stone and the kingdom of chapter 2 are set up "in the days of those kings" (2:44), during the fourth empire, so many identify it with Rome and with Christ's first coming. That kingdom then grows to fill the earth (2:35). Postmillennialists stress that this growth takes place within history. Second, Jesus' favorite title, "the Son of Man," and his answer at his trial (Mark 14:62) claim Daniel 7:13–14 for himself. The son of man ascends to the Ancient of Days, which the New Testament sees fulfilled in the ascension (Acts 1:9; Eph 1:20–22). Many Reformed interpreters likewise read the seventy weeks (9:24–27) as fulfilled in Christ's atoning work and Jerusalem's fall. They do not see them as a gap-theory timeline still waiting to be fulfilled.

title: Hosea
html:
Hosea

14 chapters

“How can I give you up, O Ephraim? How can I hand you over, O Israel?” (Hosea 11:8, ESV)

Setting. Hosea prophesied to the northern kingdom (Israel) in its last decades before Assyria conquered it in 722 BC.

Where it fits. Divided Kingdom — To the northern kingdom, c. 755–715 BC, under Jeroboam II and up to Samaria's fall (722). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Hosea's marriage (1–3): God tells Hosea to marry Gomer, who is unfaithful, and he redeems her. It is a living parable of God and Israel.
  2. Covenant lawsuit (4–10): Idolatry, political scheming, and empty religion.
  3. Love that won't let go (11–14): The Father's love for his son, and a final call to return.
Main themes. Covenant as marriage; spiritual adultery (idolatry); steadfast love; judgment and restoration.
Main characters. Hosea, Gomer, their children (Jezreel, Lo-ruhamah, Lo-ammi).
Key passages
  • 1–3 — Hosea marries Gomer and buys her back
  • 4:6 — destroyed for lack of knowledge
  • 6:6 — steadfast love, not sacrifice
  • 11:1–9 — "out of Egypt I called my son" and "how can I give you up?"
  • 14 — the invitation to return

How it points to Christ. "Out of Egypt I called my son" (11:1) is fulfilled in Jesus, the true Israel (Matt 2:15). The Bridegroom who buys back his unfaithful bride pictures Christ redeeming his church (1 Pet 2:10 uses 1:9–2:23).

Going deeper. Hosea's own marriage becomes a living parable: God loves an unfaithful people and pays to redeem them. The New Testament applies Hosea's promise ("not my people… my people," 1:10; 2:23) to Gentiles brought in by grace (Rom 9:25–26; 1 Pet 2:10). It is a powerful picture of the effectual, pursuing love of God, a love that doesn't just offer but actually wins back. Matthew 2:15 uses 11:1 to show Jesus as the true Israel, the faithful Son who succeeds where Israel failed.

Reformed note Hosea is a vivid picture of the Reformed doctrine of grace. God's love is unconditional and pursuing, and he restores his bride by his own initiative.

BibleProject video: Hosea bibleproject.com/videos/hosea/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Hosea preached in the northern kingdom (also called Ephraim or Jacob) from the time of Jeroboam II until shortly before Assyria crushed Israel in 722 BC. The book collects about 25 years of his preaching, almost all in poetry, in three sections.
  • Chapters 1–3: Hosea's marriage to Gomer, who commits adultery. God tells him to find her, pay off her lovers and recommit to her. All of this is a prophetic sign of God, the faithful husband who rescued Israel and made a covenant at Sinai, while Israel gave his gifts to Baal.
  • God could justly divorce Israel. Instead he will pursue her and renew the covenant, purely out of his own love, compassion and faithfulness. Defeat and exile are coming, but one day Israel will return and a new Davidic king will rule them.
  • Chapters 4–11: Israel lacks "knowledge" of God. The Hebrew yada means personal, relational knowing, not just facts. Hosea exposes worship that ignores the Ten Commandments and injustice, Baal altars at Bethel and Gilgal, and trust in alliances with Egypt and Assyria.
  • Chapter 11: God as a father whose son rebelled: "How can I give you up, Ephraim?" His compassion is stirred. Exile will not be his final word.
  • Chapters 12–14: a history lesson from Jacob's deceit through the wilderness and Saul shows that the family has always been unfaithful. Chapter 14 calls for repentance and promises that God will heal their waywardness and love them freely. Israel will become a spreading tree that blesses the nations.
  • A closing note from the editor tells every reader that the ways of the Lord are right: the righteous walk in them and rebels stumble in them.
A Reformed response to the video The video rightly locates the cause of restoration in God's own love, not in Israel's merit. That is the heart of the Reformed doctrine of grace. Reformed preachers have long read Hosea redeeming Gomer (3:1–2) as a picture of Christ buying his bride at a price (1 Cor 6:20; Eph 5:25–27). Paul quotes Hosea 1:10 and 2:23 for the calling of Gentiles into God's people (Rom 9:24–26), and Matthew applies 11:1 to Jesus as the true Son (Matt 2:15). Covenant theologians also point to 6:7, "like Adam they transgressed the covenant" (ESV), as one support for a covenant with Adam, though the verse is debated.

title: Joel
html:
Joel

3 chapters

“And it shall come to pass afterward, that I will pour out my Spirit on all flesh.” (Joel 2:28, ESV)

Setting. Joel's date is uncertain. The book is set after a devastating locust plague, which Joel reads as a warning of the coming Day of the Lord.

Where it fits. Undated — There are no regnal markers. Proposed dates range from the 9th century to after the Return, c. 400 BC. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. The locust plague (1): A call to lament.
  2. The Day of the Lord and a call to repent (2:1–17): "Return to me with all your heart."
  3. Promised restoration (2:18–32): The land restored and the Spirit poured out.
  4. Judgment of the nations (3): The Lord dwells in Zion.
Main themes. The Day of the Lord; repentance; the outpouring of the Spirit; judgment and restoration.
Main characters. Joel.
Key passages
  • 1 — the locust plague
  • 2:12–13 — "return to me with all your heart… rend your hearts"
  • 2:28–32 — the Spirit poured out on all flesh
  • 3 — the nations judged in the valley of decision

How it points to Christ. Peter declares that Pentecost fulfills 2:28–32 (Acts 2:16–21). The risen and exalted Christ pours out the Spirit (Acts 2:33).

Going deeper. Peter declares Joel 2 fulfilled at Pentecost (Acts 2:16–21). The "last days" began with Christ's resurrection and the gift of the Spirit, and Christians have been living in them ever since. Reformed writers stress that the Spirit is poured on "all flesh," across age, sex and social rank, and that this democratizing of the Spirit is one mark of the new covenant. The cosmic signs that accompany the day of the Lord are covenant-judgment language. Partial preterists connect them to the judgment on Jerusalem in AD 70 (Acts 2:20, 40).

Reformed note Reformed interpreters read Joel's "Day of the Lord" as something that unfolds in stages: at the cross, at Pentecost, in AD 70, and finally at Christ's return.

BibleProject video: Joel bibleproject.com/videos/joel/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Joel is unusual in three ways. It has no date, though it is probably post-exilic: there is a temple but no king. It is soaked in earlier Scripture (Exodus, Isaiah, Amos, Obadiah, Ezekiel and more). And it names no specific sin, apparently assuming readers know the prophets' charges already.
  • Chapters 1–2 are two parallel poems on "the Day of the Lord," God's powerful acts of judgment and salvation, like the plagues of Egypt.
  • Chapter 1, a past Day: a locust swarm, like Egypt's eighth plague but now turned on Israel. Joel calls elders and priests to lead the people in repentance.
  • Chapter 2, a future Day: the locusts become God's army, with cosmic signs. "Rend your hearts and not your garments," because God is "gracious and merciful, slow to anger" (quoting Exodus 34 after the golden calf). God's mercy outweighs his wrath.
  • God then "became jealous for his land and had pity on his people." He promises to drive off the invader, restore the land, and dwell among his people.
  • The final poems expand each promise. God's Spirit will fill all his people, as Isaiah, Jeremiah and Ezekiel promised. God will judge violent nations. All creation will be renewed, with a river flowing from God's presence like a new Eden.
A Reformed response to the video Peter quotes Joel 2:28–32 at Pentecost and says "this is what was uttered" (Acts 2:16). Reformed readers therefore see the outpouring of the Spirit as begun at Pentecost, not postponed to a future age. Partial preterists connect the cosmic signs with the end of the old covenant order in AD 70, while many others see a final fulfillment still to come. Paul uses 2:32 to show that "everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved," Jew and Gentile alike (Rom 10:12–13). He also applies the divine name in that verse to Jesus, a strong testimony to Christ's deity.

title: Amos
html:
Amos

9 chapters

“But let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream.” (Amos 5:24, ESV)

Setting. Amos was a shepherd and fig farmer from Judah, sent to prosperous northern Israel around 760 BC, during a time of luxury and oppression.

Where it fits. Divided Kingdom — c. 760 BC, "two years before the earthquake" (1:1), during Jeroboam II's prosperity. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Oracles against the nations, ending with Israel (1–2): Israel is the climactic target.
  2. Indictments (3–6): Oppression of the poor, empty worship, complacency.
  3. Five visions (7–9:10): Locusts, fire, the plumb line, summer fruit, and the Lord by the altar.
  4. Restoration (9:11–15): David's fallen booth raised up.
Main themes. Social justice rooted in covenant; true versus false worship; judgment; restoration of David's house.
Main characters. Amos, Amaziah the priest, Jeroboam II.
Key passages
  • 1–2 — oracles against the nations, closing in on Israel
  • 3:2 — "you only have I known; therefore I will punish you"
  • 4:1 — "cows of Bashan"
  • 5:21–24 — "let justice roll down"
  • 7–9 — five visions
  • 9:11–15 — the fallen booth of David restored

How it points to Christ. At the Jerusalem Council, James cites 9:11–12 and sees the gathering of Gentiles into the church as the rebuilding of David's fallen tent through the risen Christ (Acts 15:16–17).

Going deeper. Amos attacks religion that is busy with worship but indifferent to injustice. That is a warning to comfortable churches in every age. Biblical justice in Amos means honest courts, fair trade, and protecting the poor from exploitation, all measured by God's law, not by changing ideologies. James quotes 9:11–12 at the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15:16–18) to show that Gentiles coming to Christ is the rebuilding of David's house. That reading supports the Reformed view that the church is the continuation of Israel's story.

Reformed note Amos grounds justice in God's covenant law, not in modern ideologies. Reformed writers stress that true worship and just dealing with neighbors always go together.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • Amos was a shepherd and fig-tree farmer from near the border with Judah. He was sent north to Bethel under Jeroboam II, whose military success and wealth bred complacency, idolatry and neglect of the poor.
  • The book is a collection of sermons, poems and visions: messages to the nations and Israel (1–2), poems to Israel (3–6), and visions (7–9).
  • Chapters 1–2: Amos indicts the neighbors in a circle on the map, with Israel at the center like a target. Its indictment is three times longer: the poor sold into debt slavery and denied justice by the very people God freed from slavery in Egypt.
  • Chapters 3–6: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you." A high calling brings high responsibility. Amos exposes worship by the wealthy that ignores injustice: God hates it. "Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream."
  • Tsedaqah (righteousness) is a standard of right relationships. Mishpat (justice) is the concrete action that sets things right.
  • Idolatry, from Jeroboam I's golden calves onward, and injustice go together. "Seek me and live" and "seek good, and not evil, that you may live" amount to the same call. Rejecting the prophets brings the Day of the Lord: conquest and exile, fulfilled by Assyria about 40 years later.
  • Chapters 7–9: visions of locusts, fire and summer fruit, and God striking the Bethel temple's pillars. Then, at the end, hope: God will raise up the fallen house of David and rebuild his people to include all the nations.
A Reformed response to the video Reformed social ethics takes Amos seriously, but it ties justice to God's law and to a fair process. Amos condemns bribed courts, rigged scales and debt slavery (2:6–8; 5:10–12; 8:5–6), and calls the guilty to repent. Readers should be careful not to equate his message with any modern political program. The ending gets the last word: at the Jerusalem council, James cites 9:11–12 as fulfilled in the Gentiles turning to God through the risen Son of David (Acts 15:15–18). The restored "booth of David" is Christ's church gathered from the nations, not a future earthly temple.

BibleProject is the author and owner of this content. Visit bibleproject.com . What the video covers (our summary) Amos was a shepherd and fig-tree farmer from near the border with Judah. He was sent north to Bethel under Jeroboam II, whose military success and wealth bred complacency, idolatry and neglect of the poor. The book is a collection of sermons, poems and visions: messages to the nations and Israel (1–2), poems to Israel (3–6), and visions (7–9). Chapters 1–2: Amos indicts the neighbors in a circle on the map, with Israel at the center like a target. Its indictment is three times longer: the poor sold into debt slavery and denied justice by the very people God freed from slavery in Egypt. Chapters 3–6: "You only have I known of all the families of the earth; therefore I will punish you." A high calling brings high responsibility. Amos exposes worship by the wealthy that ignores injustice: God hates it. "Let justice roll down like waters, and righteousness like an ever-flowing stream." Tsedaqah (righteousness) is a standard of right relationships. Mishpat (justice) is the concrete action that sets things right. Idolatry, from Jeroboam I's golden calves onward, and injustice go together. "Seek me and live" and "seek good, and not evil, that you may live" amount to the same call. Rejecting the prophets brings the Day of the Lord: conquest and exile, fulfilled by Assyria about 40 years later. Chapters 7–9: visions of locusts, fire and summer fruit, and God striking the Bethel temple's pillars. Then, at the end, hope: God will raise up the fallen house of David and rebuild his people to include all the nations. A Reformed response to the video Reformed social ethics takes Amos seriously, but it ties justice to God's law and to a fair process. Amos condemns bribed courts, rigged scales and debt slavery (2:6–8; 5:10–12; 8:5–6), and calls the guilty to repent. Readers should be careful not to equate his message with any modern political program. The ending gets the last word: at the Jerusalem council, James cites 9:11–12 as fulfilled in the Gentiles turning to God through the risen Son of David (Acts 15:15–18). The restored "booth of David" is Christ's church gathered from the nations, not a future earthly temple.

title: Obadiah
html:
Obadiah

1 chapter

“For the day of the Lord is near upon all the nations. As you have done, it shall be done to you.” (Obadiah 15, ESV)

Setting. Obadiah is the shortest Old Testament book. It is an oracle against Edom, Esau's descendants, who gloated over and plundered Jerusalem when it fell, probably in 586 BC.

Where it fits. Divided Kingdom or early Exile — Against Edom, either after an attack on Jerusalem c. 848 BC or after 586 BC. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Edom's pride brought low (1–9).
  2. Edom's crimes against his brother (10–14).
  3. The Day of the Lord and Zion's restoration (15–21): "And the kingdom shall be the Lord's."
Main themes. Pride; brotherly betrayal; reaping what you sow; the kingdom of God.
Main characters. Edom (Esau), Jacob (Israel).
Key passages
  • 1–9 — Edom's pride brought down
  • 10–14 — Edom's violence against Jacob, its brother
  • 15 — the day of the Lord on all nations
  • 17–21 — deliverance on Mount Zion and "the kingdom shall be the Lord's"

How it points to Christ. The final line, "the kingdom shall be the Lord's," is fulfilled in Christ's reign. The Jacob and Esau conflict reaches its end when the Herods (Idumeans, that is, Edomites) oppose Jesus and fall.

Going deeper. The shortest book in the Old Testament continues the Jacob–Esau rivalry from Genesis. Edom gloated over Jerusalem's fall, and God promises to repay. It teaches that God takes the side of his oppressed people and opposes the proud (Jas 4:6; 1 Pet 5:5). The closing line, "the kingdom shall be the Lord's," is a fitting summary of the whole prophetic hope, one postmillennial readers expect to see increasingly realized as Christ reigns.

Reformed note Edom's fate illustrates God's righteous judgment of the proud and his faithfulness to his covenant people. Paul uses the Jacob and Esau line to teach sovereign election (Rom 9:13).

BibleProject video: Obadiah bibleproject.com/videos/obadiah/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The shortest book in the Old Testament, 21 verses of judgment on Edom, Israel's neighbor across the Dead Sea.
  • Background: Edom and Israel descend from the twin brothers Esau and Jacob, whose rivalry carried on through their nations. When Babylon conquered Jerusalem, Edom betrayed that family bond by plundering towns and capturing or killing refugees.
  • Verses 1–14: Edom's leaders are charged with pride. They live high in the desert rocks and think themselves superior, so they joined in Jerusalem's destruction. They will be brought down: "as you have done, it shall be done to you."
  • Verse 15 is the hinge: "the day of the Lord is near upon all the nations." Edom becomes an image of every proud nation. In Hebrew, edom has the same consonants as adam, "humanity."
  • Verses 16–21 build on the endings of Joel and Amos: deliverance in Zion for those who call on the Lord, and a Davidic kingdom that includes Edom and the nations. A faithful remnant will repopulate the new Jerusalem, and God's kingdom will spread to the surrounding lands.
A Reformed response to the video Reformed readers have long connected Obadiah with Malachi 1:2–3 and Romans 9:10–13 ("Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated"). That points to God's sovereign choice in election and also to Edom's real moral guilt. Both are taught side by side. The final verse, "the kingdom shall be the Lord's," fits the postmillennial expectation that Christ's kingdom will in fact spread over the nations (Ps 22:27–28). The Edomite Herods' hostility to Jesus shows the old rivalry continuing into the New Testament.

title: Jonah
html:
Jonah

4 chapters

“Salvation belongs to the Lord!” (Jonah 2:9, ESV)

Setting. Jonah son of Amittai prophesied in the reign of Jeroboam II (2 Kgs 14:25). The book is a story about a prophet who ran from God's mercy to Israel's enemy, Nineveh.

Where it fits. Divided Kingdom — Jonah prophesies under Jeroboam II (c. 793–753 BC; 2 Kgs 14:25). His mission to Nineveh comes in Assyria's weak decades. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Jonah runs (1): The storm, the sailors, and the great fish.
  2. Jonah prays (2): A psalm from the belly of the fish.
  3. Nineveh repents (3): The whole city turns, and God relents.
  4. Jonah sulks (4): The plant, the worm, and God's question: should I not pity Nineveh?
Main themes. God's sovereign mercy to the nations; disobedience and grace; repentance; the prophet's hard heart.
Main characters. Jonah, the sailors, the king of Nineveh.
Key passages
  • 1 — Jonah flees toward Tarshish
  • 2 — the prayer from the fish ("salvation belongs to the Lord")
  • 3 — Nineveh repents
  • 4 — Jonah angry and the plant

How it points to Christ. Jesus calls his resurrection "the sign of Jonah": three days and nights, then life (Matt 12:39–41). "Something greater than Jonah is here," a prophet who doesn't flee but goes willingly to save his enemies.

Going deeper. Jonah is a story about a prophet who believes the right doctrine, that God is gracious and merciful (4:2, quoting Exod 34:6), but resents it when that grace reaches his enemies. The book ends with God's unanswered question, which is aimed at the reader. Jesus points to "the sign of Jonah": three days and nights, then a message of repentance to the nations (Matt 12:39–41). Jonah's prayer, "Salvation belongs to the Lord!" (2:9), is a fine one-line summary of Reformed soteriology.

Reformed note Jonah 2:9 is a short statement of the Reformed doctrine of salvation: from start to finish, salvation is God's work. The book also shows God's sovereignty over storms, fish, plants, and worms.

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Jonah bibleproject.com/videos/jonah/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • A story about a prophet rather than a collection of his oracles. It is a "subversive story about a rebellious prophet who hates God for loving his enemies." The only other mention of Jonah (2 Kings 14:25) has him backing Jeroboam II, whom Amos opposed, so readers start out suspicious.
  • Design: chapters 1 and 3 are encounters with non-Israelites (sailors, then Ninevites), and chapters 2 and 4 are Jonah's prayers. Characters behave opposite to type: the prophet rebels, and the pagans repent. The video calls the book satire, using humor and irony.
  • Chapter 1: sent east to Nineveh, Assyria's capital, Jonah flees west to Tarshish and sleeps through a storm. He confesses the God "who made the sea and the dry land" while fleeing by sea. "Throw me overboard" may be one more way to avoid Nineveh. The sailors pray, spare him as long as they can, and end up worshipping the Lord.
  • Chapter 2: the great fish turns certain death into passage back to life. Jonah thanks God and vows to obey but never quite repents, and the fish vomits him onto land.
  • Chapter 3: his five-word sermon (in Hebrew) sets off repentance from king to cattle. God relents. The word "overturned" can mean destroyed or transformed, and Nineveh was overturned by repenting.
  • Chapter 4: Jonah admits he fled because God is "gracious… and merciful, slow to anger," quoting Exodus as a complaint, and asks to die. God gives and takes a shade plant and asks whether he should not pity a great city full of people and animals.
  • The book ends on God's question, aimed at the reader: are you okay with God loving your enemies?
A Reformed response to the video The video's literary reading brings out real irony. Reformed readers add that Jesus treated Jonah as a historical sign: "as Jonah was three days and three nights in the belly of the great fish, so will the Son of Man be… in the heart of the earth" (Matt 12:40–41). The men of Nineveh will rise at the judgment, which hardly fits pure fiction. Reading the book as satire need not mean denying the events, but that should be said clearly. The book's center is "Salvation belongs to the Lord!" (2:9), a fine summary of sovereign grace. Its picture of a repentant Gentile city encourages hope that whole peoples will turn to God.

title: Micah
html:
Micah

7 chapters

“He has told you, O man, what is good; and what does the Lord require of you but to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God?” (Micah 6:8, ESV)

Setting. Micah of Moresheth was a contemporary of Isaiah (about 735–700 BC). He spoke to both Samaria and Jerusalem.

Where it fits. Divided Kingdom → Judah alone — c. 735–700 BC, under Jotham, Ahaz, and Hezekiah. He is Isaiah's contemporary. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Judgment and hope (1–2).
  2. Corrupt leaders and the future Zion (3–5): The nations stream to the mountain of the Lord, and a ruler comes from Bethlehem (5:2).
  3. God's lawsuit and final hope (6–7): "Who is a God like you?"
Main themes. Corrupt leadership; justice and mercy; the future king from Bethlehem; God's pardoning grace.
Main characters. Micah.
Key passages
  • 1–3 — judgment on Samaria and Jerusalem's leaders
  • 4:1–5 — the mountain of the Lord and swords into plowshares
  • 5:2 — the ruler from Bethlehem
  • 6:8 — do justice, love kindness, walk humbly
  • 7:18–20 — "who is a God like you?"

How it points to Christ. Matthew 2:6 cites 5:2: the ruler born in Bethlehem "whose coming forth is from of old" is Jesus. Micah 7:18–19, about God casting all our sins into the depths of the sea, is fulfilled at the cross.

Going deeper. Micah holds together judgment and hope in sharp turns. Micah 4:1–5 (shared with Isaiah 2) pictures the nations streaming to learn God's ways and beating their swords into plowshares. Postmillennialists take it as a promise the gospel will increasingly fulfill before Christ returns. Micah 6:8 is not a substitute for the gospel. It describes the life of those who have been forgiven by the God who "casts all our sins into the depths of the sea" (7:19). Micah 5:2 locates the Messiah's birth in Bethlehem and says his "coming forth is from of old," which hints at his eternal existence.

Reformed note Micah 4:1–4, where the nations beat swords into plowshares, is a favorite postmillennial text for the peace the gospel will bring to the nations in history. 6:8 describes the life of the justified. It isn't a way to be justified.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • Micah of Moresheth was a contemporary of Isaiah in Judah. He warned that Assyria would destroy the north and ravage Jerusalem, and that Babylon would later bring worse. "I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the Lord, and with justice."
  • The book alternates accusation and hope. Chapters 1–2: God appears as at Sinai, but now in judgment after centuries of rebellion. Leaders grew rich by theft (recalling Ahab and Naboth's vineyard), and prophets sold promises of safety.
  • Chapters 3–4a: bribery, courts bent toward the rich, and the poor robbed of family land, against the Torah. Zion will be "plowed as a field." Each warning ends in hope: God as shepherd gathering a remnant, and the temple mountain exalted so that the nations stream to it and swords are beaten into plowshares.
  • Chapters 4b–5: exile to Babylon, then return. A ruler from Bethlehem will shepherd the restored people, and the remnant will be a blessing among the nations while God removes evil.
  • Chapters 6–7: more economic injustice, and the famous summary: "to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God."
  • The ending: Israel sits in shame and watches for mercy, appealing to God's character ("Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity?") and to his oath to Abraham and Jacob. "You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea."
A Reformed response to the video Matthew cites 5:2 for Jesus' birth in Bethlehem (Matt 2:5–6). The ruler's "coming forth is from of old, from ancient days," which Calvin and many Reformed interpreters see as pointing to the Son's eternal origin. Micah 6:8 is often read as a summary of what God requires. Read in context, it follows God's saving acts (6:3–5) and does not replace sacrifice and atonement. It describes the life of a people God has redeemed. The nations streaming to Zion (4:1–4) is a favorite postmillennial text, read as the gospel age, not only the eternal state.

BibleProject is the author and owner of this content. Visit bibleproject.com . What the video covers (our summary) Micah of Moresheth was a contemporary of Isaiah in Judah. He warned that Assyria would destroy the north and ravage Jerusalem, and that Babylon would later bring worse. "I am filled with power, with the Spirit of the Lord, and with justice." The book alternates accusation and hope. Chapters 1–2: God appears as at Sinai, but now in judgment after centuries of rebellion. Leaders grew rich by theft (recalling Ahab and Naboth's vineyard), and prophets sold promises of safety. Chapters 3–4a: bribery, courts bent toward the rich, and the poor robbed of family land, against the Torah. Zion will be "plowed as a field." Each warning ends in hope: God as shepherd gathering a remnant, and the temple mountain exalted so that the nations stream to it and swords are beaten into plowshares. Chapters 4b–5: exile to Babylon, then return. A ruler from Bethlehem will shepherd the restored people, and the remnant will be a blessing among the nations while God removes evil. Chapters 6–7: more economic injustice, and the famous summary: "to do justice, and to love kindness, and to walk humbly with your God." The ending: Israel sits in shame and watches for mercy, appealing to God's character ("Who is a God like you, pardoning iniquity?") and to his oath to Abraham and Jacob. "You will cast all our sins into the depths of the sea." A Reformed response to the video Matthew cites 5:2 for Jesus' birth in Bethlehem (Matt 2:5–6). The ruler's "coming forth is from of old, from ancient days," which Calvin and many Reformed interpreters see as pointing to the Son's eternal origin. Micah 6:8 is often read as a summary of what God requires. Read in context, it follows God's saving acts (6:3–5) and does not replace sacrifice and atonement. It describes the life of a people God has redeemed. The nations streaming to Zion (4:1–4) is a favorite postmillennial text, read as the gospel age, not only the eternal state.

title: Nahum
html:
Nahum

3 chapters

“The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him.” (Nahum 1:7, ESV)

Setting. Nahum prophesied Nineveh's fall (612 BC) about a century after Jonah, for Judah suffering under Assyria.

Where it fits. Judah alone — Between the fall of Thebes (663 BC, 3:8) and the fall of Nineveh (612 BC). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. The Lord's character (1): A jealous, avenging God who is good to those who take refuge in him.
  2. Nineveh's fall described (2).
  3. Woe to the bloody city (3).
Main themes. God's justice against oppressors; his goodness to the oppressed; the end of tyrants.
Main characters. Nineveh, the king of Assyria.
Key passages
  • 1:2–8 — the jealous, avenging, and good Lord
  • 1:15 — the feet of him who brings good news
  • 2–3 — the fall of Nineveh described

How it points to Christ. Nahum announces "good news" of peace (1:15), the same language Isaiah uses (52:7) and Paul applies to the gospel (Rom 10:15). Christ finally defeats every oppressor.

Going deeper. Nahum is Jonah's sequel. About a century later, Nineveh has returned to its cruelty, and this time judgment comes. The book is a strong comfort to the oppressed: God's patience is not indifference, and tyrants don't have the last word. Reformed theology sees God's justice and goodness as inseparable (1:3, 7). Nahum's "good news" (1:15) of a defeated oppressor is echoed in Isaiah 52:7 and Romans 10:15, where the greatest oppressor, sin and death, is defeated in Christ.

Reformed note Nahum reminds us that God's patience (Jonah) is not indifference. The same God who forgave Nineveh will judge it when it hardens again.

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Nahum bibleproject.com/videos/nahum/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Poems announcing the fall of Assyria and its capital Nineveh. Assyria was one of the first great empires, violent on a new scale, and it destroyed the northern kingdom. Nineveh fell to a Babylonian-led rebellion in 612 BC.
  • Chapter 1: an incomplete alphabet poem on God's appearing, like the opening of Micah and the close of Habakkuk. It quotes God's self-description from Exodus 34: "The Lord is slow to anger and great in power, and the Lord will by no means clear the guilty." The poem contrasts arrogant nations with the remnant who take refuge in God.
  • Chapter 1 never names Nineveh. It borrows Isaiah's language about Babylon's later fall and its "good news" to Zion. Nineveh becomes an image of how God brings down violent empires in every age, a message close to Daniel's.
  • Chapter 2: the battle for Nineveh in stages: the front line, chariots, the breached walls, slaughter and plunder.
  • Chapter 3: "Woe to the bloody city!" Injustice was built into the system that made Assyria successful, and its violence sowed its own destruction. The book ends with a taunt: the king's wound is fatal, and the nations he oppressed clap their hands.
  • The good news: God cares about the innocent, and his goodness requires him to bring oppressors down. "The Lord is good, a stronghold in the day of trouble; he knows those who take refuge in him."
A Reformed response to the video Nahum's bluntness about God's vengeance (1:2) is a needed corrective. Reformed theology does not treat God's wrath as merely a natural consequence. It is the holy Judge acting personally against evil. Jonah and Nahum belong together. Nineveh's repentance under Jonah was real, but it did not last, and God's patience eventually gives way to judgment. Both mercy and justice belong to the same God of Exodus 34:6–7. The "good news" and "peace" of 1:15 come to their fullest meaning in the gospel of Christ's victory over the powers (Rom 10:15; Col 2:15).

title: Habakkuk
html:
Habakkuk

3 chapters

“But the righteous shall live by his faith.” (Habakkuk 2:4, ESV)

Setting. Habakkuk prophesied in Judah shortly before the Babylonian invasion (about 609–598 BC). The book is a dialogue between the prophet and God.

Where it fits. Judah alone — c. 609–605 BC, as Babylon rises (1:6). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. First complaint and answer (1:1–11): Why do you tolerate evil? Answer: I'm raising up Babylon.
  2. Second complaint and answer (1:12–2:20): How can you use the wicked? Answer: The righteous live by faith, woes on Babylon, and the earth will be filled with God's glory.
  3. Habakkuk's prayer (3): "Though the fig tree should not blossom… yet I will rejoice in the Lord."
Main themes. Theodicy; living by faith; God's justice in his timing; joy in God when circumstances fail.
Main characters. Habakkuk, the Babylonians (Chaldeans).
Key passages
  • 1:2–4 — "how long, O Lord?"
  • 1:5–11 — God raises up the Babylonians
  • 2:4 — the righteous shall live by his faith
  • 2:14 — the earth filled with the knowledge of the Lord's glory
  • 3:17–19 — "yet I will rejoice"

How it points to Christ. Paul uses 2:4 for justification by faith (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11), and Hebrews uses it for persevering faith (Heb 10:38). Christ is the object of that faith.

Going deeper. Habakkuk models honest argument with God that ends in worship. His key verse, 2:4, is quoted three times in the New Testament (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11; Heb 10:38) and became a watchword of the Reformation for justification by faith alone. 2:14 is a central postmillennial text, a promise that the knowledge of God's glory will one day fill the earth "as the waters cover the sea." The closing hymn teaches faith that rejoices in God even when every visible support fails.

Reformed note Habakkuk 2:4 became a watchword of the Reformation. Habakkuk 2:14, "the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord as the waters cover the sea," is one of the texts postmillennialists, Wilson among them, cite most often.

BibleProject video: Habakkuk bibleproject.com/videos/habakkuk/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Habakkuk lived in Judah's last decades, as Babylon rose. Unlike other prophets, he addresses all his words to God: they are laments about believing God is good amid evil.
  • First complaint: the Torah is neglected and violence goes unchecked under corrupt leaders, so why does God do nothing? God answers that he is raising up Babylon to judge Judah.
  • Second complaint: Babylon is worse. It worships its own military power and gathers people like fish in a net. How can a holy God use it? Habakkuk takes his stand as a watchman.
  • God's answer: write the vision plainly. It awaits its appointed time: "if it seems slow, wait for it." "The righteous shall live by his faith." Babylon will fall too. God's using a nation does not mean he endorses it.
  • Five woes: extortion and debt traps, unjust gain, building with forced labor, drunken leaders, and the idolatry of money, power and security behind it all. Most nations eventually become Babylon, so the answer speaks to every generation.
  • Chapter 3: a prayer and an ancient poem of God's appearing, as at Sinai, and a future exodus in which the divine warrior strikes "the house of the wicked" and saves "your anointed."
  • Ending: "Though the fig tree should not blossom… yet I will rejoice in the Lord." Habakkuk shows what living by faith looks like.
A Reformed response to the video The video reads 2:4 as trusting the vision's hope, which is true, but it does not mention the verse's biggest role. Paul quotes it twice as the charter text for justification by faith apart from works (Rom 1:17; Gal 3:11), and Hebrews quotes it too (Heb 10:38). Luther's discovery of the righteousness of God in Romans 1:17 sparked the Reformation. 2:14 ("the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the Lord as the waters cover the sea") is a key postmillennial text. Habakkuk also models a Reformed view of providence: God governs even wicked agents for holy ends without sharing their guilt (WCF 5.4; compare Isa 10:5–7).

title: Zephaniah
html:
Zephaniah

3 chapters

“The Lord your God is in your midst, a mighty one who will save; he will rejoice over you with gladness.” (Zephaniah 3:17, ESV)

Setting. Zephaniah, a descendant of Hezekiah, prophesied during Josiah's reign (about 640–609 BC), probably before Josiah's reforms.

Where it fits. Judah alone — Under Josiah, c. 640–620 BC, probably before the reform of 622. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. The coming Day of the Lord on Judah (1).
  2. Judgment on the nations (2–3:8).
  3. Purified peoples and a rejoicing God (3:9–20).
Main themes. The Day of the Lord; humility; a purified remnant; the nations' conversion; God's joy over his people.
Main characters. Zephaniah.
Key passages
  • 1:14–18 — the great day of the Lord
  • 2 — judgment on surrounding nations
  • 3:9 — the peoples given pure speech to call on the Lord
  • 3:14–20 — the Lord rejoices over his people with singing

How it points to Christ. God promises to change the speech of the peoples so they call on his name (3:9), a reversal of Babel fulfilled at Pentecost. Christ is the mighty one in our midst who saves.

Going deeper. Zephaniah begins with one of the darkest pictures of the day of the Lord (the medieval hymn Dies Irae draws on 1:15) and ends with one of the tenderest: God singing over his redeemed people (3:17). Both are true at once, and the cross is where they meet. 3:9 promises that the nations will be given "pure speech" to call on the Lord, which many readers see as a reversal of Babel, beginning at Pentecost.

Reformed note The God who judges also sings over his redeemed (3:17). This is a fitting picture of the gospel: wrath is satisfied, so joy takes its place.

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Zephaniah bibleproject.com/videos/zephaniah/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Zephaniah preached in Judah's last decades, under Josiah, whose reforms could not undo entrenched idolatry. The book has three parts: the day of the Lord against Judah, then against the nations and Jerusalem, then hope beyond judgment.
  • Chapters 1–2:3: the poem opens by reversing Genesis 1, with creation falling back into chaos. Jerusalem's world will end: idol shrines, unjust leaders, crooked markets and the city walls. Zephaniah never names the army (Babylon). He wants to stress that God is the one orchestrating events.
  • Hope for a remnant: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land… perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord."
  • 2:4–3:8: judgment on Philistia, Moab, Ammon and even Assyria, and finally on Jerusalem, whose leaders are so corrupt that God treats them like another foreign nation. God will gather the nations and pour out his burning anger.
  • 3:9–20, the surprise: the fire purifies. God will change the peoples' speech so they all call on the Lord's name, fulfilling the promise to Abraham. A humbled remnant rejoices in the restored city.
  • God himself sings: "he will rejoice over you with gladness… he will exult over you with loud singing." He gathers the outcast, the lame and the shamed and honors them. Justice and love together are the world's hope.
A Reformed response to the video Zephaniah 1:14–18 inspired the medieval hymn Dies Irae. The book does not soften God's wrath, and Reformed readers should not either. The purifying fire of 3:8–9 is not universalism. Its fruit is "a people humble and lowly" who take refuge in the Lord (3:12), the elect remnant from every nation. The gift of "pure speech" to the peoples (3:9) reverses Babel, and Christians have long seen it begun at Pentecost (Acts 2:5–11). 3:17, God singing over his people, is a tender picture of his delight in those he has saved.

The book has three parts: the day of the Lord against Judah, then against the nations and Jerusalem, then hope beyond judgment. Chapters 1–2:3: the poem opens by reversing Genesis 1, with creation falling back into chaos. Jerusalem's world will end: idol shrines, unjust leaders, crooked markets and the city walls. Zephaniah never names the army (Babylon). He wants to stress that God is the one orchestrating events. Hope for a remnant: "Seek the Lord, all you humble of the land… perhaps you may be hidden on the day of the anger of the Lord." 2:4–3:8: judgment on Philistia, Moab, Ammon and even Assyria, and finally on Jerusalem, whose leaders are so corrupt that God treats them like another foreign nation. God will gather the nations and pour out his burning anger. 3:9–20, the surprise: the fire purifies. God will change the peoples' speech so they all call on the Lord's name, fulfilling the promise to Abraham. A humbled remnant rejoices in the restored city. God himself sings: "he will rejoice over you with gladness… he will exult over you with loud singing." He gathers the outcast, the lame and the shamed and honors them. Justice and love together are the world's hope. A Reformed response to the video Zephaniah 1:14–18 inspired the medieval hymn Dies Irae . The book does not soften God's wrath, and Reformed readers should not either. The purifying fire of 3:8–9 is not universalism. Its fruit is "a people humble and lowly" who take refuge in the Lord (3:12), the elect remnant from every nation. The gift of "pure speech" to the peoples (3:9) reverses Babel, and Christians have long seen it begun at Pentecost (Acts 2:5–11). 3:17, God singing over his people, is a tender picture of his delight in those he has saved.

title: Haggai
html:
Haggai

2 chapters

“The latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former.” (Haggai 2:9, ESV)

Setting. Haggai preached four dated messages in 520 BC to returned exiles who had stopped rebuilding the temple and were building their own houses instead.

Where it fits. Return — Four messages dated to 520 BC, Darius I's 2nd year. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Consider your ways (1): The people put their own houses first, and they obey.
  2. The greater glory (2:1–9): God will shake the nations and fill this house with glory.
  3. Defilement and blessing (2:10–19).
  4. Zerubbabel the signet ring (2:20–23).
Main themes. Priorities; God's presence; obedience; the future glory of God's house; the Davidic line.
Main characters. Haggai, Zerubbabel, Joshua the high priest.
Key passages
  • 1:2–11 — "consider your ways": paneled houses and a ruined temple
  • 1:12–15 — the people obey and the Lord stirs their spirit
  • 2:6–9 — the shaking of the nations and the latter glory
  • 2:20–23 — Zerubbabel the signet ring

How it points to Christ. The greater glory came when Christ himself entered the temple. Zerubbabel, God's "signet ring," is in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:12–13), and Hebrews 12:26–28 applies the shaking of all things to Christ's unshakable kingdom.

Going deeper. Haggai challenges God's people to put his house first rather than their own comfort, and it shows God's blessing following obedience. Its promise that the latter house will have greater glory was fulfilled when Christ himself, God in the flesh, came to that temple. Hebrews 12:26–28 applies the shaking of 2:6 to the present age: everything that can be shaken will be removed, and we are receiving "a kingdom that cannot be shaken." That fits well with a postmillennial confidence in Christ's advancing kingdom.

Reformed note Haggai teaches that God's worship should come first in a believer's life and a community's priorities. It is a call the Reformed tradition applies to the church and to Christian culture-building.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • The year is 520 BC, about 70 years after the exile. Persia has let the exiles return. The governor Zerubbabel, a son of David, and the high priest Joshua lead the rebuilding (Ezra 1–6). Four messages are dated over four months.
  • Chapter 1: misplaced priorities. The people live in "paneled houses, while this house lies in ruins." Drought and poor harvests echo the covenant curses of Deuteronomy. Leaders and people respond and start rebuilding (Ezra 5).
  • 2:1–9, a month later: morale sags because the new temple looks like nothing next to Solomon's. Haggai recalls the promises of Isaiah and Micah: God will shake the nations, their treasures will come, and "the latter glory of this house shall be greater than the former… and in this place I will give peace."
  • 2:10–19, two months later: a question about ritual purity. Uncleanness spreads by contact, but holiness does not. Without repentance from injustice and apathy, even the temple they are building will be unclean. The video frames this as a choice, like Moses before the land: faithfulness leads to blessing.
  • 2:20–23: God will overthrow kingdoms as he did Pharaoh's chariots and make Zerubbabel his "signet ring," the Davidic hope in that generation. The book leaves the question open: will this generation and this son of David be faithful? Read on in Zechariah and Malachi.
A Reformed response to the video The video says that in a sense Israel's future "lay in their hands." Haggai does treat obedience as real and as a means God uses. But it also says who caused the obedience: "the Lord stirred up the spirit of Zerubbabel… and the spirit of all the remnant" (1:14). God both commands and enables, and his appointed means never compete with his sovereignty (WCF 5.3; Phil 2:12–13). The "greater glory" of 2:7–9 was fulfilled when the Lord himself came to this second temple (Mal 3:1; John 2:19–21). Hebrews 12:26–28 applies the shaking of 2:6 to the unshakable kingdom we are receiving now. Zerubbabel the "signet ring" stands in the line of Christ (Matt 1:12–13), so the promise was not lost when he died.

title: Zechariah
html:
Zechariah

14 chapters

“Behold, your king is coming to you; righteous and having salvation is he, humble and mounted on a donkey.” (Zechariah 9:9, ESV)

Setting. Zechariah was a priest-prophet and contemporary of Haggai (from 520 BC). He encouraged the returnees with visions and messianic oracles.

Where it fits. Return — Begins in 520 BC. Chapters 9–14 may be later, perhaps after 480 BC †. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Call to return (1:1–6).
  2. Eight night visions (1:7–6:15): Horsemen, horns, a measuring line, Joshua cleansed, the lampstand, the flying scroll, and Joshua crowned as the Branch.
  3. Fasting versus faithfulness (7–8).
  4. Two oracles (9–14): The humble king, the rejected shepherd sold for thirty pieces of silver, the one they pierced, the struck shepherd, and the Lord as king over all the earth.
Main themes. Return and restoration; cleansing from sin; the Branch (priest-king); the shepherd rejected; God's universal reign.
Main characters. Zechariah, Joshua the high priest, Zerubbabel.
Key passages
  • 1–6 — eight night visions
  • 3 — Joshua the high priest's filthy garments replaced
  • 4:6 — "not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit"
  • 9:9 — the humble king on a donkey
  • 12:10 — "him whom they have pierced"
  • 13:7 — strike the shepherd
  • 14 — the Lord king over all the earth

How it points to Christ. Zechariah is full of passion-week texts: the triumphal entry (9:9), thirty pieces of silver (11:12–13), "they look on me, on him whom they have pierced" (12:10), and "strike the shepherd" (13:7). Christ is the Branch who unites priest and king (6:12–13).

Going deeper. Zechariah is the Old Testament book most quoted in the Gospels' passion narratives: the king on a donkey, thirty pieces of silver, the pierced one, the shepherd struck and the sheep scattered. Chapter 3 is a vivid picture of justification. The accused priest's filthy clothes are removed and replaced with clean robes, by God's act alone. 4:6 reminds the church that the kingdom advances by the Spirit, not by worldly power. Postmillennialists take that as the method of the kingdom's growth, not a reason to doubt it.

Reformed note The cleansing of Joshua the high priest (3), whose filthy garments are replaced with clean ones, is a vivid Old Testament picture of imputed righteousness.

BibleProject video: Zechariah bibleproject.com/videos/zechariah/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Set after the return from exile. With Haggai, Zechariah urged the people to rebuild the temple (Ezra 5–6). Jeremiah's 70 years are nearly up, but life is hard, so why haven't the promises come?
  • Structure: a call to return (1:1–6), eight night visions (1–6), a sermon (7–8), then two collections of oracles about the messianic future (9–11 and 12–14).
  • The night visions are arranged in matching pairs. Visions 1 and 8, horsemen and chariots patrolling the earth: the world is at rest under Persia. Is now the time? God is determined to fulfill his promises but leaves the timing open.
  • Visions 2 and 7, Israel's past: horns (Assyria and Babylon) scattered by craftsmen (Persia), and a woman in a basket, Israel's long rebellion, carried off to Babylon on stork wings. Visions 3 and 6, the new Jerusalem: a man measuring the city, a beacon for the nations, and a flying scroll that purges thieves and liars.
  • Visions 4 and 5, at the center: the high priest Joshua's filthy garments replaced with clean ones (grace and forgiveness), and a golden lampstand fed by two olive trees, the two anointed leaders. "Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit."
  • Then a crown is set on Joshua as a sign of a coming priest-king, the Branch, "if you will diligently obey." In chapters 7–8, mourners ask whether they can stop fasting, and Zechariah turns the question back on them: be a people ready for the kingdom by doing justice and keeping covenant.
  • Chapters 9–11: a humble king comes to Zion on a donkey. He is pictured as a shepherd rejected by people and leaders, and he is valued at thirty pieces of silver. Chapters 12–14: God defeats evil among the nations, pours out "a spirit of grace and pleas for mercy" so that Israel mourns "him whom they have pierced," opens a fountain for sin, and makes Jerusalem a new Eden, with living waters flowing out and the nations coming to worship.
A Reformed response to the video The video presents the kingdom as depending on the people's faithfulness. Zechariah does call for repentance, but the climax is God's initiative: God pours out the Spirit of grace, and only then do they mourn (12:10). God himself opens the fountain for sin (13:1). The New Testament quotes Zechariah's messianic texts more than almost any other prophet's: the donkey (Matt 21:5; John 12:15), the thirty pieces of silver (Matt 27:9–10), the pierced one (John 19:37; Rev 1:7), and the struck shepherd (Matt 26:31). Joshua crowned as priest and king (6:12–13) is fulfilled in Christ, who unites both offices (Heb 7). Many postmillennial readers take 14:9, "the Lord will be king over all the earth," as the goal toward which the gospel age is moving.

title: Malachi
html:
Malachi

4 chapters

“For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name will be great among the nations.” (Malachi 1:11, ESV)

Setting. Malachi ("my messenger") prophesied around 450–430 BC, around Nehemiah's time, to a spiritually indifferent post-exilic community.

Where it fits. Return — c. 433–420 BC, around Nehemiah's second term. It is the last Old Testament prophet. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Six disputes: God's love (1:2–5), polluted offerings (1:6–14), corrupt priests (2:1–9), faithless marriages (2:10–16), God's justice (2:17–3:5), robbing God (3:6–12), and the righteous and the wicked (3:13–4:3).
  2. Remember Moses, and await Elijah (4:4–6).
Main themes. God's electing love; true worship; covenant faithfulness in marriage; tithes; the coming messenger and day.
Main characters. Malachi, the priests, the people.
Key passages
  • 1:2–5 — "I have loved you"
  • 1:6–14 — polluted offerings and God's name great among the nations
  • 2:10–16 — faithlessness in marriage (ESV 2:16: "the man who does not love his wife but divorces her… covers his garment with violence")
  • 3:1 — the messenger who prepares the way
  • 3:6–12 — tithes and the windows of heaven
  • 4:5–6 — Elijah before the day of the Lord

How it points to Christ. The messenger who prepares the way (3:1) and "Elijah" (4:5) are fulfilled in John the Baptist, and the Lord who suddenly comes to his temple is Jesus (Mark 1:2; Matt 11:10–14).

Going deeper. Malachi closes the Old Testament prophets with a cooled-off people who still worship, but grudgingly. It is a mirror for nominal churches. Its marriage passage (2:13–16) grounds faithfulness in God's covenant purpose of "godly offspring." Reformed teaching on marriage often stresses this text. The last words promise Elijah, whom Jesus identifies as John the Baptist (Matt 11:14; 17:12–13). After four hundred years of silence, the next voice in the story is a herald in the wilderness.

Reformed note Paul cites 1:2–3 in Romans 9:13 ("Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated") to teach unconditional election, as Calvin stressed. 1:11 is a promise that God's name will one day be honored among the nations worldwide.
