BibleProject video: Malachi bibleproject.com/videos/malachi/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • About a century after the return, the temple stands but things are going badly (compare Ezra–Nehemiah). The returned community proved as unfaithful as its ancestors, and exile had not changed hard hearts.
  • The book is built as six disputes. God makes a claim, Israel objects ("How have you…?"), and God has the last word. The first three expose corruption, and the last three confront it.
  • 1. "I have loved you." "How have you loved us?" God points to his choice of Jacob over Esau, whose nation came to ruin. 2. The temple despised: blind, lame and sick animals offered, with priests joining in. 3. Treachery against God and wives: marrying worshippers of other gods (Nehemiah 13) and a wave of divorces. Malachi calls it covenant betrayal.
  • 4. "Where is the God of justice?" God will send his messenger to prepare the way, then come himself like a refiner's fire to purify his people. 5. "Return to me." "How shall we return?" They are robbing God by withholding the tithe (one tenth) that supported the temple, and he promises blessing for faithfulness.
  • 6. "It is vain to serve God," since the arrogant prosper. Here God answers with a story: those who fear the Lord talk together, and "a book of remembrance" is written. The video sees this as a reflection on the gift of Scripture. For them "the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings."
  • The last three verses close the whole Law and Prophets: "Remember the law of my servant Moses," and "I will send you Elijah the prophet" to turn hearts before the day of the Lord. Scripture is a unified story that points ahead to a messenger and to God's own coming.
A Reformed response to the video The New Testament identifies the messenger of 3:1 and the Elijah of 4:5 as John the Baptist (Matt 11:10–14; Mark 1:2; Luke 1:17). It identifies the Lord who "will suddenly come to his temple" as Jesus. So the Christ whom Malachi points to is God himself coming. Paul uses 1:2–3 ("Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated") for God's sovereign election (Rom 9:13). Reformed Christians differ on whether the tithe binds the church today. All agree that generous, regular giving to support the ministry is a New Testament duty (1 Cor 9:13–14; 2 Cor 9:6–7). On divorce, see the key passage note on 2:16 above.

( Timelines ) The Flow of the Book Six disputes : God's love (1:2–5), polluted offerings (1:6–14), corrupt priests (2:1–9), faithless marriages (2:10–16), God's justice (2:17–3:5), robbing God (3:6–12), and the righteous and the wicked (3:13–4:3). Remember Moses, and await Elijah (4:4–6) . Main themes. God's electing love; true worship; covenant faithfulness in marriage; tithes; the coming messenger and day. Main characters. Malachi, the priests, the people. Key passages 1:2–5 — "I have loved you" 1:6–14 — polluted offerings and God's name great among the nations 2:10–16 — faithlessness in marriage (ESV 2:16: "the man who does not love his wife but divorces her… covers his garment with violence") 3:1 — the messenger who prepares the way 3:6–12 — tithes and the windows of heaven 4:5–6 — Elijah before the day of the Lord How it points to Christ. The messenger who prepares the way (3:1) and "Elijah" (4:5) are fulfilled in John the Baptist, and the Lord who suddenly comes to his temple is Jesus (Mark 1:2; Matt 11:10–14). Going deeper. Malachi closes the Old Testament prophets with a cooled-off people who still worship, but grudgingly. It is a mirror for nominal churches. Its marriage passage (2:13–16) grounds faithfulness in God's covenant purpose of "godly offspring." Reformed teaching on marriage often stresses this text. The last words promise Elijah, whom Jesus identifies as John the Baptist (Matt 11:14; 17:12–13). After four hundred years of silence, the next voice in the story is a herald in the wilderness. Reformed note Paul cites 1:2–3 in Romans 9:13 ("Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated") to teach unconditional election, as Calvin stressed. 1:11 is a promise that God's name will one day be honored among the nations worldwide. What the video covers (our summary) About a century after the return, the temple stands but things are going badly (compare Ezra–Nehemiah). The returned community proved as unfaithful as its ancestors, and exile had not changed hard hearts. The book is built as six disputes. God makes a claim, Israel objects ("How have you…?"), and God has the last word. The first three expose corruption, and the last three confront it. 1. "I have loved you." "How have you loved us?" God points to his choice of Jacob over Esau, whose nation came to ruin. 2. The temple despised: blind, lame and sick animals offered, with priests joining in. 3. Treachery against God and wives: marrying worshippers of other gods (Nehemiah 13) and a wave of divorces. Malachi calls it covenant betrayal. 4. "Where is the God of justice?" God will send his messenger to prepare the way, then come himself like a refiner's fire to purify his people. 5. "Return to me." "How shall we return?" They are robbing God by withholding the tithe (one tenth) that supported the temple, and he promises blessing for faithfulness. 6. "It is vain to serve God," since the arrogant prosper. Here God answers with a story: those who fear the Lord talk together, and "a book of remembrance" is written. The video sees this as a reflection on the gift of Scripture. For them "the sun of righteousness shall rise with healing in its wings." The last three verses close the whole Law and Prophets: "Remember the law of my servant Moses," and "I will send you Elijah the prophet" to turn hearts before the day of the Lord. Scripture is a unified story that points ahead to a messenger and to God's own coming. A Reformed response to the video The New Testament identifies the messenger of 3:1 and the Elijah of 4:5 as John the Baptist (Matt 11:10–14; Mark 1:2; Luke 1:17). It identifies the Lord who "will suddenly come to his temple" as Jesus. So the Christ whom Malachi points to is God himself coming. Paul uses 1:2–3 ("Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated") for God's sovereign election (Rom 9:13). Reformed Christians differ on whether the tithe binds the church today. All agree that generous, regular giving to support the ministry is a New Testament duty (1 Cor 9:13–14; 2 Cor 9:6–7). On divorce, see the key passage note on 2:16 above.

title: The New Testament as a Whole
html:
The New Testament as a Whole

BibleProject overview
BibleProject video: New Testament Overview bibleproject.com/videos/new-testament-overview/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • "Testament" means covenant partnership. The Old Testament (TaNaK) is 39 books over more than a thousand years. The New Testament is 27 books written within 30–40 years by first-generation followers of Jesus, collected early and read with the Old Testament as one story that leads to Jesus.
  • Its layout: four Gospels, Acts, thirteen letters of Paul (arranged longest to shortest), Hebrews, James, Peter, John and Jude, and Revelation.
  • The Bible is one epic in several acts. Act 1, God and humanity: the garden temple, rebellion, exile, Babylon, and the promise of a new human who will crush evil. Act 2, God and Israel: the same pattern, longer and more violent, ending in exile to Babylon, but the promise of a priest-king from Abraham's line survives. Act 3, the prophets and poets: the day of the Lord, and a royal priest who suffers like a servant for the sins of Israel and the world and is exalted.
  • The Gospels: Jesus is Abraham's son and the new human, "a human, and more," Israel's God become the faithful Israelite. He defeats evil by letting it kill him on the paradoxical throne of the cross, and rises as the prototype of a new humanity.
  • Acts and the letters: the Spirit spreads Jesus' multiethnic family. Our lives become part of the story: exile and home, Egypt and the Passover Lamb, dust and resurrection.
  • Revelation: the slain Lamb leads his people out of Babylon into the New Jerusalem garden temple, where heaven and earth are reunited and humans rule as God's image. These "human words" carry "a divine word of hope."
A Reformed response to the video The story arc is excellent. Reformed readers will want to supply what BibleProject leaves implicit: the cross as penal substitution, God's just wrath borne by Christ (Rom 3:25–26; Isa 53:5–6), and not only as a demonstration that "non-violence, forgiveness and self-giving love are the most powerful things in the universe." On that point see Packer, "What Did the Cross Achieve?", and Stott and Packer generally.

title: Matthew
html:
Matthew

28 chapters

“All authority in heaven and on earth has been given to me. Go therefore and make disciples of all nations.” (Matthew 28:18–19, ESV)

Setting. Matthew, the tax collector turned apostle, wrote mainly for Jewish Christians, probably in the 60s AD. He shows that Jesus is the promised Messiah who fulfills the Law and the Prophets.

Where it fits. New Testament — Jesus' life, c. 6/4 BC–AD 30/33. Written c. AD 50s–60s, before 70. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Birth and preparation (1–4): The genealogy from Abraham and David, the birth, the baptism, and the temptation.
  2. Five great discourses alternating with narrative: The Sermon on the Mount (5–7), the mission discourse (10), the kingdom parables (13), life in the community (18), and the Olivet Discourse (24–25).
  3. Passion and resurrection (26–28): The cross, the empty tomb, and the Great Commission.
Main themes. Fulfillment ("that it might be fulfilled"); the kingdom of heaven; Jesus as the new Moses and Son of David; true righteousness; the church; mission to the nations.
Main characters. Jesus, Joseph, Mary, John the Baptist, Peter, the Twelve, the Pharisees, Pilate.
Key passages
  • 1:1–17 — the genealogy from Abraham through David
  • 5–7 — the Sermon on the Mount
  • 13 — the kingdom parables (mustard seed and leaven)
  • 16:13–20 — Peter's confession and "I will build my church"
  • 24–25 — the Olivet Discourse
  • 26–27 — the passion
  • 28:18–20 — the Great Commission

How it points to Christ. Matthew presents Jesus as Immanuel ("God with us," 1:23), who will be with his people "to the end of the age" (28:20). He is the true Israel, the greater Moses, and the King who gives his life "as a ransom for many" (20:28).

Going deeper. Matthew presents Jesus as the fulfillment of Israel's Scriptures: the new Moses giving the law on a mountain, the Son of David, and the Son of Man from Daniel 7 who receives "all authority." Postmillennialists find their basic method in the parables of chapter 13. The kingdom begins small, like a mustard seed, and slowly works through the whole world, like leaven through dough. They read the Great Commission as a command that will succeed: "disciple the nations," not just individuals in them. Wilson and Sproul (The Last Days According to Jesus) read much of Matthew 24 as fulfilled in the destruction of Jerusalem in AD 70, inside "this generation" (24:34).

Reformed note The Great Commission is central to Doug Wilson's postmillennialism: Christ already has all authority, and he commands the discipling of whole nations, not just a remnant. Sproul (The Last Days According to Jesus) and Wilson both read much of the Olivet Discourse, "this generation will not pass away" (24:34), as fulfilled in the fall of Jerusalem in AD 70.
Reading BibleProject well BibleProject's two Matthew videos center on "the kingdom of heaven" coming to earth, which is a good emphasis. Reformed readers will also want to keep the cross at the center of how that kingdom comes: the King reigns by first bearing sin (26:28).
Recommended free Reformed commentaries: Matthew
  • Calvin's Commentaries: Harmony of the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) — John Calvin. The fountainhead of Reformed exegesis: plain sense, Christ-centred, and pastoral (vols. 31–33; link opens vol. 31).ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom31
  • Surveying the Text: Matthew — Douglas Wilson. Wilson's one-sermon panorama of the whole book: its structure, themes, and Christ, with postmillennial and covenantal punch.dougwils.com/the-church/s8-expository/surveying-the-text-matthew.html
  • TGC Bible Commentary: Matthew — Douglas Sean O'Donnell (TGC Bible Commentary). A free, modern, section-by-section commentary in TGC's Reformed-evangelical stream, with good help on biblical theology.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/matthew/
More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Matthew 1-13 bibleproject.com/videos/matthew-1-13/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Matthew is anonymous, but early, reliable tradition links it to Matthew the tax collector. It gathers the apostles' memorized eyewitness teaching into a carefully designed book: an introduction, five sections each ending in a long teaching block, and a conclusion.
  • It presents Jesus three ways: the Davidic Messiah, a new and authoritative Moses, and Immanuel, "God with us."
  • The genealogy (son of David, son of Abraham) and the fulfilled prophecies show he is "no mere human. He is God with us." Like Moses, he comes out of Egypt, passes through water, spends forty days in the wilderness and teaches from a mountain.
  • The kingdom is "God's rescue operation for his whole world… through King Jesus." The Sermon on the Mount describes an upside-down kingdom open to all. Jesus fulfills the Torah and transforms hearts to love God and neighbor, including enemies.
  • Nine healing stories, in three sets of three, are interleaved with calls to follow. Jesus sends the Twelve (ch. 10) and warns that Israel's leaders will persecute them.
  • Responses are mixed: crowds are enthusiastic, John and Jesus' family are puzzled, the leaders hostile. The kingdom parables (ch. 13) say the kingdom will keep spreading anyway. BibleProject encourages readers to look up Matthew's Old Testament quotations in context.
BibleProject video: Matthew 14-28 bibleproject.com/videos/matthew-14-28/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The leaders expect a conquering Messiah (Psalm 2, Daniel 2) and plot against Jesus. He feeds a Jewish crowd and a Gentile crowd in the wilderness, as Moses fed Israel.
  • Peter confesses "the Messiah, the Son of the living God" but pictures military victory. Jesus teaches from Isaiah that the Messiah will reign by suffering and dying for his people and the nations.
  • The fourth teaching block and the teaching around it describe the upside-down kingdom: honor through service, forgiveness instead of revenge, wealth given away.
  • At the triumphal entry and the temple disruption, Jesus asserts royal authority over a temple compromised by hypocrisy. The leaders try to trap him in debate, fail, and decide to kill him.
  • The fifth block: woes on the Pharisees, weeping over Jerusalem, and a warning that the leaders' path of revolt will bring Jerusalem and the temple to ruin. Jesus will be vindicated by resurrection and will one day return.
  • At the Last Supper the Passover bread and wine become signs that his death is a redeeming sacrifice. Old Testament citations increase around the cross: he is Isaiah's Servant, "judged on their behalf."
  • The risen king gives the Great Commission, and the book ends as it began, with Immanuel: "I am with you."
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject reads Jesus' warning in Matthew 24 as being about Jerusalem's fall in AD 70 as well as his final return. Partial preterists like Doug Wilson read the chapter much the same way. Sproul's The Last Days According to Jesus works through the question carefully.

title: Mark
html:
Mark

16 chapters

“For even the Son of Man came not to be served but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.” (Mark 10:45, ESV)

Setting. According to early tradition (Papias), John Mark recorded Peter's preaching for believers in Rome facing persecution, probably in the 60s AD. It is the shortest and fastest-moving Gospel ("immediately").

Where it fits. New Testament — Jesus' ministry, c. AD 28–30/33. Written c. AD 50s–60s, by tradition from Peter's preaching in Rome. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Who is Jesus? (1–8:30): Authority over demons, disease, nature, and sin, while people keep misunderstanding him. It climaxes in Peter's confession: "You are the Christ."
  2. The way of the cross (8:31–10:52): Three predictions of the passion, and the call to deny yourself, take up your cross, and follow.
  3. Jerusalem, death, and resurrection (11–16): The temple judged, the Last Supper, Gethsemane, the cross ("Truly this man was the Son of God!"), and the empty tomb.
Main themes. The secret of the Messiah's identity; the suffering Son of Man; discipleship as cross-bearing; faith versus fear; the kingdom coming in power.
Main characters. Jesus, Peter, James and John, the disciples, the Roman centurion, the women at the tomb.
Key passages
  • 1:1 — "the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God"
  • 1:14–15 — "the kingdom of God is at hand"
  • 4 — the sower
  • 8:27–38 — Peter's confession and the first passion prediction
  • 10:45 — the ransom saying
  • 14:36 — the cup in Gethsemane
  • 15:34–39 — the cry of dereliction and the centurion's confession

How it points to Christ. Mark's Gospel turns on the cross. Jesus is the Christ and the Son of God, and he wins by dying as a ransom in our place (10:45; 14:24). The torn temple curtain (15:38) opens the way to God.

Going deeper. Mark moves fast ("immediately" appears again and again) and pivots at Peter's confession (8:29), after which everything heads toward the cross. Mark's Jesus is the powerful Son who chooses to suffer. Mark 10:45 and the "cup" of 14:36 (the Old Testament cup of God's wrath) are central for the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution. Discipleship in Mark is cross-shaped: whoever would come after him must deny himself.

Reformed note Mark 10:45 and the "cup" Jesus drinks in Gethsemane (14:36, the Old Testament cup of God's wrath) are central for the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution. On 9:1, see Calvin and Wilson: the kingdom came "with power" within that generation.
Recommended free Reformed commentaries: Mark
  • Calvin's Commentaries: Harmony of the Gospels (Matthew, Mark, Luke) — John Calvin. The fountainhead of Reformed exegesis: plain sense, Christ-centred, and pastoral (vols. 31–33; link opens vol. 31).ccel.org/ccel/calvin/calcom31
  • Surveying the Text: Mark — Douglas Wilson. Wilson's one-sermon panorama of the whole book: its structure, themes, and Christ, with postmillennial and covenantal punch.dougwils.com/the-church/s8-expository/surveying-the-text-mark.html
  • Exposition of the Gospel of Mark (MP3 series) — R. C. Sproul. Sproul's verse-by-verse sermons from Saint Andrew's.monergism.com/gospel-mark-mp3-series
  • TGC Bible Commentary: Mark — Mark L. Strauss (TGC Bible Commentary). A free, modern, section-by-section commentary in TGC's Reformed-evangelical stream, with good help on biblical theology.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/mark/
More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Mark bibleproject.com/videos/mark/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Early tradition links Mark to John Mark, a coworker of Paul and partner of Peter. Papias says Mark recorded Peter's memories. Mark gives his own view only in the first line ("the good news about Jesus the Messiah, the Son of God") and lets Jesus' words and actions do the rest.
  • The book is a drama in three acts. In Galilee everyone asks "who is this?" On the road the disciples struggle to understand what kind of Messiah he is. In Jerusalem comes the paradox of a king crowned through suffering.
  • Isaiah and Malachi promised that God himself would come, and Jesus arrives in his place. At the baptism the heavens open and God says "You are my beloved Son." Jesus heals, casts out evil and forgives sins, which only God can do.
  • The parables of chapter 4 describe a hidden kingdom: soils and a mustard seed.
  • Peter's confession expects a military king, but Jesus is the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 and calls his followers to carry the cross. "The Son of Man came… to give his life as a ransom for many." The Transfiguration shows Jesus as God's glory in a body.
  • In Jerusalem he takes royal authority over the temple and predicts its fall "within a generation." At the Last Supper he gives new meaning to the Passover. At the cross, darkness falls, Jesus cries out, and a Roman centurion is the first person to confess "the Son of God."
  • BibleProject notes that the longer ending is missing from the earliest manuscripts and thinks Mark probably ended abruptly on purpose (16:8, the women's fear), leaving readers to decide whether to run or to proclaim.
A Reformed response to the video Reformed scholars are divided about whether Mark meant to end at 16:8. Most accept the manuscript evidence BibleProject describes, and the ESV brackets 16:9–20 with a note. None of the gospel's central teaching depends on the longer ending.

Key passages 1:1 — "the gospel of Jesus Christ, the Son of God" 1:14–15 — "the kingdom of God is at hand" 4 — the sower 8:27–38 — Peter's confession and the first passion prediction 10:45 — the ransom saying 14:36 — the cup in Gethsemane 15:34–39 — the cry of dereliction and the centurion's confession How it points to Christ. Mark's Gospel turns on the cross. Jesus is the Christ and the Son of God, and he wins by dying as a ransom in our place (10:45; 14:24). The torn temple curtain (15:38) opens the way to God. Going deeper. Mark moves fast ("immediately" appears again and again) and pivots at Peter's confession (8:29), after which everything heads toward the cross. Mark's Jesus is the powerful Son who chooses to suffer. Mark 10:45 and the "cup" of 14:36 (the Old Testament cup of God's wrath) are central for the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution. Discipleship in Mark is cross-shaped: whoever would come after him must deny himself. Reformed note Mark 10:45 and the "cup" Jesus drinks in Gethsemane (14:36, the Old Testament cup of God's wrath) are central for the Reformed doctrine of penal substitution. On 9:1, see Calvin and Wilson: the kingdom came "with power" within that generation. BibleProject is the author and owner of this content. Visit bibleproject.com . What the video covers (our summary) Early tradition links Mark to John Mark, a coworker of Paul and partner of Peter. Papias says Mark recorded Peter's memories. Mark gives his own view only in the first line ("the good news about Jesus the Messiah, the Son of God") and lets Jesus' words and actions do the rest. The book is a drama in three acts. In Galilee everyone asks "who is this?" On the road the disciples struggle to understand what kind of Messiah he is. In Jerusalem comes the paradox of a king crowned through suffering. Isaiah and Malachi promised that God himself would come, and Jesus arrives in his place. At the baptism the heavens open and God says "You are my beloved Son." Jesus heals, casts out evil and forgives sins, which only God can do. The parables of chapter 4 describe a hidden kingdom: soils and a mustard seed. Peter's confession expects a military king, but Jesus is the suffering servant of Isaiah 53 and calls his followers to carry the cross. "The Son of Man came… to give his life as a ransom for many." The Transfiguration shows Jesus as God's glory in a body. In Jerusalem he takes royal authority over the temple and predicts its fall "within a generation." At the Last Supper he gives new meaning to the Passover. At the cross, darkness falls, Jesus cries out, and a Roman centurion is the first person to confess "the Son of God." BibleProject notes that the longer ending is missing from the earliest manuscripts and thinks Mark probably ended abruptly on purpose (16:8, the women's fear), leaving readers to decide whether to run or to proclaim. A Reformed response to the video Reformed scholars are divided about whether Mark meant to end at 16:8. Most accept the manuscript evidence BibleProject describes, and the ESV brackets 16:9–20 with a note. None of the gospel's central teaching depends on the longer ending.

title: Luke
html:
Luke

24 chapters

“For the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost.” (Luke 19:10, ESV)

Setting. Luke, a physician and Paul's companion, wrote an "orderly account" for Theophilus (1:3), probably in the early 60s AD. It is the first of a two-volume work with Acts.

Where it fits. New Testament — Dated by Augustus and Tiberius (2:1; 3:1). Written c. AD 60–62. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Births and preparation (1–4:13): Mary's and Zechariah's songs, the birth, and the temptation.
  2. Ministry in Galilee (4:14–9:50): The Nazareth sermon from Isaiah 61.
  3. Journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19:27): Parables of the lost (15), the good Samaritan, and the rich and the poor.
  4. Jerusalem: death and resurrection (19:28–24): The Emmaus road, where Jesus explains himself from "all the Scriptures."
Main themes. Salvation for outsiders (the poor, women, tax collectors, Gentiles); reversal; the Holy Spirit; prayer; joy; the journey to the cross.
Main characters. Jesus, Mary, Elizabeth, Zechariah, John the Baptist, Zacchaeus, the two thieves, Cleopas.
Key passages
  • 1:46–55 — Mary's Magnificat
  • 2:1–20 — the birth in Bethlehem
  • 4:16–21 — the Nazareth sermon
  • 15 — the lost sheep, coin and sons
  • 19:1–10 — Zacchaeus
  • 23:39–43 — the thief on the cross
  • 24:13–35 — the road to Emmaus
  • 24:44–49 — "everything written about me… must be fulfilled"

How it points to Christ. On the Emmaus road Jesus shows that all of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms are about him (24:27, 44). That is the key to reading the whole Bible, including this guide.

Going deeper. Luke writes an "orderly account" so that Theophilus may have certainty (1:3–4). Christian faith rests on history, not myth. Luke shows Jesus seeking the outsider (tax collectors, sinners, women, Samaritans, the poor), and his parables of grace (ch. 15) are among the clearest pictures of free justification in the Bible. The thief on the cross is the classic example: saved with no works at all, by faith in a dying King. Luke 24:27, 44 is the warrant for reading the whole Old Testament as pointing to Christ, the method behind this whole guide.

Reformed note Luke 24:27 is the warrant for the Reformed practice of reading the Old Testament with Christ at the center, as Calvin did in his commentaries.
Reading BibleProject well BibleProject's two Luke videos (and their Luke–Acts series) highlight reversal and the "upside-down kingdom." That is a good emphasis, as long as it stays rooted in the gospel of forgiveness through the cross (24:46–47) and isn't reduced to social reversal.

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Luke 1-9 bibleproject.com/videos/luke-1-9/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Luke is volume one of Luke–Acts, written by Paul's companion Luke the doctor. It is an "orderly account" of things "fulfilled," the climax of God's story with Israel and the world.
  • The opening pairs the births of John and Jesus. Their songs, full of psalm and prophet echoes, cast John as the promised messenger and Jesus as David's king who will bless the nations as God promised Abraham. Simeon calls the child "a light for the nations."
  • John's baptism gathers a renewed Israel. Luke's genealogy runs back to Adam, so Jesus is for all humanity.
  • In Nazareth Jesus reads Isaiah 61. Luke stresses the social side of the kingdom: "release" (aphesis) recalls the Jubilee, and "the poor" (ani) includes everyone of low status and every outsider.
  • Stories show that good news in action: the sick, a leper, Levi the tax collector, a forgiven sinful woman. Jesus appoints twelve leaders for a new Israel and preaches the Sermon on the Plain about radical generosity, servant leadership and forgiveness.
  • Jesus reveals he will die as Isaiah's suffering servant. At the Transfiguration Moses and Elijah talk about his coming "exodus" (9:31) in Jerusalem, the new Moses leading a freedom march from sin and evil.
BibleProject video: Luke 10-24 bibleproject.com/videos/luke-10-24/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The journey to Jerusalem (9:51–19) presents discipleship as learning on the road: being sent on mission, prayer, trust, and more teaching on money and generosity than anywhere else in the Gospels.
  • Outsiders are transformed (Samaritans, Zacchaeus), and the kingdom is pictured as a great banquet. "He came to seek and to save the lost."
  • Meals with the leaders turn into confrontations, summed up in the prodigal son and the resentful older brother. The only entry requirement is humility and repentance.
  • Jesus weeps over Jerusalem, whose rejection of his kingdom of peace will lead to revolt against Rome. He acts out the temple's coming destruction and predicts Roman armies around the city "within a generation."
  • The Last Supper is a new exodus meal. Luke stresses Jesus' innocence (Pilate says so three times, and Herod finds no fault). Jesus forgives the soldiers and promises the thief "today… in paradise."
  • On the Emmaus road the disciples recognize Jesus in the breaking of bread. BibleProject's point is that when we impose our own agenda Jesus stays hidden, and we see him when we submit to the self-giving way of the cross.
  • The risen Jesus opens the Scriptures, sends forgiveness to the nations and tells the disciples to wait for the Spirit (Acts).
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject gives particular weight to the social side of Luke's "good news to the poor," which is truly there. Reformed readers welcome it but keep the order straight: the deepest release is forgiveness of sins (Luke 24:47). Mercy to the poor grows out of the gospel. It is not a replacement for it.

title: John
html:
John

21 chapters

“But these are written so that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that by believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31, ESV)

Setting. The apostle John, "the disciple whom Jesus loved," wrote late in the first century, probably from Ephesus. His stated purpose is evangelistic (20:31).

Where it fits. New Testament — Jesus' ministry, including three or more Passovers. Written c. AD 85–90 at Ephesus (some say before 70 †). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Prologue (1:1–18): The Word was God and became flesh.
  2. The Book of Signs (1:19–12:50): Seven signs, from water into wine to the raising of Lazarus, along with the "I am" sayings and growing conflict.
  3. The Upper Room (13–17): Foot-washing, the promise of the Spirit, and the high priestly prayer.
  4. The Book of Glory (18–21): Arrest, the cross ("It is finished"), resurrection, Thomas, and the restoration of Peter.
Main themes. The deity of Christ; signs and belief; light and life; glory revealed in the cross; the Spirit; abiding in Christ; sovereign grace.
Main characters. Jesus, John the Baptist, Nicodemus, the Samaritan woman, Lazarus, Martha and Mary, Thomas, Peter, Pilate.
Key passages
  • 1:1–18 — the Word became flesh
  • 3:1–21 — the new birth and "God so loved the world"
  • 6 — the bread of life and the Father's drawing
  • 10 — the Good Shepherd
  • 11 — Lazarus raised
  • 14:6 — the way, the truth and the life
  • 17 — the high priestly prayer
  • 20:28 — "My Lord and my God!"

How it points to Christ. Jesus is the eternal Word, the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world (1:29), the true temple, bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine, and the "I AM" himself (8:58).

Going deeper. John is the most explicitly theological Gospel. Its prologue (1:1–18) and Thomas's confession (20:28) together state the full deity of Christ, the heart of the Nicene faith. John 6 and 10 are central texts for Reformed teaching on grace. No one can come unless the Father draws him (6:44). All the Father gives will come (6:37). The sheep hear and are kept, and no one can snatch them out of the Father's hand (10:27–29). That is unconditional election and perseverance in Jesus' own words. The seven "I am" sayings echo the divine name of Exodus 3:14.

Reformed note D.A. Carson's Pillar commentary on John is a Reformed and evangelical standard, and he argues that 20:31 is aimed at drawing unbelievers to faith. John is rich in sovereign grace: "All that the Father gives me will come to me" (6:37), and "No one can come to me unless the Father… draws him" (6:44).

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: John 1-12 bibleproject.com/videos/john-1-12/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The author is "the disciple whom Jesus loved." BibleProject notes a debate over whether he is John son of Zebedee or a Jerusalem disciple later called John the Elder. The stated purpose is "that you may believe… and… have life in his name" (20:31).
  • The prologue alludes to Genesis 1. The Word is distinct from God ("with God") and yet is God, and he became human, God's tabernacle among us. The one God of Israel is Father and Son.
  • Chapter 1 gives Jesus seven titles, a first sign of John's love of sevens. Each story in chapters 2–12 follows a pattern: a sign or claim, then misunderstanding, then a choice.
  • Jesus fulfills four Jewish institutions: the wedding wine (the generosity of the messianic party), the temple ("destroy this temple"), the rabbi Nicodemus ("born again," a new heart), and the sacred well (living water, eternal life as a new quality of life that begins now).
  • The feasts: on the Sabbath he works as his Father works (equal with God). At Passover he is the bread of life. At Tabernacles he offers water and is "the light of the world." At Hanukkah he is the one set apart, "I and the Father are one."
  • The seventh sign is the raising of Lazarus. Jesus knowingly gives up his own life to give his friend life, which points to the cross.
BibleProject video: John 13-21 bibleproject.com/videos/john-13-21/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Jesus washes the disciples' feet, a picture of God's self-giving love and of the cross, and gives the new command to love one another as he has loved.
  • The farewell discourse: Jesus goes away so that the Spirit (the Advocate) can come as his personal presence everywhere, drawing believers into the love between the Father and the Son. "Abide" as branches in the vine.
  • The Spirit equips the disciples to love, to bear witness to the truth by naming sin and announcing God's love for the world, and to stand firm under persecution: "I have overcome the world."
  • At the arrest, "I am" (ego eimi) is the climax of the seven "I am" sayings and seven absolute "I am" moments, echoing the divine name of Exodus 3. Jesus reveals his divine name at the very moment he gives up his life.
  • "My kingdom is not from this world." It is for this world, but its values come from God. At the cross the true King conquers evil by letting it conquer him.
  • The resurrection is the climactic sign, vindicating the author of life. Jesus breathes the Spirit and sends the disciples. In the epilogue, the great catch comes through listening and obeying, Peter is restored and commissioned, and the beloved disciple bears witness by writing.

The Spirit equips the disciples to love, to bear witness to the truth by naming sin and announcing God's love for the world, and to stand firm under persecution: "I have overcome the world." At the arrest, "I am" (ego eimi) is the climax of the seven "I am" sayings and seven absolute "I am" moments, echoing the divine name of Exodus 3. Jesus reveals his divine name at the very moment he gives up his life. "My kingdom is not from this world." It is for this world, but its values come from God. At the cross the true King conquers evil by letting it conquer him. The resurrection is the climactic sign, vindicating the author of life. Jesus breathes the Spirit and sends the disciples. In the epilogue, the great catch comes through listening and obeying, Peter is restored and commissioned, and the beloved disciple bears witness by writing.

title: Acts
html:
Acts

28 chapters

“But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you, and you will be my witnesses in Jerusalem and in all Judea and Samaria, and to the end of the earth.” (Acts 1:8, ESV)

Setting. Acts is Luke's second volume, covering about AD 30–62. It tells how the risen Christ, through his Spirit, spread the gospel from Jerusalem to Rome.

Where it fits. New Testament — From Pentecost (AD 30/33) to Paul in Rome (c. 60–62), from Tiberius to Nero. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Jerusalem (1–7): The ascension, Pentecost, the early church, and Stephen's martyrdom.
  2. Judea and Samaria (8–12): Philip, Saul's conversion, Peter and Cornelius (Gentiles receive the Spirit).
  3. To the ends of the earth (13–28): Paul's three missionary journeys, the Jerusalem Council (15), arrest, trials, and Paul preaching in Rome "without hindrance."
Main themes. The Holy Spirit; witness; the resurrection; the church as one people of Jews and Gentiles; God's sovereign advance of the word despite opposition.
Main characters. Peter, John, Stephen, Philip, Paul (Saul), Barnabas, Cornelius, Lydia, Silas, Timothy, Priscilla and Aquila.
Key passages
  • 1:8 — witnesses to the ends of the earth
  • 2 — Pentecost and Peter's sermon
  • 7 — Stephen's speech and martyrdom
  • 9 — Saul's conversion
  • 10–11 — Cornelius and the Gentiles
  • 15 — the Jerusalem Council
  • 17:22–31 — Paul at the Areopagus
  • 28:30–31 — Paul preaching in Rome "without hindrance"

How it points to Christ. Acts is volume two of what "Jesus began to do and teach" (1:1). The ascended Christ keeps acting from heaven, pouring out the Spirit and adding to his church.

Going deeper. Acts is the story of the risen Christ continuing what he "began to do and teach" (1:1) through his Spirit and his church. The gospel spreads outward in widening circles from Jerusalem to Rome, against every obstacle. That is why postmillennialists treat Acts as a picture of how the kingdom grows. Acts 13:48, "as many as were appointed to eternal life believed," is a key text on election joined with evangelism. Election never stifles mission. It guarantees mission will succeed. Paul's sermon at Athens is a model of presuppositional apologetics as Frame and Van Til describe it: he begins with God as Creator and Judge, not with neutral ground.

Reformed note Acts 13:48, "as many as were appointed to eternal life believed," is a key text on election. Presbyterians cite 2:39 ("the promise is for you and for your children") for infant baptism. Covenantal Baptists point to the rest of the verse ("everyone whom the Lord our God calls") and to the pattern of believers being baptized. Postmillennialists see in Acts the beginning of the gospel's worldwide, unstoppable advance.

BibleProject video: Acts 1-12 bibleproject.com/videos/acts-1-12/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Acts is volume two of Luke–Acts. If the Gospel is what Jesus "began to do and teach," Acts is what he went on doing, so BibleProject suggests the book might be better called "the Acts of Jesus and the Spirit."
  • The risen Jesus teaches the kingdom for forty days and promises the Spirit, the prophets' hope of God's presence living in a new temple and transforming hearts. Acts 1:8 lays out the book: Jerusalem, Judea and Samaria, the ends of the earth. At the ascension, Daniel 7's cloud enthrones the Son of Man.
  • At Pentecost, wind and fire echo the glory filling the tabernacle and temple, but now God's fiery presence fills a people instead of a building. Pilgrims from every nation and tribe of Israel point to Israel being reunited and the message going to the nations.
  • The "tale of two temples": the new community fulfills what the Jerusalem temple was meant to be (healing, generosity, provision for the poor as the Torah required) while the temple leaders arrest the apostles.
  • Stephen's speech shows Israel always rejecting God's messengers. His martyrdom scatters the church, and that tragedy carries the gospel outward.
  • Philip goes to Samaria, Saul is converted, Peter's vision opens the way to Cornelius's household and the Spirit falls on Gentiles. Antioch becomes the first great multiethnic church, where believers are first called "Christians," and it sends out the first missionaries.
BibleProject video: Acts 13-28 bibleproject.com/videos/acts-13-28/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Paul's three missionary journeys (Asia Minor, then Greece, then the same regions again). He always starts at the synagogue, and some believe while others drive him out.
  • The Jerusalem Council (Acts 15): Peter, Paul and James show that God always meant to include the nations. Gentiles must leave pagan temple worship but need not become ethnically Jewish or take on the Torah's laws. Membership rests on "trusting Jesus and then following his teachings."
  • Clashes with Greco-Roman culture (Philippi, Athens, Ephesus): Jesus as the one true God's revelation exposes the idols, and Christians are accused of treason against Caesar, of proclaiming "another king." Roman officials repeatedly find no crime.
  • The church was something new: diverse, treating men and women, rich and poor, slave and free as equals, loyal to King Jesus alone and peaceful.
  • Paul is arrested in Jerusalem and tried before the Sanhedrin, Felix, Festus and Agrippa. His hope is the resurrection fulfilled in Jesus. He appeals to Caesar, and BibleProject notes his imprisonment gave time for his most important letters.
  • After the shipwreck, he is under house arrest in Rome and the book closes with him preaching the kingdom "unhindered," right under Caesar's nose.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject describes the church as a peaceful community whose very existence turned Roman values upside down, and it often speaks of "allegiance" to King Jesus. Reformed readers agree that Christ's lordship has public consequences: Wilson's "Jesus is Lord, Caesar is not" is a postmillennial way of putting it. They also insist that saving faith is resting on Christ alone, and that faithful obedience is its fruit, not part of what justifies (WCF 11, 14).

title: Romans
html:
Romans

16 chapters

“For all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God, and are justified by his grace as a gift, through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.” (Romans 3:23–24, ESV)

Setting. Paul wrote to the church in Rome, a mix of Jewish and Gentile believers, from Corinth around AD 57. He wanted to set out his gospel and win their support for a mission to Spain.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from Corinth c. AD 57, before Paul's last trip to Jerusalem. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. The gospel and human sin (1–3:20): Gentiles and Jews alike are under sin.
  2. Justification by faith (3:21–5): God's righteousness is revealed, Christ is the propitiation, Abraham is counted righteous, and Adam and Christ are compared.
  3. New life in the Spirit (6–8): Dead to sin, the struggle with the law, and no condemnation, ending in "If God is for us, who can be against us?"
  4. God's faithfulness to Israel (9–11): Election, Israel's unbelief, and the future grafting in of "all Israel."
  5. Living the gospel (12–16): Living sacrifices, love, the governing authorities, the weak and the strong, and greetings.
Main themes. The righteousness of God; justification by faith; propitiation; union with Christ; sanctification by the Spirit; election; Jew and Gentile together.
Main characters. Paul, Phoebe, Priscilla and Aquila, Abraham, Adam (as types).
Key passages
  • 1:16–17 — the gospel is the power of God for salvation
  • 1:18–32 — suppression of the truth
  • 3:21–26 — righteousness by faith and propitiation
  • 4 — Abraham justified by faith
  • 5:12–21 — Adam and Christ
  • 8 — no condemnation and the golden chain (8:29–30)
  • 9–11 — God's purpose in election and Israel's future
  • 12:1–2 — living sacrifices

How it points to Christ. Christ is the one God "put forward as a propitiation by his blood" (3:25), the second Adam whose obedience makes many righteous (5:19), and the one in whom there is no condemnation (8:1).

Going deeper. Romans is the fullest statement of the gospel in Scripture. Luther called it "the chief part of the New Testament," and Calvin said that whoever understands it has a door opened to the treasures of Scripture. Romans 3:21–26 is the center of the Reformed doctrine of justification. God is shown to be both "just and the justifier" because Christ's death satisfied his justice as a propitiation. Romans 5 grounds imputation in two federal heads, Adam and Christ, and Romans 8:29–30 sets out the "golden chain" of salvation from foreknowledge to glory. Many Reformed postmillennialists (and older Reformed writers such as Charles Hodge and John Murray) read 11:12, 15 and 25–26 as promising a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Israel, which will be "life from the dead" for the world.

Reformed note Calvin called justification "the main hinge on which religion turns" (Institutes 3.11.1). Romans 4:5 and 5:19 ground the Reformed doctrine of imputed righteousness, which Sproul defended in Faith Alone. Romans 9 is the classic text on unconditional election. Many Reformed interpreters, postmillennialists especially, read 11:25–26 as a future large-scale conversion of ethnic Israel.
Reading BibleProject well BibleProject's Romans videos stress God's covenant faithfulness and the forming of one multiethnic family. Those are real themes, and they reflect the influence of "New Perspective" scholars like N.T. Wright. Reformed readers will want to keep at the center what Paul also clearly teaches: God's forensic declaration that the ungodly are righteous through faith alone, based on Christ's imputed righteousness.

BibleProject video: Romans 1-4 bibleproject.com/videos/romans-1-4/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Paul, a former Pharisee commissioned by the risen Jesus as apostle to the Gentiles, writes late in his career. When Claudius's expulsion of the Jews ended and Jewish believers returned, the Roman church had become largely Gentile and was split over Sabbath, kosher food and circumcision. Paul writes to unify it and to make Rome his base for a mission to Spain.
  • The gospel is God's saving power, and it reveals God's righteousness: that he does what is right and keeps his promises.
  • Paul retells Genesis 3–11. Idolatry, giving ultimate allegiance to created things, has distorted humanity, which stands "guilty as charged." Israel, with the Torah, is no better, and in fact more accountable.
  • Jesus as our representative and sacrifice absorbed sin's just consequences and offers resurrection life. "Jesus became what we are so that we might become what he is."
  • Justification "literally means to declare righteous": a new status (forgiven, right with God), a new family (God's covenant people) and a new future (a transformed life). It is all a gift received through faith.
  • Abraham was declared righteous by faith (Genesis 15) before the Torah, so he is father of a multiethnic family of all who trust Jesus.
BibleProject video: Romans 5-16 bibleproject.com/videos/romans-5-16/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Adam versus Jesus, the new Adam: one humanity enslaved to sin and death, a new one headed by the obedient Jesus. In baptism the old humanity dies and is raised with Christ, so "what's true of him is now true of them."
  • Romans 7: the Torah's commands are good but cannot fix the heart. They work like a magnifying glass, concentrating the human problem in Israel.
  • Romans 8: Jesus, Israel's representative, has dealt with sin, and the Spirit transforms hearts to fulfill the law of love. This renewal is the first step toward renewing all creation.
  • Romans 9–11: being Abraham's physical descendant never automatically made anyone a faithful member. God has always chosen a subset to carry the line of promise, and he turns rejection (Pharaoh, the golden calf) to redemptive ends. Many Israelites base the covenant on performing the Torah. In the olive tree, branches are broken off and Gentiles grafted in, and Paul trusts that one day Israel will acknowledge Jesus.
  • Romans 12–16: unity through love and forgiveness, using diverse gifts. Food laws and Sabbath are non-essential issues where believers must respect each other. Phoebe, a leader in the church at Cenchreae, likely carried the letter.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject's account of justification as a declared status received by faith is sound, but it never names the imputation of Christ's righteousness, which Reformed teaching considers essential (2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9; WCF 11). It reads Romans 9 in terms of the line of promise. Calvin, Sproul and Grudem read it as personal, unconditional election (9:11–16). On Romans 11, many Reformed and postmillennial writers expect a large-scale future turning of Israel to Christ. That fits BibleProject's hope but goes further than the cautious way it is stated in the video.

Food laws and Sabbath are non-essential issues where believers must respect each other. Phoebe, a leader in the church at Cenchreae, likely carried the letter. A Reformed response to the video BibleProject's account of justification as a declared status received by faith is sound, but it never names the imputation of Christ's righteousness, which Reformed teaching considers essential (2 Cor 5:21; Phil 3:9; WCF 11). It reads Romans 9 in terms of the line of promise. Calvin, Sproul and Grudem read it as personal, unconditional election (9:11–16). On Romans 11, many Reformed and postmillennial writers expect a large-scale future turning of Israel to Christ. That fits BibleProject's hope but goes further than the cautious way it is stated in the video.

title: 1 Corinthians
html:
1 Corinthians

16 chapters

“For the word of the cross is folly to those who are perishing, but to us who are being saved it is the power of God.” (1 Corinthians 1:18, ESV)

Setting. Paul wrote from Ephesus around AD 54 to a gifted but divided and worldly church he had planted in the port city of Corinth.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from Ephesus c. AD 54/55, a few years after Paul founded the church (c. 50–52). (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Divisions and the wisdom of the cross (1–4).
  2. Sexual immorality, lawsuits, and the body (5–6).
  3. Answers to their questions (7–16): Marriage, food offered to idols, worship and head coverings, the Lord's Supper, spiritual gifts, love (13), and the resurrection (15).
Main themes. The cross as God's wisdom; church unity; holiness of the body; Christian freedom and love; orderly worship; resurrection.
Main characters. Paul, Apollos, Cephas, Chloe's people, Sosthenes.
Key passages
  • 1:18–31 — the folly of the cross
  • 2:14 — the natural person and the things of the Spirit
  • 6:9–11 — "such were some of you"
  • 11:23–26 — the Lord's Supper
  • 12–14 — spiritual gifts and the body
  • 13 — love
  • 15 — the resurrection and 15:25, "he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet"

How it points to Christ. Christ crucified is the power and wisdom of God (1:23–24). He is the firstfruits of the resurrection, and "he must reign until he has put all his enemies under his feet" (15:25).

Going deeper. Paul answers a gifted but proud, divided and worldly church by bringing everything back to the cross and the resurrection. Chapter 15 is the Bible's fullest teaching on the resurrection of the body, and its argument is historical: if Christ is not raised, our faith is futile. 15:24–26 is a central postmillennial text. Christ reigns now and must keep reigning until every enemy is subdued, with death last, before he returns. On spiritual gifts, Reformed teachers divide between cessationists (for example Sproul and the confessional tradition) and continuationists (Grudem, The Gift of Prophecy).

Reformed note 15:25 is a cornerstone postmillennial text for Wilson and others: Christ reigns now, from heaven, until his enemies are subdued, and death is the last enemy. On spiritual gifts (12–14), Wayne Grudem is a well-known Reformed continuationist (The Gift of Prophecy), while many in the Reformed tradition are cessationists.

BibleProject video: 1 Corinthians bibleproject.com/videos/1-corinthians/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Corinth was a wealthy, idol-filled port where Paul spent eighteen months (Acts 18). Bad reports followed, and the letter takes up five problems, answering each with part of the gospel story, so that every area of life is seen "through the lens of the gospel."
  • Divisions over Paul, Apollos and Peter (chs. 1–4): the church is not a popularity contest, and its leaders are only servants of Jesus.
  • Sex (chs. 5–7): some called immorality freedom. Jesus died for sin, and the body will be raised, so "what you do with your body matters." No compromise on sexual integrity.
  • Idol meat (chs. 8–10): don't eat if it would suggest Christians also worship other gods. Otherwise, eat freely, since idols are nothing. The governing principle is love that gives itself for others.
  • Worship (chs. 11–14): disorderly tongues and prophecy. The church is a body with many parts, all for "building up," and the greatest gift is love.
  • The resurrection (ch. 15): it is essential and backed by hundreds of eyewitnesses. Without it faith is futile. It is victory over death and the ground of unity, purity and love. "The gospel is not just moral advice… It's an announcement about Jesus."

title: 2 Corinthians
html:
2 Corinthians

13 chapters

“For our sake he made him to be sin who knew no sin, so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” (2 Corinthians 5:21, ESV)

Setting. Paul's most personal letter, written from Macedonia around AD 55–56 after a painful visit and a severe letter. He defends his ministry against "super-apostles."

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from Macedonia c. AD 55/56. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Paul's ministry explained (1–7): Comfort in affliction, the glory of the New Covenant, treasure in jars of clay, and the ministry of reconciliation.
  2. The collection for Jerusalem (8–9): Grace-driven generosity.
  3. Paul's defense (10–13): Boasting in weakness, the thorn in the flesh, and "my grace is sufficient for you."
Main themes. Power in weakness; New Covenant ministry; reconciliation; generosity; true versus false apostles.
Main characters. Paul, Titus, the "super-apostles".
Key passages
  • 3 — the ministry of the new covenant
  • 4:7 — treasure in jars of clay
  • 5:17 — new creation
  • 5:21 — the great exchange
  • 8–9 — the collection and cheerful giving
  • 11–12 — the "super-apostles," Paul's sufferings and the thorn
  • 12:9 — "my grace is sufficient for you"

How it points to Christ. 5:21 is the "great exchange": our sin credited to Christ, and his righteousness credited to us. Christ, though rich, became poor for our sake (8:9).

Going deeper. 2 Corinthians is Paul's most personal letter, a defense of ministry shaped by weakness and suffering rather than by impressive performance. It corrects the triumphalism that judges ministry by visible power. Postmillennial hope rests on Christ's power at work through weak people, not on the church's strength. 5:21 is the classic text of the "great exchange": our sin credited to Christ, and his righteousness credited to us. Calvin, Luther and Packer all treat it as a summary of the gospel. 8–9 is the New Testament's main teaching on generous giving, grounded in Christ, who "though he was rich… became poor."

Reformed note The Reformed tradition reads 5:21 as double imputation, the heart of substitutionary atonement and justification. Packer's essay "What Did the Cross Achieve?" (1973) is a classic defense of this penal logic.

BibleProject video: 2 Corinthians bibleproject.com/videos/2-corinthians/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The letter comes after a "painful visit" and a "tearful letter." Most of the church has repented, and Paul affirms his love. Three parts: reconciliation (chs. 1–7), the neglected collection (chs. 8–9), and the remaining opponents (chs. 10–13).
  • The Corinthians had become ashamed of Paul: poor, persecuted, unimpressive as a speaker. Paul pictures the apostles as captives in Christ's triumphal procession. The Corinthians themselves, written on by the Spirit (Jeremiah and Ezekiel), are his letter of recommendation.
  • The old covenant's glory faded and could not transform. The new covenant's glory is the risen Jesus, and his Spirit transforms people into his likeness.
  • The cross turns ideas of glory upside down. It reconciles sinners to God, reveals God's self-giving love and establishes a "cruciform" way of life. Rejecting Paul's suffering means rejecting Jesus.
  • The collection for Jerusalem is the gospel told in money terms: "though he was rich, yet for your sake he became poor."
  • The "super-apostles": Paul could outmatch their credentials but boasts in weakness: "My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness."

title: Galatians
html:
Galatians

6 chapters

“Yet we know that a person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” (Galatians 2:16, ESV)

Setting. Paul wrote urgently (around AD 48–55) to churches in Galatia being pressured by teachers who said Gentiles must be circumcised and keep the law to belong.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written c. AD 48/49, before the Jerusalem Council (South Galatian view). Others date it to the mid-50s †. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Paul's gospel is from God (1–2): His call, independence, and confronting Peter at Antioch.
  2. Justification by faith (3–4): Abraham's faith, Christ becoming a curse for us, the law as guardian, sons and heirs, and Hagar and Sarah.
  3. Freedom in the Spirit (5–6): Not license. Walk by the Spirit and bear one another's burdens.
Main themes. Justification by faith alone; the one true gospel; the role of the law; adoption; freedom; the fruit of the Spirit.
Main characters. Paul, Peter (Cephas), Barnabas, James, Titus, the "agitators".
Key passages
  • 1:6–9 — no other gospel
  • 2:11–21 — Paul opposes Peter and "justified by faith in Christ"
  • 3:10–14 — Christ became a curse for us
  • 3:28–29 — one in Christ and Abraham's offspring
  • 5:1 — freedom
  • 5:16–26 — the fruit of the Spirit
  • 6:14 — boasting only in the cross

How it points to Christ. "Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law by becoming a curse for us" (3:13). He is the singular offspring of Abraham (3:16).

Going deeper. Galatians is the Magna Carta of Christian freedom and Luther's favorite letter. Adding anything to Christ as a condition of justification, even good things like circumcision, is "another gospel." Paul's argument from Abraham (3:6–9) shows the one covenant of grace running through both testaments: believers are Abraham's offspring (3:29). That is the foundation of Reformed covenant theology, which Baptists and Presbyterians share even though they disagree over baptism. Freedom in Christ isn't license. It is life in the Spirit, which bears fruit.

Reformed note Galatians was Luther's favorite letter and a battle-standard of the Reformation. Reformed theology reads 3:8 ("the Scripture… preached the gospel beforehand to Abraham") as proof that there is one way of salvation, by grace through faith, across both Testaments.

BibleProject video: Galatians bibleproject.com/videos/galatians/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Jewish Christians had come to the Galatian churches demanding that Gentile believers be circumcised and keep the Torah's boundary markers. Paul writes "brokenhearted and angry": they have turned to "a different gospel."
  • Paul defends his apostleship, received from the risen Jesus and later affirmed by Peter and James. He recounts confronting Peter at Antioch for withdrawing from Gentile tables.
  • "A person is not justified by works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ." BibleProject notes that the Greek phrase could mean Jesus' own faithfulness or our trust in him, but either way people are justified "through trusting in what God did for them through Jesus, not by what they do for themselves." Galatians 2:20: what is true of Christ becomes true of those who trust him.
  • Abraham was justified by faith in God's promise of blessing to the nations. The Torah came later and was temporary: it magnified sin and "imprisoned everyone under sin," and it served as a guardian until the Messiah came. As Israel's faithful King, Jesus bore the law's curse, so the blessing goes to all peoples.
  • Chapters 5–6: the Torah is summed up in loving one's neighbor, and the Spirit gives the power to obey. The works of the flesh versus the fruit of the Spirit, which needs cultivating: "keep in step with the Spirit."
  • What matters is "new creation," a multiethnic family of faith fulfilling "the law of Christ."
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject leaves the "faith of Christ" phrase open. The ESV and most Reformed interpreters (Calvin, Packer, Grudem) take it as faith in Christ, while not denying that Christ's own active obedience is the ground of our justification. BibleProject's stress on Torah "boundary markers" overlaps with the New Perspective on Paul. Reformed critics such as Carson, among others, have responded that Paul's argument goes deeper than boundary markers: justification excludes all works, including moral law-keeping (Gal 3:10–12).

Reformed critics such as Carson, among others, have responded that Paul's argument goes deeper than boundary markers: justification excludes all works, including moral law-keeping (Gal 3:10–12).

title: Ephesians
html:
Ephesians

6 chapters

“For by grace you have been saved through faith. And this is not your own doing; it is the gift of God, not a result of works.” (Ephesians 2:8–9, ESV)

Setting. Paul wrote from prison (around AD 60–62), probably as a circular letter to churches in and around Ephesus.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from prison (Rome) c. AD 60–62. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Spiritual blessings in Christ (1): Chosen before the foundation of the world, adopted, redeemed, and sealed.
  2. Saved by grace and made one (2–3): Dead to alive, Jew and Gentile one new man, and the mystery revealed.
  3. Walk worthy (4–6): Unity and gifts, the new self, walking in love and light, households (wives and husbands, children, servants), and the armor of God.
Main themes. Election and grace; union with Christ; the church as Christ's body, temple, and bride; unity; the new life; spiritual warfare.
Main characters. Paul, Tychicus.
Key passages
  • 1:3–14 — every spiritual blessing, chosen before the foundation of the world
  • 2:1–10 — dead in sins, made alive by grace
  • 2:11–22 — Jew and Gentile one new man
  • 4:1–16 — unity and gifts for building up the body
  • 5:22–33 — marriage and the mystery of Christ and the church
  • 6:10–20 — the armor of God

How it points to Christ. Everything is "in Christ." God's plan is to unite all things in him (1:10), and the church is his body and bride, for whom he gave himself (5:25).

Going deeper. Ephesians gives the widest vision of God's purpose: "to unite all things in him" (1:10). Election in Christ before creation (1:4–5), resurrection of the spiritually dead (2:1–5), and salvation as God's gift (2:8–9) are all classic Reformed texts. Chapter 5 grounds Christian marriage in the gospel itself. The husband loves sacrificially as Christ loved the church, and the wife respects and follows as the church does Christ. Wilson's Reforming Marriage draws heavily on this passage. Ephesians 1:22, Christ "head over all things for the church," supports the postmillennial confidence that his rule is active now.

Reformed note 1:4–5 is the classic text for predestination in Calvin and the Reformed confessions. Doug Wilson's Reforming Marriage builds its picture of a husband's headship as sacrificial, Christ-like love largely on 5:22–33, a theme Wilson returns to often.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • Ephesus was a center of pagan worship where Paul ministered for over two years (Acts 19). He writes from prison. Chapters 1–3 tell the gospel story, and "therefore" (4:1) leads to how to live it out in church, community and family.
  • The opening blessing (1:3–14): from eternity the Father chose and blessed a covenant people (BibleProject points to Genesis 12:1–3). In Jesus anyone can be adopted, sins are covered, and God's plan is to unite all things in Christ. Father, Son and Spirit all appear in the poem.
  • Chapter 2: dead in sin and deceived by dark powers, saved by grace and raised with Christ for good works. The Torah's commands acted like a dividing wall, but in Jesus it is broken down and "one new man" is made.
  • Chapter 3: Paul's wonder at his calling, and a prayer to grasp Christ's love.
  • Chapter 4: one body, Spirit, Lord, faith, baptism, but unity is "not the same thing as uniformity." Diverse gifts build up the temple. Take off the old humanity and put on the new, renewed in God's image.
  • Being filled with the Spirit shows itself in singing, thanksgiving and mutual submission. Wives respect their husbands and husbands lay down their lives as Christ did, which reenacts the gospel, and the same applies to parents and children and to masters and slaves. The armor of God comes from Isaiah's portrait of the Messiah.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject reads Ephesians 1:4 mainly as God choosing a covenant people, Abraham's family. Reformed theology (Calvin, Sproul, Grudem, WCF 3) also reads it as God's eternal, personal choice of individuals "in him… before the foundation of the world," without losing the corporate aspect. BibleProject's account of marriage, the husband as responsible, self-giving head and the wife as respectful, is close to the classic Reformed and complementarian reading Wilson defends.

title: Philippians
html:
Philippians

4 chapters

“For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain.” (Philippians 1:21, ESV)

Setting. Paul wrote from prison (probably Rome, around AD 61) to a beloved church that had supported him. It is a letter full of joy.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from prison (Rome) c. AD 61–62. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Partnership and joy in prison (1).
  2. The mind of Christ (2): The Christ hymn (2:5–11), with Timothy and Epaphroditus as examples.
  3. Righteousness from God, not from law (3): Count everything as loss to gain Christ.
  4. Contentment and thanks (4): "I can do all things through him who strengthens me."
Main themes. Joy in suffering; humility; the mind of Christ; righteousness by faith; perseverance; contentment.
Main characters. Paul, Timothy, Epaphroditus, Euodia and Syntyche.
Key passages
  • 1:6 — he who began a good work will complete it
  • 1:21 — to live is Christ, to die is gain
  • 2:5–11 — the Christ hymn
  • 2:12–13 — work out your salvation, for God works in you
  • 3:7–11 — counting all loss to gain Christ
  • 4:4–7 — rejoice and do not be anxious
  • 4:13 — I can do all things

How it points to Christ. In 2:5–11 Christ, who is truly God, humbled himself to death on a cross, and God highly exalted him so that every knee will bow. It is the pattern of humiliation and exaltation.

Going deeper. Philippians is a letter of joy written from prison. Its center, 2:5–11, is one of the highest Christological passages in the New Testament. The eternal Son "emptied himself" by adding humanity, not by giving up deity (Grudem's Systematic Theology discusses why the "kenotic" theory is wrong). 2:12–13 holds together human effort and divine sovereignty: we work because God works in us. 1:6 is a key text for the perseverance of the saints. 3:9 contrasts "a righteousness of my own" with "the righteousness from God that depends on faith," which is imputation in Paul's own words.

Reformed note Reformed theology insists that Christ "emptied himself" (2:7) by adding humanity and taking the form of a servant, not by giving up any of his deity. 1:6, "he who began a good work in you will bring it to completion," is a key text for the perseverance of the saints.

  • Surveying the Text: Philippians — Douglas Wilson. Wilson's one-sermon panorama of the whole book: its structure, themes, and Christ, with postmillennial and covenantal punch.dougwils.com/the-church/s8-expository/surveying-the-text-philippian…

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Philippians bibleproject.com/videos/philippians/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Philippi was a patriotic Roman colony and Paul's first church in Europe (Acts 16). Paul writes from prison to thank the church for the gift Epaphroditus brought.
  • The letter is a series of short reflections around the poem of 2:6–11, and each takes up words from it to show believers living out Jesus' story.
  • Paul's imprisonment has advanced the gospel. "To live is Christ, and to die is gain." For Paul the real sacrifice is staying alive to serve others.
  • The poem: equal with God, the Messiah, unlike Adam, did not grasp. He emptied himself, became a servant and was obedient to death on a cross. God exalted him so that every knee will bow, words from Isaiah 45 that apply the Lord's universal worship to Jesus. "The one true God of Israel consists of God the Father and the Lord Jesus."
  • Timothy and Epaphroditus model this mindset. Paul counts his former Torah-zeal and status as loss (the word is ruder in Greek) in order to know Christ and the power of his resurrection.
  • "Our citizenship is in heaven," not as an escape from earth: Jesus will come from there to bring new creation. Euodia and Syntyche should reconcile. "Do not be anxious." Think on whatever is true and lovely. Paul has learned contentment "through him who strengthens me."

title: Colossians
html:
Colossians

4 chapters

“He is the image of the invisible God, the firstborn of all creation.” (Colossians 1:15, ESV)

Setting. Paul wrote from prison (around AD 60–62) to a church he hadn't visited, which was threatened by a mix of philosophy, mysticism, and Jewish ritualism.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from prison (Rome) c. AD 60–62, alongside Philemon. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. The supremacy of Christ (1): Creator, sustainer, head of the church, and reconciler.
  2. Fullness in Christ (2): Don't be taken captive by human philosophy or rules.
  3. New life in Christ (3–4): Set your minds above, put off and put on, the household, and prayer.
Main themes. The supremacy and sufficiency of Christ; union with Christ in death and resurrection; true spirituality; the household.
Main characters. Paul, Epaphras, Onesimus, Tychicus, Mark, Luke.
Key passages
  • 1:13–14 — transferred into the kingdom of his beloved Son
  • 1:15–20 — the supremacy of Christ in creation and redemption
  • 2:9 — the whole fullness of deity bodily
  • 2:13–15 — the record of debt nailed to the cross and powers disarmed
  • 3:1–4 — set your minds on things above
  • 3:18–4:1 — the household

How it points to Christ. "In him the whole fullness of deity dwells bodily" (2:9). Christ disarmed the powers and canceled the record of our debt by nailing it to the cross (2:14–15).

Going deeper. Colossians answers a hollow, add-on spirituality by showing that Christ is all-sufficient. Every created thing, visible and invisible, was made through him and for him, and he holds it all together. This is the backbone of a Reformed vision of all of life under Christ's lordship, the conviction behind Kuyper's famous claim that there is not one square inch of creation over which Christ does not cry "Mine!" (Kuyper's words, not Paul's). 2:14–15 says the cross both cancelled our debt and defeated the powers. Penal substitution and Christus Victor belong together here, as many Reformed writers stress.

Reformed note 2:14–15 joins penal substitution (the debt canceled) with Christ's victory over the powers, so both aspects of the atonement stand together here. Presbyterians and covenantal Baptists read 2:11–12 (circumcision and baptism) differently, but both find the believer's union with Christ in it.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • Paul writes from prison to a church he had not founded (Epaphras planted it), which faced pressure from mystical polytheism and from demands to keep Torah.
  • The poem of 1:15–20 has two stanzas. Jesus is the image of God and the "firstborn," royal over all things, sharing the Creator's identity, and every power was made by and for him. He is also head of a new body and firstborn from the dead: the fullness of God dwells in him, and through the cross God reconciles all things.
  • Paul's sufferings are a share in Christ's afflictions and a cause for joy. "Christ in you, the hope of glory."
  • Christ triumphed over the "elemental spirits" and fulfilled the Torah, so nothing needs to be added to him (food laws, festivals, circumcision).
  • "Set your minds on things above," meaning where Jesus now reigns, not escape to heaven. Put off the old self and put on the new, where there is not "Greek and Jew… slave, free; but Christ is all."
  • The household code reshapes the authoritarian Roman household around Christ's lordship. Through Onesimus (see Philemon), "no part of human existence remains untouched" by Jesus' rule.

title: 1 Thessalonians
html:
1 Thessalonians

5 chapters

“He who calls you is faithful; he will surely do it.” (1 Thessalonians 5:24, ESV)

Setting. One of Paul's earliest letters (around AD 50–51), written from Corinth to a young church that had come to faith amid persecution.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from Corinth c. AD 50/51, just after the church was founded. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Thanksgiving for their faith (1–3): Paul's conduct and Timothy's good report.
  2. Living to please God (4:1–12): Holiness and brotherly love.
  3. The Lord's coming (4:13–5:11): Those who have died in Christ will rise, so be watchful.
  4. Final instructions (5:12–28).
Main themes. Faith, love, and hope; holiness; Christ's return; encouragement in grief.
Main characters. Paul, Silas, Timothy.
Key passages
  • 1:9–10 — turned from idols to serve the living God
  • 2 — Paul's ministry among them
  • 4:1–8 — sexual holiness
  • 4:13–18 — the dead in Christ and the Lord's coming
  • 5:1–11 — the day of the Lord like a thief
  • 5:16–18 — rejoice, pray, give thanks

How it points to Christ. Christ, who died and rose, will return visibly, and his people will be with him forever (4:14–17).

Going deeper. Written to a young church under pressure, 1 Thessalonians shows how quickly the gospel changes lives: idols abandoned and hope renewed. 4:13–18 is a passage of comfort, not a timetable. Most Reformed interpreters (Calvin among them) read it as Christ's one visible second coming with resurrection, not a secret rapture before a tribulation. The word for "meet" (apantesis) was used for citizens going out to greet a visiting king and escort him back into the city. Many scholars note this, and it fits the idea that Christ's people rise to welcome him as he comes to reign on earth.

Reformed note Reformed interpreters usually read 4:13–18 as Christ's single, visible, public return at the end, not a secret rapture before a separate return.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • This is probably Paul's earliest letter. After about a month in Thessalonica, many Jews and Greeks gave their allegiance to Jesus, and the church was accused of defying Caesar with "another king" (Acts 17). Paul and Silas had to flee.

  • They "turned to God from idols to serve the living and true God, and to wait for his Son from heaven," at the cost of isolation and family hostility.
  • Paul was like a mother and a father to them, sharing "our own selves." Leadership means loving service, not power, and he took no money. Their suffering joins in Jesus' story. Timothy reports they are thriving.

  • On believers who have died: the dead in Christ will be raised. To "meet the Lord in the air" uses the language of a city delegation going out to welcome a visiting ruler and escort him back, so believers meet Jesus and accompany him to establish his kingdom on earth. "Peace and security" mocks Roman propaganda, and believers are children of the day.

title: 2 Thessalonians
html:
2 Thessalonians

3 chapters

“As for you, brothers, do not grow weary in doing good.” (2 Thessalonians 3:13, ESV)

Setting. Written shortly after 1 Thessalonians, to correct confusion. Some thought the Day of the Lord had already come, and some had stopped working.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from Corinth a few months after 1 Thessalonians, c. AD 51. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Comfort in persecution and coming justice (1).
  2. The man of lawlessness (2): The Day won't come before the rebellion.
  3. Work and discipline (3): Idleness rebuked.
Main themes. God's just judgment; the man of lawlessness; perseverance; ordinary faithful work.
Main characters. Paul, Silas, Timothy.
Key passages
  • 1:5–10 — God's righteous judgment at Christ's revealing
  • 2:1–12 — the day of the Lord, the rebellion and the man of lawlessness
  • 2:13–15 — chosen for salvation, so stand firm
  • 3:6–13 — warning against idleness

How it points to Christ. The Lord Jesus will be revealed from heaven, and he will destroy the lawless one "with the breath of his mouth" (2:8).

Going deeper. Some in Thessalonica thought the day of the Lord had already come and had stopped working. Paul corrects their eschatology and their ethics together. 2:13 is a strong text on election: "God chose you as the firstfruits to be saved." Interpretations of the man of lawlessness vary widely among Reformed writers. Classic Protestants (including the Westminster Confession 25.6 in its original form) identified him with the papacy. Some partial preterists connect him to first-century figures. Others see a pattern of evil climaxing before Christ returns. The ethical lesson is clear on any view: eschatology should make us faithful workers, not idle watchers.

Reformed note Reformed views differ on the "man of lawlessness." Some, including partial preterists in Wilson's tradition, place him in the first century around AD 70, while others see a figure still to come. All agree that Christ wins decisively.
