BibleProject video: 2 Thessalonians bibleproject.com/videos/2-thessalonians/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Persecution has grown worse and the church is confused about Jesus' return. Three sections, each closing with a prayer: hope under persecution, clarity about the day of the Lord, a challenge to the idle.
  • Their suffering is part of the kingdom. Jesus will bring justice on persecutors, who will be banished "away from the presence of the Lord." BibleProject describes this as the rejecters getting what they wanted, distance from their Creator.
  • Someone was claiming in Paul's name that the day of the Lord had already come. Paul admits the passage is "too short" and puzzling. Drawing on Isaiah and Daniel, he describes a pattern of rulers who exalt themselves (BibleProject mentions Caligula and Nero) that will peak in a final rebel whom Jesus will defeat. The aim is comfort, not speculation, and the events will be public (cf. Mark 13).
  • The "idle" were probably dependent clients of wealthy patrons, living disordered lives. Paul worked with his own hands. "What you hope for shapes what you live for."

title: 1 Timothy
html:
1 Timothy

6 chapters

“The saying is trustworthy and deserving of full acceptance, that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, of whom I am the foremost.” (1 Timothy 1:15, ESV)

Setting. Paul wrote to Timothy, his delegate at Ephesus (mid-60s AD), about how to order the church and confront false teaching.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written after Paul's first Roman imprisonment, c. AD 62–64. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Confronting false teachers and Paul's testimony (1).
  2. Worship and order (2–3): Prayer for all, men and women in worship, and qualifications for overseers and deacons.
  3. Timothy's ministry (4–6): Godliness, widows, elders, slaves, and the dangers of loving money.
Main themes. Sound doctrine; church order; godliness; the church as "pillar and buttress of the truth" (3:15).
Main characters. Paul, Timothy, Hymenaeus and Alexander.
Key passages
  • 1:15 — Christ came to save sinners
  • 2:1–4 — prayer for kings and all people
  • 2:5 — one mediator
  • 2:8–15 — men and women in worship
  • 3:1–13 — elders and deacons
  • 3:15–16 — the church, pillar of the truth, and the mystery of godliness
  • 6:6–10 — godliness with contentment

How it points to Christ. "There is one God, and there is one mediator between God and men, the man Christ Jesus, who gave himself as a ransom for all" (2:5–6).

Going deeper. 1 Timothy is a manual for ordering the church as "the household of God." Paul ties right doctrine to right order and right living. Its qualifications for elders focus on character and household leadership more than talent. 2:12–13 grounds restricting the office of teaching elder to men in the order of creation, not in local culture. That is the complementarian reading held by Grudem, Carson and Wilson. 2:1–4 calls the church to pray for rulers so that the gospel may spread in peace, a quiet but important public role.

Reformed note The Reformed tradition, Presbyterian and Reformed Baptist alike, draws its pattern of qualified elders and deacons from chapter 3. Grudem's complementarian reading of 2:11–15 is widely followed in Reformed churches.

BibleProject video: 1 Timothy bibleproject.com/videos/1-timothy/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Paul sent Timothy, his protégé from Lystra, to Ephesus to confront leaders spreading false teaching. The letter has an opening and closing commission around two practical sections, linked by three poems exalting King Jesus.
  • The false teachers (Hymenaeus, Alexander) speculated about Genesis genealogies and divided the church. True teaching produces love. The law exposes sin and leads to grace: "Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners."
  • Prayer for rulers and peace, because God "desires all people to be saved," and there is "one mediator… who gave himself as a ransom for all."
  • Men caught up in angry disputes should pray. Wealthy women dressing ostentatiously, and some teaching the false doctrine, are told not to teach or exercise authority. BibleProject lays out three views of 2:12 (a prohibition for every church; a limit on women's authority over men while women still teach; a rule for Ephesus only) and stresses that the women were to be taught well.
  • Elders should be men of proven character with well-ordered families. Deacons (BibleProject: "men and women") serve. "Great… is the mystery of godliness."
  • False asceticism is answered from Genesis 1: food and marriage are good gifts. The widow list, older men behaving badly, a little wine for Timothy's stomach, slaves and witness, greedy teachers. "Godliness with contentment is great gain." The rich are to be rich in good works.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject lists the views on 2:12 without settling them, and its framing (wealthy women spreading heresy) leans toward a local reading. Grudem, Carson, Piper and Wilson hold that Paul grounds the restriction in creation order (2:13), so it applies in every church: the office of elder and authoritative teaching to the gathered church belong to qualified men. Women's many gifts and ministries are still honored (Phoebe, Priscilla).

title: 2 Timothy
html:
2 Timothy

4 chapters

“All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness.” (2 Timothy 3:16, ESV)

Setting. Paul's last letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution (around AD 64–67). He passes the torch to Timothy.

Where it fits. New Testament — Paul's last letter, written from prison in Rome under Nero, c. AD 64–67. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Don't be ashamed; guard the deposit (1).
  2. Be strong: soldier, athlete, farmer, and an approved workman (2).
  3. Difficult times, and the sufficiency of Scripture (3).
  4. Preach the word, and Paul's farewell: "I have fought the good fight" (4).
Main themes. Faithfulness unto death; suffering; the inspiration and sufficiency of Scripture; passing on the faith.
Main characters. Paul, Timothy, Lois and Eunice, Onesiphorus, Demas, Luke, Mark.
Key passages
  • 1:9–10 — saved by grace given before the ages began
  • 1:12 — I know whom I have believed
  • 2:2 — entrust to faithful men who will teach others
  • 2:15 — rightly handling the word
  • 3:1–9 — difficult times
  • 3:14–17 — Scripture breathed out by God
  • 4:1–5 — preach the word
  • 4:6–8 — "I have fought the good fight"

How it points to Christ. Christ "abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" (1:10). He is the righteous judge who will give the crown.

Going deeper. 2 Timothy is Paul's last letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution. 3:16–17 is the foundational text for the doctrine of Scripture. "Breathed out by God" means Scripture's origin is God himself, which is the basis of inerrancy and sufficiency as Packer ("Fundamentalism" and the Word of God), Sproul and Frame (The Doctrine of the Word of God) defend them. 2:2 sets out the four generations of discipleship that keep the gospel moving through history. The charge to "preach the word… in season and out of season" (4:2) is the Reformed pulpit's mandate.

Reformed note 3:16 is the classic inerrancy text. Sproul and Packer were leading voices behind the Chicago Statement on Biblical Inerrancy (1978).

BibleProject video: 2 Timothy bibleproject.com/videos/2-timothy/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • This is Paul's last and most personal letter, written from a Roman prison during a trial that is going badly. He asks Timothy to come and take up the mission.
  • Timothy's faith came through Lois and Eunice and the Scriptures. "Do not be ashamed": others such as Phygelus and Hermogenes deserted Paul.
  • The soldier, the athlete, the farmer: following Jesus takes endurance. The "trustworthy saying": "If we have died with him, we will also live with him… if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself."
  • The false teachers say "the resurrection has already happened," a private, hyper-spiritual faith that has given up the hope of new creation. Timothy should avoid quarrels and keep "the main thing the main thing."
  • The Scriptures make one "wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus." "All Scripture is breathed out by God" (the Spirit guiding the authors so they wrote what God wanted) and is useful for teaching, reproof, correction and training in righteousness.
  • "Bring the cloak… and the parchments" before winter. Beware Alexander. Everyone deserted Paul, "but the Lord stood by me."
text: 2 Timothy 4 chapters “All Scripture is breathed out by God and profitable for teaching, for reproof, for correction, and for training in righteousness.” (2 Timothy 3:16, ESV) Setting. Paul's last letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution (around AD 64–67). He passes the torch to Timothy. Where it fits. New Testament — Paul's last letter, written from prison in Rome under Nero, c. AD 64–67. ( Timelines ) The Flow of the Book Don't be ashamed; guard the deposit (1) . Be strong : soldier, athlete, farmer, and an approved workman (2). Difficult times, and the sufficiency of Scripture (3) . Preach the word, and Paul's farewell : "I have fought the good fight" (4). Main themes. Faithfulness unto death; suffering; the inspiration and sufficiency of Scripture; passing on the faith. Main characters. Paul, Timothy, Lois and Eunice, Onesiphorus, Demas, Luke, Mark. Key passages 1:9–10 — saved by grace given before the ages began 1:12 — I know whom I have believed 2:2 — entrust to faithful men who will teach others 2:15 — rightly handling the word 3:1–9 — difficult times 3:14–17 — Scripture breathed out by God 4:1–5 — preach the word 4:6–8 — "I have fought the good fight" How it points to Christ. Christ "abolished death and brought life and immortality to light through the gospel" (1:10). He is the righteous judge who will give the crown. Going deeper. 2 Timothy is Paul's last letter, written from a Roman prison shortly before his execution. 3:16–17 is the foundational text for the doctrine of Scripture. "Breathed out by God" means Scripture's origin is God himself, which is the basis of inerrancy and sufficiency as Packer ( "Fundamentalism" and the Word of God ), Sproul and Frame ( The Doctrine of the Word of God ) defend them. 2:2 sets out the four generations of discipleship that keep the gospel moving through history. The charge to "preach the word… in season and out of season" (4:2) is the Reformed pulpit's mandate. Reformed note 3:16 is the classic inerrancy text. What the video covers (our summary) This is Paul's last and most personal letter, written from a Roman prison during a trial that is going badly. He asks Timothy to come and take up the mission. Timothy's faith came through Lois and Eunice and the Scriptures. "Do not be ashamed": others such as Phygelus and Hermogenes deserted Paul. The soldier, the athlete, the farmer: following Jesus takes endurance. The "trustworthy saying": "If we have died with him, we will also live with him… if we are faithless, he remains faithful, for he cannot deny himself." The false teachers say "the resurrection has already happened," a private, hyper-spiritual faith that has given up the hope of new creation. Timothy should avoid quarrels and keep "the main thing the main thing." The Scriptures make one "wise for salvation through faith in Christ Jesus." "All Scripture is breathed out by God" (the Spirit guiding the authors so they wrote what God wanted) and is useful for teaching, reproof, correction and training in righteousness. "Bring the cloak… and the parchments" before winter. Beware Alexander. Everyone deserted Paul, "but the Lord stood by me."

title: Titus
html:
Titus

3 chapters

“For the grace of God has appeared, bringing salvation for all people.” (Titus 2:11, ESV)

Setting. Paul wrote to Titus, his coworker on Crete (mid-60s AD), about appointing elders and teaching sound doctrine to a culture known for dishonesty.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written c. AD 62–64, between Paul's imprisonments. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Appoint qualified elders and silence false teachers (1).
  2. Teach what fits sound doctrine to every age group; grace trains us (2).
  3. Be devoted to good works; saved by mercy, not works (3).
Main themes. Sound doctrine and godly living; grace that saves and trains; good works; church leadership.
Main characters. Paul, Titus.
Key passages
  • 1:2 — God, who never lies, promised before the ages began
  • 1:5–9 — appointing elders in every town
  • 1:15–16 — professing God but denying him by works
  • 2:1–10 — sound doctrine for every age group
  • 2:11–14 — grace that trains us
  • 3:4–7 — the washing of regeneration and justification by grace

How it points to Christ. Christ "gave himself for us to redeem us from all lawlessness and to purify for himself a people for his own possession who are zealous for good works" (2:14).

Going deeper. Titus ties doctrine to everyday life more tightly than any other letter: "sound doctrine" produces sober, loving households and good works that "adorn" the teaching of God (2:10). 3:4–7 is a compact summary of salvation. We are saved by God's mercy, not by our works, through regeneration by the Spirit, and justified by grace. The letter's aim is the transformation of a hard culture ("Cretans are always liars," 1:12) through ordered churches and godly families. That is the slow, leavening work postmillennialists expect the gospel to do.

Reformed note 3:4–7 is a compact summary of Reformed soteriology: salvation is by God's mercy and not by our works, through regeneration by the Spirit, and we are justified by grace and made heirs.

BibleProject video: Titus bibleproject.com/videos/titus/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Paul sends Titus, his Greek coworker, to bring order to house churches on Crete. The island was notorious (kretizo, "to be a Cretan," meant to lie), full of mercenaries and violence, but its harbors made it strategic for mission.
  • The opening, "God, who never lies," contrasts the Christian God with the Cretans' Zeus, who seduced and deceived. God's character is faithfulness and truth.
  • Task 1: appoint elders, mature husbands and fathers whose integrity, self-control and generosity stand out against Cretan culture. Task 2: silence the "circumcision party," teachers driven by myths, human commands and money. Paul quotes the Cretan poet Epimenides: "Cretans are always liars, evil beasts, lazy gluttons."
  • Wrecked households were discrediting the gospel, so Paul sets out godly older men and women, young women and men, and slaves, so as to "adorn the doctrine of God our Savior." Paul looks for the gospel to show its power in public life, through ordinary participation lived by a different value system, not through upheaval or withdrawal.
  • "The grace of God has appeared… training us to renounce ungodliness."
  • Christians as ideal citizens. The poem of 3:4–7: God's kindness saved us, "not because of works," by "the washing of regeneration and renewal of the Holy Spirit," justified by grace, heirs of eternal life.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject's call to engage culture neither by "culture war" nor by assimilation is wise. Postmillennial writers like Wilson would add that this patient, faithful leavening (Matt 13:33) is exactly how Christ's kingdom actually reshapes whole cultures over time, Crete included.

title: Philemon
html:
Philemon

1 chapter

“No longer as a bondservant but more than a bondservant, as a beloved brother.” (Philemon 16, ESV)

Setting. A short personal letter from Paul in prison to Philemon, a Colossian believer, about his runaway slave Onesimus, who had become a Christian.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from prison (Rome) c. AD 60–62. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Thanksgiving for Philemon's love (1–7).
  2. Paul's appeal for Onesimus (8–20): Receive him as you would receive me, and charge his debt to me.
  3. Final requests (21–25).
Main themes. The gospel reshaping relationships; reconciliation; brotherhood in Christ; substitution ("charge that to my account").
Main characters. Paul, Philemon, Onesimus, Apphia, Archippus.
Key passages
  • 1:4–7 — thanksgiving for Philemon's love
  • 1:8–16 — the appeal for Onesimus, "no longer as a bondservant but… a beloved brother"
  • 1:17–19 — "charge that to my account"
  • 1:21 — confident that you will do even more

How it points to Christ. Paul's offer to pay Onesimus's debt (18) is a small picture of what Christ did for us: he took our debt on himself and welcomed us as brothers.

Going deeper. The shortest of Paul's letters is a living picture of the gospel. Paul offers to take on Onesimus's debt ("charge that to my account") and asks Philemon to receive him as he would receive Paul. Luther wrote in his preface to Philemon that "we are all his Onesimus," meaning that Christ does for us what Paul does for Onesimus. Philemon also shows how the gospel works on social institutions. It does not start a revolution. Instead it plants a brotherhood that undermines slavery from within, a point Wilson and other postmillennialists have stressed.

Reformed note Luther famously said, "We are all his Onesimus." The letter shows the gospel changing social structures from the inside, which is a theme Reformed writers who stress cultural transformation emphasize.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • Paul's shortest letter and "one of the most explosive." Onesimus, a slave who had wronged his owner Philemon, a Colossian house-church leader, and run away, came to Paul in prison and became a believer.
  • The key word is koinonia, "partnership" or shared participation, as the basis of Paul's appeal.
  • Paul asks Philemon to receive Onesimus "no longer as a slave… but as a beloved brother," a social equal and family member, which overturned Roman norms and went far beyond what the law required.
  • "If he has wronged you… charge that to my account." Paul acts out the gospel of reconciliation by taking Onesimus's debt on himself (2 Cor 5:19).
  • This is the only letter in which Paul doesn't explicitly mention the cross, because he is demonstrating it. The gospel is "extremely personal and never private," and in the new humanity status lines lose their meaning (Col 3:11).

title: Hebrews
html:
Hebrews

13 chapters

“For by a single offering he has perfected for all time those who are being sanctified.” (Hebrews 10:14, ESV)

Setting. Hebrews is an anonymous "word of exhortation" (13:22), probably written before AD 70, to Jewish Christians tempted to drift back from Christ to the old covenant system.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written before the temple fell in AD 70. The sacrifices are still being offered (10:1–2). Probably the 60s. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. The Son is greater than angels (1–2).
  2. Greater than Moses, and a greater rest (3–4).
  3. Christ our great high priest after the order of Melchizedek (5–7).
  4. The better covenant, sanctuary, and sacrifice (8–10).
  5. The great cloud of faith (11).
  6. Endure, and come to Mount Zion (12–13).
Main themes. The supremacy of Christ; Christ's priesthood; the New Covenant; once-for-all sacrifice; warnings against apostasy; persevering faith.
Main characters. Christ, Melchizedek, Moses, Joshua, Abraham, the heroes of faith in chapter 11.
Key passages
  • 1:1–4 — God has spoken by his Son
  • 2:14–18 — Christ shares our flesh to destroy the devil
  • 4:14–16 — our sympathetic high priest
  • 6:4–8 — the warning against falling away
  • 7 — Melchizedek
  • 8 — the new covenant (Jer 31)
  • 9:11–28 — once for all by his own blood
  • 11 — the hall of faith
  • 12:1–2 — looking to Jesus
  • 12:22–29 — Mount Zion and a kingdom that cannot be shaken

How it points to Christ. Christ is everything the old covenant pictured: the final word of God (1:1–2), the priest who offered himself, the sacrifice that removes sin, and the forerunner who entered the true Holy Place.

Going deeper. Hebrews is the New Testament's great commentary on the Old Testament's worship. Tabernacle, priesthood and sacrifice were "a shadow of the good things to come" (10:1), fulfilled in Christ's once-for-all sacrifice. This book is central to covenant theology and to the Baptist–Presbyterian debate. Baptists (the 1689 Confession) stress that the new covenant is made up of those who know the Lord (8:11). Presbyterians stress continuity with the household structure of the old. Hebrews 12:28 has believers "receiving a kingdom that cannot be shaken," already in hand. Many partial preterists read the "shaking" of 12:26–27 and the old covenant "ready to vanish away" (8:13) as fulfilled in AD 70.

Reformed note Hebrews is the most important book for covenant theology. Covenantal Baptists stress the "better covenant" with better members (8:6–13), and Presbyterians stress continuity. The Reformed tradition reads the warning passages (6, 10) as real means God uses to keep his elect persevering, not proof that true believers can be lost.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • The author is anonymous (perhaps a coworker of Paul like Barnabas or Apollos, "we just don't know") and learned from the apostles' circle. The readers were probably Jewish Christians, under persecution and tempted to fall away.
  • Four comparisons, each with a warning: Jesus is greater than the angels (who, in tradition, delivered the Torah), so pay attention; greater than Moses, builder of all creation, so don't rebel as the wilderness generation did and miss God's "rest"; greater than Aaron's priests, a priest-king "after the order of Melchizedek" (Psalm 110), sinless and eternal; a greater sacrifice, offered "once for all," founding Jeremiah's new covenant.
  • "He is the radiance of the glory of God and the exact imprint of his nature," as sunlight is to the sun or a wax seal to the signet ring: "There is no God apart from Jesus."
  • He shares our humanity and sympathizes with us.
  • The closing exhortation: follow the great examples of faith (ch. 11) and endure. The warnings are meant to make you "uncomfortable," not afraid. They show that rejecting such a Savior is foolish.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject doesn't go into the hard questions the warning passages raise (6:4–6; 10:26–29). Reformed interpreters read them as real means God uses to keep his elect persevering, addressed to a mixed covenant community where some who are outwardly in the covenant show by falling away that they were never truly regenerate (1 John 2:19; WCF 17). Covenantal Baptists (1689 LBCF) and Presbyterians handle membership in the covenant community differently, and that affects how they apply these texts.

He shares our humanity and sympathizes with us. The closing exhortation: follow the great examples of faith (ch. 11) and endure. The warnings are meant to make you "uncomfortable," not afraid. They show that rejecting such a Savior is foolish. A Reformed response to the video BibleProject doesn't go into the hard questions the warning passages raise (6:4–6; 10:26–29). Reformed interpreters read them as real means God uses to keep his elect persevering, addressed to a mixed covenant community where some who are outwardly in the covenant show by falling away that they were never truly regenerate (1 John 2:19; WCF 17). Covenantal Baptists (1689 LBCF) and Presbyterians handle membership in the covenant community differently, and that affects how they apply these texts.

title: James
html:
James

5 chapters

“So also faith by itself, if it does not have works, is dead.” (James 2:17, ESV)

Setting. James, the brother of Jesus and a leader of the Jerusalem church, wrote early (perhaps the 40s AD) to scattered Jewish believers. It reads like New Testament wisdom literature.

Where it fits. New Testament — Possibly the earliest NT letter, c. AD 45–49, by Jesus' brother in Jerusalem. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Trials and wisdom (1): Count it all joy; be doers of the word.
  2. Faith that works (2): No partiality, and faith shown by works.
  3. The tongue and true wisdom (3).
  4. Humility, worldliness, and wealth (4–5:6).
  5. Patience, prayer, and restoring the wanderer (5:7–20).
Main themes. Living faith; trials; the tongue; wisdom from above; the rich and the poor; prayer.
Main characters. James, with Abraham, Rahab, Job, and Elijah as examples.
Key passages
  • 1:2–4 — joy in trials
  • 1:17 — every good gift from the Father of lights
  • 1:22–25 — doers of the word
  • 2:1–13 — no partiality
  • 2:14–26 — faith without works is dead
  • 3:1–12 — taming the tongue
  • 4:13–17 — "if the Lord wills"
  • 5:13–18 — prayer

How it points to Christ. James echoes the Sermon on the Mount on nearly every page. True faith in "our Lord Jesus Christ, the Lord of glory" (2:1) shows itself in obedience.

Going deeper. James is the New Testament's wisdom book, packed with echoes of the Sermon on the Mount and of Proverbs. Luther notoriously called it "an epistle of straw" compared to the main Gospel books (in his 1522 preface). But the Reformed tradition, following Calvin, harmonized James and Paul. Paul denies that works justify us before God. James denies that a faith with no works is real faith. Paul's opponents added works to faith. James's opponents subtracted works from faith. Both say that saving faith is living faith.

Reformed note Paul and James don't conflict. Paul says we are justified before God by faith alone, and James says true faith proves itself by works. The Reformation maxim, often traced to Calvin, is that faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is never alone.

BibleProject video: James bibleproject.com/videos/james/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The author is "Jacob" (Iakobos, Ya'akov), Jesus' half-brother, a "pillar" of the Jerusalem church through twenty years of famine and persecution until he was killed.
  • This is not a letter to one church's problems but a summary of wisdom for every community, meant to "get in your business." It draws heavily on the Sermon on the Mount and Proverbs 1–9, in short sayings and memorable one-liners.
  • Chapter 1 introduces all the themes. Trials are paradoxical gifts that produce endurance and make us "perfect" (a word James uses seven times), meaning whole and integrated. Ask God for wisdom without doubting. Wealth fades like flowers. Don't blame God, the generous Father who gave us new birth. Be doers of "the perfect law, the law of liberty."
  • Chapters 2–5 contain twelve short teachings. On favoritism: faith that neglects the poor "is dead," because genuine faith always results in obedience.
  • On speech: blessing and cursing from the same mouth, slander, bending the truth. "Our words tell the real truth about our character."
  • On wealth: "your riches have rotted." Patient hope for Jesus' return and faith-filled prayer.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject rightly says that dead faith shows itself by its lack of works. Reformed teaching adds how James fits with Paul: Paul is talking about how a sinner is declared righteous before God (by faith alone), and James about how true faith is shown to be real (it is never alone). "Faith alone justifies, but the faith that justifies is not alone," a summary of Calvin's teaching that Sproul often repeated.

title: 1 Peter
html:
1 Peter

5 chapters

“He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree, that we might die to sin and live to righteousness.” (1 Peter 2:24, ESV)

Setting. The apostle Peter wrote from "Babylon" (Rome) in the early 60s to scattered believers in Asia Minor, the "elect exiles," who were facing slander and suffering.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written from "Babylon" (Rome) c. AD 62–64, on the eve of Nero's persecution. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Living hope and holiness (1–2:10): New birth, a holy people, and living stones in a spiritual house.
  2. Exiles in society (2:11–3:12): Honor authorities, servants, wives and husbands.
  3. Suffering for righteousness (3:13–4:19): Christ's example and his victory.
  4. Shepherds and the flock (5).
Main themes. Elect exiles; living hope; holiness; suffering and glory; submission and witness; the church as God's people.
Main characters. Peter, Silvanus, Mark.
Key passages
  • 1:1–2 — elect exiles, chosen according to the foreknowledge of God
  • 1:3–9 — born again to a living hope
  • 2:4–10 — living stones and a royal priesthood
  • 2:13–17 — honor the emperor
  • 2:21–25 — the suffering servant
  • 3:15 — always ready to give a defense
  • 3:18–22 — Christ suffered once for sins
  • 5:6–11 — the devil like a roaring lion

How it points to Christ. Christ is the suffering Servant of Isaiah 53 (2:22–25), the righteous one who died for the unrighteous to bring us to God (3:18), and the Chief Shepherd who will appear.

Going deeper. 1 Peter is written to "elect exiles," Christians scattered and suffering in Asia Minor. Peter gives them Israel's titles (2:9, from Exod 19:6) and calls them God's people now. That is a key text for the Reformed view that the church is the one people of God in continuity with Israel. 2:24 ("He himself bore our sins in his body on the tree") is central to the doctrine of substitution. 3:15 is the classic charter for apologetics, and Frame argues it requires us to set apart Christ as Lord in our reasoning, not just our worship.

Reformed note Wayne Grudem's Tyndale commentary on 1 Peter is a respected Reformed work. It includes a long appendix arguing that 3:19–20 refers to Christ preaching through Noah. 1:1–2 joins election and the work of the Trinity in salvation.

What the video covers (our summary)
  • Simon, renamed Kephas/Peter ("rock"), writes from Rome ("Babylon"), with Silvanus composing the letter, to mainly Gentile churches across Asia Minor who face harassment.
  • He greets them as "elect exiles," Israel's language applied to Gentiles, who now belong to Abraham's family of wanderers.
  • The opening song: "born again to a living hope through the resurrection." Suffering refines faith like fire and burns away false hopes.
  • New-exodus identity: gird your minds, redeemed by the blood of the Lamb, a people with God's word in their hearts, "living stones" in a new temple, "a royal priesthood" to the nations.
  • Submit to Roman authority even when it is unjust, without violent resistance. Slaves and wives in pagan households resist evil the way Jesus did. Christian husbands are to honor their wives as "heirs with you of the grace of life."
  • Christ suffered for the unrighteous, was vindicated and is exalted over every power. Baptism, like Noah's flood, is not magic but "an appeal to God for a good conscience." Elders should shepherd as servants. "Resist" the devil, who prowls like a lion. Rome is the new Babylon.

title: 2 Peter
html:
2 Peter

3 chapters

“For no prophecy was ever produced by the will of man, but men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit.” (2 Peter 1:21, ESV)

Setting. Peter's farewell letter, written shortly before his martyrdom (around AD 64–68), warning against false teachers and scoffers.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written shortly before Peter's martyrdom, c. AD 64–67. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Grow in grace, and the reliability of the apostolic and prophetic word (1).
  2. False teachers described and condemned (2).
  3. The Day of the Lord will come; God's patience (3).
Main themes. Spiritual growth; the authority of Scripture; false teaching; the certainty of judgment; God's patience.
Main characters. Peter, the false teachers, Noah and Lot as examples.
Key passages
  • 1:3–11 — his divine power has granted all things for life and godliness
  • 1:16–21 — eyewitnesses of his majesty and men carried along by the Spirit
  • 2 — false teachers
  • 3:3–13 — the scoffers and the day of the Lord
  • 3:15–16 — Paul's letters among "the other Scriptures"

How it points to Christ. Peter was an eyewitness of Christ's majesty at the Transfiguration (1:16–18), the same scene that follows Mark 9:1. Christ's kingdom is eternal (1:11).

Going deeper. 2 Peter is Peter's farewell, warning against false teachers who deny Christ's return and turn grace into license. 1:20–21 is a key text, with 2 Timothy 3:16, for the inspiration of Scripture: men spoke from God "as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit." 3:15–16 treats Paul's letters as Scripture already. 3:9 ("not wishing that any should perish") is debated. Many Reformed interpreters note that the context speaks of God's patience toward "you," his elect, who must all be gathered before the end. Postmillennialists read the long delay as giving time for the gospel to fill the earth.

Reformed note 1:21 is a classic inspiration text. On 3:9, Reformed interpreters note that "not wishing that any should perish" is addressed to believers ("toward you") and describes God's patience in gathering all his elect.

BibleProject video: 2 Peter bibleproject.com/videos/2-peter/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • This is Peter's farewell from Rome before his execution under Nero, written to the same churches as 1 Peter. It has one challenge and two warnings about corrupt teachers.
  • Through Jesus we become "partakers of the divine nature," sharing God's life and love. That calls for growth in seven virtues crowned by love.
  • To skeptics who say the apostles made it up: Peter is an eyewitness of the Transfiguration. The prophets' words are not invented, because "men spoke from God as they were carried along by the Holy Spirit."
  • The false teachers deny a final reckoning so they can indulge their greed and lust, turning Paul's freedom into license. Peter points to three judgments: angels (Genesis 6 as read in 1 Enoch), the flood, and Sodom, with Lot rescued. They are "slaves of corruption": a dog returns to its vomit.
  • "Where is the promise of his coming?" The God whose word created all things can act again. "With the Lord one day is as a thousand years," and the delay is patience, so that people may repent.
  • The day of the Lord is fire. BibleProject argues that stoicheia probably means the heavenly bodies (as in Isaiah 34), so the sky is peeled back and the earth "exposed." The aim is not to scrap creation but to purge evil, so that "new heavens and a new earth in which righteousness dwells" emerge. Paul's letters are "hard to understand" and get twisted, but all the apostles agree.

title: 1 John
html:
1 John

5 chapters

“In this is love, not that we have loved God but that he loved us and sent his Son to be the propitiation for our sins.” (1 John 4:10, ESV)

Setting. The apostle John wrote to churches (probably around Ephesus, late first century) shaken by false teachers who had left and who denied that Christ had come in the flesh.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written c. AD 85–95 at Ephesus, against early Gnostic-type error. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Walking in the light (1–2): Confession, an advocate, and obedience.
  2. Children of God (3): Practicing righteousness and loving one another.
  3. Testing the spirits, and God is love (4).
  4. Faith that overcomes, and assurance (5): "That you may know that you have eternal life."
Main themes. Assurance; fellowship with God; truth, obedience, and love as tests of genuine faith; the incarnation; propitiation.
Main characters. John, the "antichrists" (false teachers).
Key passages
  • 1:5–10 — walking in the light and confessing sin
  • 2:1–2 — Jesus our advocate and propitiation
  • 2:18–27 — antichrists
  • 3:1–3 — children of God
  • 4:1–6 — test the spirits
  • 4:7–21 — God is love
  • 5:13 — that you may know you have eternal life

How it points to Christ. Jesus Christ the righteous is our advocate and the propitiation for our sins (2:1–2; 4:10). He came "in the flesh" (4:2).

Going deeper. 1 John is written "so that you may know that you have eternal life" (5:13), and assurance is its theme. John gives three tests: right belief (Jesus came in the flesh), obedience and love. Reformed pastors have long used them, not to create doubt, but to strengthen assurance alongside the promises. 2:2 ("propitiation… for the sins of the whole world") is debated in discussions of definite atonement. Many Reformed interpreters, following John Owen (The Death of Death in the Death of Christ), read "whole world" as people of every nation, not only Jews.

Reformed note 1 John gives the biblical basis for the Reformed and Puritan doctrine of assurance. D.A. Carson's The Difficult Doctrine of the Love of God helps hold together "God is love" (4:8) and propitiation (4:10).

title: 2 John
html:
2 John

1 chapter

“And this is love, that we walk according to his commandments.” (2 John 6, ESV)

Setting. A brief letter from "the elder" (John) to "the elect lady and her children," probably a church, warning against welcoming traveling false teachers.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written c. AD 85–95, with 1 and 3 John. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Greeting in truth and love (1–3).
  2. Walk in love and truth (4–6).
  3. Don't receive deceivers (7–11).
  4. Closing (12–13).
Main themes. Truth and love together; discernment; Christ come in the flesh.
Main characters. The elder, the elect lady.
Key passages
  • 1:1–3 — truth and love
  • 1:4–6 — walking in the commandment of love
  • 1:7–11 — deceivers who deny Christ come in the flesh, and refusing them hospitality

How it points to Christ. The person of Christ is the test: whoever abides in the teaching of Christ has both the Father and the Son (9).

Going deeper. 2 John holds truth and love together. Love "walks according to his commandments," and real love refuses to give a platform to those who deny the incarnation. Christian hospitality has doctrinal boundaries.

Reformed note 2 John shows that biblical love is never indifferent to doctrine. That balance runs through Reformed confessional churches.

title: 3 John
html:
3 John

1 chapter

“I have no greater joy than to hear that my children are walking in the truth.” (3 John 4, ESV)

Setting. A personal note from the elder to Gaius, commending hospitality to traveling missionaries and rebuking the domineering Diotrephes.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written c. AD 85–95, with 1 and 2 John. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Joy in Gaius's faithfulness (1–4).
  2. Support gospel workers (5–8).
  3. Diotrephes rebuked and Demetrius commended (9–12).
Main themes. Hospitality; supporting missions; humble versus domineering leadership.
Main characters. The elder, Gaius, Diotrephes, Demetrius.
Key passages
  • 1:2–4 — walking in the truth
  • 1:5–8 — supporting traveling missionaries
  • 1:9–10 — Diotrephes, who likes to put himself first
  • 1:11 — imitate good, not evil

How it points to Christ. Missionaries go out "for the sake of the name" (7), the name of Christ, and supporting them makes us "fellow workers for the truth."

Going deeper. 3 John is a small window into early church life: commending faithful hospitality to missionaries (Gaius), rebuking a domineering leader (Diotrephes), and endorsing a good man (Demetrius). It shows that church leadership is service, not self-promotion.

Reformed note 3 John is a small but practical text for church leadership: elders should be servants, not like Diotrephes, "who likes to put himself first" (9).

title: Jude
html:
Jude

1 chapter

“Contend for the faith that was once for all delivered to the saints.” (Jude 3, ESV)

Setting. Written by Jude, the brother of James and of Jesus, to warn churches against immoral false teachers who had crept in unnoticed.

Where it fits. New Testament — Written c. AD 65, by Jesus' brother. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. The call to contend (1–4).
  2. Old Testament and traditional examples of judgment (5–16): Israel, the angels, Sodom, Cain, Balaam, and Korah.
  3. Remember, build yourselves up, show mercy (17–23).
  4. Doxology (24–25).
Main themes. Contending for the faith; judgment on apostasy; perseverance; God's keeping power.
Main characters. Jude, Michael the archangel, Enoch (cited).
Key passages
  • 1:3 — contend for the faith once for all delivered to the saints
  • 1:4 — ungodly people who pervert grace into sensuality
  • 1:5–16 — examples of judgment
  • 1:20–23 — build yourselves up and show mercy
  • 1:24–25 — the doxology, "to him who is able to keep you from stumbling"

How it points to Christ. Christ is the Master and Lord whom the false teachers deny (4), and the one able to keep us from stumbling (24).

Going deeper. Jude meant to write about our "common salvation" but felt he had to urge believers to fight for the faith "once for all delivered." That phrase is a key text for the closure of the canon and the sufficiency of Scripture. Jude cites 1 Enoch (vv. 14–15) and a tradition about Michael (v. 9). Reformed writers note that quoting a true statement from a non-canonical source doesn't make the source Scripture, just as Paul quotes pagan poets (Acts 17:28; Titus 1:12). The doxology at the end is the book's comfort: God is able to keep his people.

Reformed note Jude begins with those who are "kept for Jesus Christ" (1) and ends with the God "who is able to keep you from stumbling" (24). Both are strong texts for the perseverance and preservation of the saints.

More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources
BibleProject video: Jude bibleproject.com/videos/jude/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • Judah, one of Jesus' brothers, became a believer after the resurrection and traveled as a teacher. He writes to a church of mostly Messianic Jews steeped in Scripture and Jewish literature.
  • He had planned a longer work but urgently calls them to "contend for the faith" against intruders who "pervert the grace of our God into sensuality." Jude goes after their way of life, which reveals their bad theology.
  • Two sets of three examples. Rebels judged: the wilderness generation, the angels (Genesis 6 as read in 1 Enoch) and Sodom. Corrupters of others: Cain, Balaam, Korah. In addition, Michael disputing over Moses' body (from the Testament of Moses).
  • Jude piles up Old Testament images: selfish shepherds (Ezekiel), waterless clouds (Proverbs), wild waves (Isaiah). He quotes 1 Enoch 1, which itself echoes Old Testament day-of-the-Lord texts, along with the apostles' warnings.
  • Build yourselves up on "your most holy faith" as God's temple, pray in the Spirit, keep yourselves in God's love, wait for mercy, and rescue others. The doxology praises "him who is able to keep you from stumbling."
  • BibleProject: a book need not be in the Bible to carry an important message. The Apocrypha (Deuterocanon) and pseudepigrapha "are part of the biblical tradition."
A Reformed response to the video Protestant and Reformed teaching (WCF 1.3) holds that quoting a book, as Paul quotes pagan poets, does not make it Scripture. Jude's citations of 1 Enoch and the Testament of Moses make a true point inspired by the Spirit, without endorsing those books. BibleProject's language about the Apocrypha being "part of the biblical tradition" is looser than the Reformed canon allows. Reformed interpreters are also divided on Genesis 6: Calvin held the "Sethite" view, while others follow the angelic reading BibleProject adopts.

title: Revelation
html:
Part

Revelation

The Bible's closing book: a prophetic, apocalyptic letter showing the slain Lamb on the throne and the new creation coming down.

Revelation
text: Part Revelation The Bible's closing book: a prophetic, apocalyptic letter showing the slain Lamb on the throne and the new creation coming down. Revelation

title: Revelation
html:
Revelation

22 chapters

“The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ, and he shall reign forever and ever.” (Revelation 11:15, ESV)

Setting. The apostle John wrote it while exiled on Patmos, to seven churches in Asia Minor facing persecution and compromise. It may date to the 60s (early date) or around AD 95 (late date).

Where it fits. New Testament — Written c. AD 95 on Patmos under Domitian, or c. AD 68 before Jerusalem's fall (Gentry, Wilson) †. (Timelines)

The Flow of the Book
  1. Christ among the churches (1–3): The risen Son of Man and seven letters.
  2. The throne and the Lamb (4–5): Only the slain Lamb is worthy to open the scroll.
  3. Seals and trumpets (6–11): Cycles of judgment, the sealed people of God, and the two witnesses.
  4. The dragon and the beasts (12–14): The cosmic conflict behind earthly persecution.
  5. Bowls and the fall of Babylon (15–19): The rider on the white horse.
  6. The millennium, final judgment, and the new creation (20–22): The new Jerusalem, God dwelling with man, and the tree of life.
Main themes. The sovereignty of God; the victory of the Lamb; faithful witness under persecution; judgment on Babylon; worship; new creation.
Main characters. John, the risen Christ, the Lamb, the dragon, the beasts, Babylon the harlot, the bride.
Key passages
  • 1:5–6 — ruler of kings on earth, who made us a kingdom
  • 1:9–20 — the vision of the risen Son of Man
  • 2–3 — letters to seven churches
  • 4–5 — the throne room and the Lamb who was slain
  • 6–16 — seals, trumpets and bowls
  • 12 — the woman, the dragon and the child
  • 17–18 — the fall of Babylon
  • 19:11–21 — the rider on the white horse
  • 20 — the thousand years
  • 21–22 — the new heavens and new earth

How it points to Christ. The whole book is "the revelation of Jesus Christ" (1:1). The Lion of Judah turns out to be a Lamb who was slain (5:5–6), and he conquers by his blood and reigns forever.

Going deeper. Revelation is apocalyptic prophecy, written in symbols drawn from the Old Testament, and the Reformed tradition holds four views of it. Futurists see most of it in the future. Historicists (common among Reformers and Puritans) see it unfolding through church history. Idealists see timeless patterns. Preterists see much of it fulfilled in the first century. Wilson (When the Man Comes Around) and Kenneth Gentry (Before Jerusalem Fell) hold an early date (before AD 70) and read much of chapters 4–19 as God's judgment on apostate Jerusalem and his vindication of the church. Warfield ("The Millennium and the Apocalypse") read the thousand years of chapter 20 as the present age of Christ's reign. On any view, the core message is plain. The Lamb who was slain is on the throne and is now "the ruler of kings on earth" (1:5). He will finish what he began and make all things new.

Reformed note Reformed believers hold several views of Revelation. Many are amillennial. Doug Wilson (When the Man Comes Around) is postmillennial and partial preterist, reading much of the book as fulfilled in the first century, especially God's judgment on apostate Jerusalem in AD 70, and R.C. Sproul also favored an early date. Wayne Grudem holds historic premillennialism. All agree that Christ wins, the dead are raised, and God makes all things new.
Reading BibleProject well BibleProject reads Revelation symbolically as a call to faithful witness modeled on the slain Lamb. That reading is helpful and fairly close to an idealist or amillennial approach. Wilson's preterist and postmillennial reading puts more weight on historical fulfillment in the first century and on hope for the gospel's victory in history.
Recommended free Reformed commentaries: Revelation
  • Commentary on the Whole Bible: Revelation — Matthew Henry. Calvin wrote no commentary here. Henry's Puritan-era classic is devotional, verse by verse, and full of application.ccel.org/ccel/henry/mhc6/mhc6.Rev.i.html
  • Surveying the Text: Revelation — Douglas Wilson. Wilson's one-sermon panorama of the whole book: its structure, themes, and Christ, with postmillennial and covenantal punch.dougwils.com/the-church/s8-expository/surveying-the-textrevelation.…
  • The Returning King — Vern Poythress. A clear, non-sensational guide by Frame's colleague, strong on symbolism. Free, personal use only.frame-poythress.org/ebooks/the-returning-king/
  • TGC Bible Commentary: Revelation — Brian J. Tabb (TGC Bible Commentary). A free, modern, section-by-section commentary in TGC's Reformed-evangelical stream, with good help on biblical theology.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/revelation/
More free material: Monergism: sermons and commentaries · Ligonier and Sproul resources · A Commentary upon the Book of Revelation (James Durham)
BibleProject video: Revelation 1-11 bibleproject.com/videos/revelation-1-11/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • "Revelation," not "Revelations." Its author is John, either the beloved disciple or another Jewish-Christian prophet. It is three things at once. An apocalypse: symbolic visions that unveil heaven's view of history. A prophecy: a word from God in a time of crisis. A circular letter to seven real churches in Asia. Its meaning is anchored in the first century, and its symbols are explained by Old Testament texts. It is "not a secret predictive code."
  • On Patmos, John sees the risen Jesus among seven lampstands. His messages to the seven churches address affluent apathy, compromise (idol feasts and immorality), and faithful suffering under persecution. Each church is called to "conquer," with rewards taken from the closing new-creation vision.
  • The throne room: "holy, holy, holy." No one can open the sealed scroll, which holds God's kingdom purposes from the prophets and Daniel. John hears of "the Lion of the tribe of Judah," then turns and sees a slain Lamb standing. The kingdom comes through the crucified Messiah, and the cross is his enthronement.
  • The seals, trumpets and bowls nest inside one another and each ends at the final judgment. So BibleProject reads them as three views of the same period, from the resurrection to the return. The horsemen stand for war, conquest, famine and death, "a tragically average day in human history." The martyrs cry out. The 144,000 is a census John hears, while what he sees is a countless multiethnic army redeemed by the Lamb's blood.
  • The trumpets replay the Exodus plagues, but the nations don't repent. John eats the opened scroll. The temple is measured and protected, standing for God's people. The two witnesses (lampstands, i.e. the church) prophesy like Moses and Elijah, are killed by the beast, and are raised, and then the nations repent.
  • The center of the book: judgment alone does not bring repentance, but "it is God's mercy shown through Jesus' followers that will bring the nations to repentance." The seventh trumpet: "The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of his Christ."
BibleProject video: Revelation 12-22 bibleproject.com/videos/revelation-12-22/
What the video covers (our summary)
  • The "signs." The dragon, the ancient serpent of Genesis 3, attacks the woman and her child (the Messiah and his people). He is defeated by the cross and thrown down, and the saints conquer "by the blood of the Lamb and by the word of their testimony." The real enemy is spiritual, not Rome.
  • There are two beasts, in Daniel's imagery: violent military power, and the economic and propaganda machine that worships it. The mark on forehead and hand is an "anti-Shema," a demand for total allegiance. 666 is the value of "Nero Caesar" in Hebrew letters, a recent example of the beastly pattern that runs from Babylon to Persia, Greece and Rome.
  • The Lamb on Zion with his followers, "an eternal gospel," "Come out of Babylon," and two harvests (grain gathered, grapes trodden).
  • The bowls replay the plagues, and many still curse God. Armageddon is drawn from Ezekiel's Gog, the rebel nations gathered for judgment.
  • Babylon the prostitute is Rome, painted with every Old Testament oracle against Babylon, Tyre and Edom: a portrait of the human condition throughout history.
  • The rider on the white horse is already robed in blood "before the battle even begins," his own blood, and his only weapon is the sword from his mouth. The impenitent receive the destiny they chose.
  • On the 1,000 years, BibleProject presents two options: a literal millennium after Jesus' return, or a symbol of the present victory of Christ and the martyrs. The main point is clear either way.
  • The bride, the new heavens and earth, and a new Eden that is also a city where cultures flourish. There is no temple, because God and the Lamb fill everything, and a renewed humanity rules as God's image.
A Reformed response to the video BibleProject's dating (under Domitian), its warning against reading the book as a timetable, and its two millennial options leave out the postmillennial reading. Wilson (in his Revelation commentary When the Man Comes Around) and Kenneth Gentry (Before Jerusalem Fell) argue for a date before AD 70, with much of chapters 6–19 fulfilled in the judgment on Jerusalem and Rome's persecution ("what must soon take place," 1:1). Warfield (in "The Millennium and the Apocalypse") read Revelation 20 as the present reign of Christ and his saints. Postmillennialists expect that reign to bring a great ingathering of the nations before Christ returns. BibleProject's own claim that the Lamb's mercy, shown through his people, "will bring the nations to repentance" is in fact very close to that hope.

title: Resources & Further Reading
html:
Resources & Further Reading

BibleProject (inspiration for this guide's structure)

  • Every video linked in this guide follows the pattern bibleproject.com/videos/<title>/
  • Book overview videos: bibleproject.com/explore/book-overviews
  • Downloads (free posters, transcripts, and study notes): bibleproject.com/downloads
  • About their study notes: bibleproject.com/articles/study-notes-for-the-bible

Free Reformed resources for the whole Bible

  • Monergism: sermons, MP3s, and free ebooks for every book of the Bible, sorted by book. monergism.com/topics/sermon-manuscripts-mp3s-scripture
  • John Calvin's commentaries (45 volumes, Christian Classics Ethereal Library). ccel.org/ccel/calvin/commentaries
  • Matthew Henry's Commentary on the Whole Bible (CCEL). ccel.org/ccel/henry/mhc
  • Douglas Wilson, "Surveying the Text": one sermon per book of the Bible, free on his blog. The edited Canon Press book is not free. dougwils.com/scripture-reference-index. Christ Church sermon archive: christkirk.com/sermons
  • R.C. Sproul / Ligonier: all of Sproul's teaching series are now free to stream, including Dust to Glory, a survey of the whole Bible. ligonier.org/posts/now-free-forever-rc-sprouls-teaching-series · learn.ligonier.org/series/dust-to-glory · resources by book: learn.ligonier.org/scripture
  • TGC Bible Commentary (The Gospel Coalition, D.A. Carson's network): a free online commentary that is growing book by book. thegospelcoalition.org/commentary
  • D.A. Carson, For the Love of God, vol. 1: daily readings through the whole Bible (free PDF from TGC). media.thegospelcoalition.org/documents/carson/1998_for_the_love_of_God.pdf
  • John Frame and Vern Poythress: free ebooks for personal use, including Poythress on Genesis 1–3, the Law of Moses, and Revelation. frame-poythress.org/ebooks
  • John Piper / Desiring God: sermons sorted by book. desiringgod.org/scripture

Not free online, and so not linked: Wayne Grudem's Systematic Theology and his 1 Peter (TNTC), the ESV Study Bible notes, Wilson's published commentaries, and most of Carson's commentaries (Pillar, EBC). They are listed below as recommended reading.

Reformed works mentioned in this guide

  • John Calvin, Institutes of the Christian Religion, and his commentaries on most of Scripture
  • R.C. Sproul, The Holiness of God; Faith Alone; The Last Days According to Jesus; ed., Reformation Study Bible
  • J.I. Packer, Knowing God; "What Did the Cross Achieve? The Logic of Penal Substitution" (1973)
  • Wayne Grudem, Systematic Theology; 1 Peter (Tyndale NT Commentaries); The Gift of Prophecy
  • John Frame, The Doctrine of God; The Doctrine of the Knowledge of God; The Doctrine of the Christian Life
  • D.A. Carson, The Gospel According to John (Pillar); How Long, O Lord?; The Difficult Doctrine of the Love of God
  • Douglas Wilson, Heaven Misplaced (postmillennialism); When the Man Comes Around (Revelation); Joy at the End of the Tether (Ecclesiastes); Reforming Marriage; To a Thousand Generations (covenant and baptism); Standing on the Promises; Recovering the Lost Tools of Learning
  • Kenneth Gentry, Before Jerusalem Fell (dating Revelation); B.B. Warfield, "The Millennium and the Apocalypse"; John Owen, The Death of Death in the Death of Christ
  • Meredith Kline, Treaty of the Great King (Deuteronomy as covenant treaty)
  • The 1689 Second London Baptist Confession and the Westminster Confession of Faith
